title: eNTRy rule optimization of phenotypic hits for Klebsiella pneumoniae activity under in vivo relevant conditions
description: As part of the Gr-ADI consortium this proposal aims to address a critical gap in Gram-negative antibiotic discovery: poor intracellular accumulation of phenotypic hits. Following the eNTRy rules (1), we will upcycle phenotypic hits identified against an efflux-impaired Klebsiella pneumoniae strain to increase activity against wild-type strains, thereby expanding the pool of chemical starting points for further drug discovery efforts. Using an expanded AI/ML-optimized Entryway analysis1, hits will be scored and prioritized for synthesis based on predicted accumulation, with the objective to build-in intracellular accumulation through minimal computational filtering/medicinal chemistry rounds. Hit accumulation will be inferred by improved activity against wild-type K. pneumoniae relative to the efflux impaired strain, through a multiplex assay that will be developed to assess activity against both strains simultaneously. This assay will also be used for de novo screening of additional compound libraries under in vivo relevant conditions, accelerating identification and prioritization of promising novel hits potentially acting through inhibition of in vivo essential targets. The major outcomes of this project are novel hits against wild-type K. pneumoniae for further progression and validated methodologies for improving intracellular accumulation of hits. These methodologies could also boost antibiotic discovery efforts against other Gram-negative WHO priority pathogens.

title: Youth Mental Health Hub at SXSW London 2026
description: The Child Mind Institute, in partnership with Wellcome Trust, proposes to deliver the inaugural Youth Mental Health Hub at SXSW London 2026: a curated platform for spotlighting practical, evidence-informed approaches to youth mental health. Embedded within a major international forum spanning technology, media, culture, and public conversation, the Hub will bring greater visibility and coherence to youth mental health programming across the week. Through 4-7 linked sessions and related engagement activities, the Hub will convene contributors from clinical care, science, technology, sport, media, and lived experience to examine approaches that can strengthen prevention, early support, family and community resilience, and public understanding. Working topics include family resilience, sport- and community- based pathways to support, responsible uses of AI, mental health in the media, and youth mental health in contexts of conflict and recovery. The project will produce a distinctive youth mental health presence at SXSW London, foster exchange among UK, U.S., and international partners, and generate a post-event summary to support further dissemination and collaboration.

title: Africa Fungal Disease Summit
description: The Africa Fungal Disease Summit 2026, co-hosted by GAFFI and Africa CDC, will take place from 2–4 March 2026 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. It responds to the growing but neglected burden of fungal diseases in Africa, which significantly contribute to mortality—particularly among people living with HIV, cancer, TB, and other chronic conditions. Limited access to diagnostics, treatment, and surveillance systems, alongside rising antifungal resistance, has created an urgent need for coordinated action. The summit aims to catalyse a continent- wide response by bringing together policymakers, researchers, clinicians, donors, and civil society to advance locally led solutions. It will align with global and regional frameworks, including the WHO Fungal Priority Pathogens List, Africa CDC strategies, and AU health agendas. Key objectives include increasing awareness, sharing best practices, strengthening partnerships, prioritising research, and developing actionable country-level roadmaps. The programme will focus on seven thematic areas, including diagnostics and treatment access, research and development, policy integration, financing, and regional planning. Expected outcomes include improved coordination across stakeholders, strengthened health systems, and clear implementation pathways to reduce morbidity and mortality. The summit represents a milestone in positioning fungal diseases as a major public health priority in Africa.

title: Building an integrated platform for facility, community, patient and research information systems through a health information exchange
description: Disease management in resource-constrained settings is often siloed in facility, community, patient and research interventions. The evolution of a health information exchange (HIE) in the Western Cape, South Africa, together with the launch of a health and demographic surveillance system, C-SHARP, where community-based research and complex interventions can be supported, has created a platform through each of these levels can now integrate data. This proposal aims to test the feasibility and utility this approach, using non- communicable diseases (diabetes and hypertension) as an example, but with the long-term goal of developing a disease-agnostic research platform, which tracks patients through all levels of care, including at home, and enables novel research questions to be addressed. We plan to enhance the open-source community and patient software platforms supporting ambulatory community-based clinical data collection, with full data integration to the population-wide HIE. Then we will document the experience of patients, community health workers and facility clinicians working with the newly integrated platforms, assess measures of uptake, completeness, timeliness, access, new diagnoses ascertainment and where possible clinical outcomes. We will also quantify the additive routine contribution of the service platform to research-collected longitudinal population data.
recipient: The Health Foundation of South Africa

title: Convergent transcriptional consequences of recurrent somatic variants in MASLD
description: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects a third of the world’s population, is rising in incidence, and can progress to chronic liver disease and liver cancer. While the contribution of environmental and inherited germline drivers of hepatic steatosis are well- established, recent whole-genome sequencing studies have shown the widespread acquisition of clonal expansions in livers of patients with MASLD. These clones are driven by somatic variants in key genes governing lipid and carbohydrate metabolism; the converging acquisition of recurrent variants suggest they confer selective advantage to hepatocytes in the lipotoxic microenvironment of MASLD. However, the mechanistic basis of this advantage is not well-understood, and it is unclear if individual variants exert their effect through a shared or divergent transcriptional response. Perturb-seq is a novel functional genomics tool that offers a powerful tool to systematically map genotype/phenotype correlations across a wide range of settings. Using this approach in mosaic in vivo and in vitro models, we will study the biological processes downstream of recurrent MASLD-assosciated somatic variants. As a secondary aim, we will probe the synergistic interaction of somatic mosaicism with known germline variants and microenvironmental stress to identify common regulatory pathways.

title: An Artificial Intelligence-Driven Antifungal Drug Target Discovery Platform
description: Fungal antimicrobial resistance is a growing global health threat, particularly from critical priority pathogens such as Aspergillus fumigatus and Candida auris. There is a clear unmet need for novel antifungal agents with new mechanisms, low toxicity, and high resistance barriers. We propose an integrated, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven antifungal drug discovery platform to systematically identify and validate novel drug targets. Our approach harnesses cutting-edge technologies, CRISPR-based oligo recombineering, cysteine-reactivity profiling, and AI-guided prediction of gene essentiality, toxicity, and resistance emergence, to accelerate the discovery of durable antifungal agents. This platform will focus on C. auris, building genome-wide libraries and targetable chemogenomic maps. Structure- guided lead discovery will be supported by state-of-the-art AI pipelines and compound libraries. Predictive models for toxicity and resistance will ensure prioritization of safe and durable drug targets. Pangenome approaches will explore the evolutionary constraints of target sites; bolstering binding efficacy and target specificity, whilst enabling detection of emerging resistance. Expected outcomes include the identification of novel, non-human homologous targets; public release of chemogenomic and resistance prediction datasets; and an advanced AI-enabled pipeline adaptable to emerging and future antifungal threats. This project will transform antifungal discovery, future- proof therapies against resistance, and deliver early target enablement.

title: Mapping host responses in the nasal mucosa during respiratory viral infections to identify cellular determinants of severe disease
description: Respiratory viruses impose a significant burden on healthcare systems worldwide, with the greatest impact on children in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). While previous studies, primarily in high-income settings, have characterized virally-induced mucosal cell states, their relevance in LMIC populations, where genetic diversity, environmental exposures, and nutritional factors differ, remains unknown. We aim to uncover the full spectrum of respiratory virus-induced epithelial and immune cell states in the nasal mucosa of children in Bangladesh. Our primary focus will be studying the response to Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in children under the age of two years at two sites (one community, one clinical) in Bangladesh, representing diverse demographic and environmental contexts. Using single-cell transcriptomics, cell culture models including air-liquid interface, and flow cytometry assays, we will define pathogenic cell states linked to severe disease by RSV, gradually expanding to other viruses, and investigate viral and host factors driving these states. We will also assess demographic and socioeconomic risk factors underlying severe respiratory disease in children in LMICs. This work will be a collaboration between research groups in Bangladesh and the USA and will generate critical insights into respiratory viral pathogenesis and foster capacity for cutting-edge cellular and molecular research in Bangladesh.

title: Piloting Federated Learning to Re-design Health Data Systems in Africa
description: African health systems generate rich data through HDSS longitudinal cohorts, and real-world data from electronic health records in hospitals, yet this potential remains untapped. Data remains fragmented across institutions and borders, regulatory frameworks differ, and centralised pooling increases violation of national data protection laws and institutional trust. This project pilots federated learning across four sites in Cameroon, Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, and Burkina Faso using DataSHIELD, which sends analytical code to the data rather than moving data itself. Each institution retains control of its data within national jurisdiction, contributing only non-disclosive summary outputs. Building on the existing continental data initiatives that are creating localized solutions such as a TRE-in-a-box by the APCC, or centralized data pooling by INSPIRE Network, and training in DataSHIELD by the DSWB team, this advances to live, governed, multi-country federated analysis with use cases from 2 HDSS sites and 2 hospitals a first in any African health context. We aim to conduct analyses on population health indicators and non- communicable diseases, evaluate technical and operational feasibility, governance performance, produce open-access protocols, training materials, templates to support broader adoption of privacy-preserving analytics across Africa. Findings : Inform the future of health data systems in Africa and allow cross-border evidence generation.
recipient: African Population and Health Research Centre

title: Prevention of Household Tuberculosis with Optimal Nutrition (PHOTON)
description: The Prevention of Household Tuberculosis with Optimal Nutrition (PHOTON) study investigates whether targeted nutritional supplementation can reduce tuberculosis (TB) transmission among household contacts (HHCs) of TB index cases in Indonesia and Tanzania, two high-burden settings where undernutrition is a major modifiable driver of TB risk. Emerging evidence suggests B vitamins, particularly B3 (niacin), enhance nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent immune pathways critical for Mycobacterium tuberculosis control, while multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) and balanced energy-protein (BEP) food product address broader nutrient deficiencies in TB- endemic populations. PHOTON is a multi-site, cluster-randomized controlled trial evaluating the efficacy of six months of daily high-dose B vitamins (HB), MMS, and BEP in reducing the incidence of bacteriologically confirmed symptomatic TB (BCsTB) among HHCs. Four intervention arms (placebo, HB, HB+MMS, and HB+MMS+BEP) will allow component-specific and combined efficacy assessment. Secondary objectives include evaluating effects on NAD/NADP status, vitamin and protein biomarkers, clinical TB, morbidity, mortality, and adherence. Exploratory objectives include assessing the cost-effectiveness of nutritional TB prevention strategies and establishing harmonized biorepositories. PHOTON will generate robust evidence on whether nutritional intervention can reduce TB incidence, informing scalable, low-cost interventions for high-burden communities. Keywords: tuberculosis, household contacts, nutrition, B-vitamins, niacin, NAD+, micronutrients, balanced energy-protein, prevention, randomized controlled trial.

title: PREVENTION OF HOUSEHOLD TUBERCULOSIS WITH OPTIMAL NUTRITION (PHOTON)
description: Prevention of tuberculosis by nutritional supplementation is a promising approach to reduce TB incidence but is not widely tested. The primary objective of the PHOTON trial is to evaluate whether a six-month regimen of daily High vitamin B (HB), alone or combined with Multiple micronutrients (MMS) and Balanced Energy and Protein (BEP), reduces the incidence of bacteriologically confirmed symptomatic TB among household contacts (HHCs) of TB patients over two years. The PHOTON is a cluster-randomized controlled trial which will be conducted in Indonesia and Tanzania in the span of 5 years. Household will be the unit of randomization. The trial includes four arms: (1) placebo; (2) HB; (3) HB + MMS) and (4) HB + MMS + BEP. Non-pregnant TB-free household contacts aged 5–65 years who reside in study area will be eligible for enrolment. Based on a projected 2-year TB incidence of 1.7% and 1.8%, the study targets 42,000 and 36,143 HHCs to detect a 30–40% reduction in TB incidence in Indonesia and Tanzania. The primary endpoint is the incidence of microbiologically confirmed TB among HHCs within 24 months. Secondary outcomes include clinical TB, adherence, safety, and cost-effectiveness. Nutritional and immunity biomarkers will be explored as mediators of TB risk.
recipient: National Institute for Medical Research, Tanzania

title: Beyond inclusion: enabling equitable genomic discovery in Caribbean populations across the UK and the Caribbean
description: Caribbean populations remain the most underrepresented people in global genomic datasets. While initiatives have increased inclusion of broad 'African ancestry' groups, the routine collapsing of Caribbean populations into these aggregated African categories, obscures their distinct demographic history, admixture architecture and allele frequency distributions. This is not just an equity gap; it is a significant discovery constraint. For example, in cardiometabolic disease, where Caribbean populations in the UK and Caribbean experience a disproportionate burden, the absence of Caribbean ancestry- relevant genomic data limits variant interpretation, fine-mapping resolution and polygenic score validity. This proposed programme reframes Caribbean underrepresentation as a methodological problem and proposes that equitable; community co-produced research is a scientific requirement for genomic discovery. Over 24 months, four integrated aims will deliver: 1.)a Transatlantic Intergenerational UK-Caribbean Panel to govern ancestry operationalisation and embed community perspectives within analytical decisions; 2.)the first systematic audit of Caribbean representation across cardiometabolic genomic resources; 3.)proof-of-principle genomic analyses in 14,000 individuals across established cohorts; and 4.)a transdisciplinary governance and interpretation framework for responsible genomic research in postcolonial contexts. Together, these outputs will help establish the analytic, governance and infrastructural foundations for a future large-scale Caribbean genomic discovery consortium, generating evidence about how ancestry-specific inclusion reshapes genomic science.
programme: Genomics in Context Awards: collaborative research at intersection of genomics

title: Generative classifiers and causal image labelling for safer, better medical AI
description: Machine learning classification models are prone to learning bystander features and developing bias 1. This harms their performance in new ‘out of domain’ datasets and can lead to problems such as racial bias 2,3. There have been attempts to address these issues by modifying the data they are trained on, or through using specific learning strategies. I propose to solve these problems by implementing and evaluating generative classifiers – models which are trained to learn all features in an input image, rather than only the simplest discriminative features. This concept is now feasible due to advances in generative models. I will further refine this approach using causal generative models, which are constrained by a defined understanding of the data generating process. In addition, I will invert the approach of image labelling for machine learning tasks, where the image determines the label via expert labelling. This is the opposite of the true data generating process, where the disease/label causes imaging features to develop. I will give computer vision models the opportunity to learn features associated with early disease, which are difficult to spot or not currently appreciated.

title: Trust Talks!: Constructive Conversations about health and creative adaptation to climate change
description: Trust Talks! offers an innovative approach to facilitate constructive conversations in low-income communities in Northwest England through meaningful collaboration with community organisations. The project responds to the Wellcome Trust priority areas of climate and health by focusing on the theme of “Health, well-being and creative adaptation to climate change”. The underpinning principles behind Trust Talks! are collaboration community organisation through the provision of decision-making power and financial resources to those with the greatest proximity to communities and low trust in institutions, to co-design constructive conversations. Previous research has revealed dominant narratives about a lack of agency in climate change and adaptation. The use of psychosocial tools offers an innovative way to facilitate new, exploratory ways of thinking, challenging taken-for-granted assumptions about the roles of science, research, and climate change and create space for envisioning an optimistic future. The Climate Psychology Alliance (CPA) will use innovative methods to facilaite conversations between communities and researchers, enabling people to not only explore fears and uncertainties about the ecological crisis, but also to aspirations and hopes. It will explore the sense of possibility and science for envisioning optimistic futures, exploring solutions, adaptations, and mitigation that are perceived as feasible within people’s daily lives.

title: 2026 Global Innovation Conference for Research, Policy, and Practice
description: The Impact Funders Forum will host the 2026 Global Innovation Conference for Research, Policy, and Practice on November 17-19, 2026, in Singapore. The conference will be co-hosted with local partner, the Centre for Evidence and Implementation. Building on two previous conferences, the convening will bring together an international community of experts studying and innovating in evidence-informed policy and practice. The conference will reflect priorities of the Impact Funders Forum and Wellcome, including building on efforts to advance knowledge and action on research impact, enhancing infrastructure and technology for improved evidence generation, synthesis, and delivery, and bringing together expertise from across science, innovation, and society to design equitable solutions that improve outcomes. Likely conference focal areas include: • Scholarship about what makes research more useful, used, trusted, and impactful • Research impact assessment frameworks • Innovative models for evidence-informed policymaking, including through evidence synthesis • Practical guidance and training on the responsible use of emerging technologies, especially artificial intelligence • Changes in the global research ecosystem, including in funding, talent pipeline, public trust in science, and more. The convening will provide dedicated space for this cross- disciplinary and cross-issue community to work together to strengthen the connections between research, policy, and practice around the world.

title: The Parliamentarians’ Guide to Health, Climate and Nature
description: The Parliamentarians’ Guide to Health, Climate and Nature is a flagship initiative to strengthen UK legislative action on the climate, nature and health crises. Although the right to health is recognised in the Paris Agreement, policy has been slow to integrate health with climate and nature. The Guide will translate the latest science for a parliamentary audience and bring to life the real-world impacts and policy opportunities of tackling health, climate and nature together. The project will convene leading academic authors to produce concise, authoritative chapters, to equip decision-makers with key data, evidence and analysis. Peers for the Planet will lead content briefing, author liaison and parliamentary engagement, drawing on the expertise of our Chair, Professor Baroness Kathy Willis, and Vice-Chair, Baroness Rosie Boycott, to ensure relevance and cross-party resonance. The Guide will be launched at a parliamentary reception in November 2026 and disseminated widely in print and digital formats to MPs, active Peers and wider policy networks. Expected impacts include increased parliamentary knowledge of the latest science, helping to counter misinformation, stronger ties between legislators and the scientific community, and durable evidence assets to support scrutiny of legislation.

title: Transfer and exploitation of Mosnodenvir and related assets
description: Dengue fever is the most widespread mosquito-borne viral disease globally, with ~4 billion people at risk of dengue virus infection each year. It heavily impacts (sub)tropical regions and increasingly threatens previously low-risk areas, including the US and Europe. Mosnodenvir is a first-in-class small molecule antiviral drug that inhibits the dengue virus NS3–NS4B interaction, preventing viral replication and achieving pico- to nanomolar in-vitro potency across all four serotypes. This antiviral was discovered by KU Leuven (with the support of the Wellcome Trust) together with Johnson & Johnson (JnJ). It has advanced through Phase 1 studies, with no key safety signals reported, and prophylactic antiviral efficacy has been shown in Phase 2 human challenge studies and an early halted Phase 2 community-based field study showing favorable PK/PD. Mosnodenvir has received U.S. orphan drug status for treatment and fast-track designation for prophylaxis and is protected with a large established patent portfolio. After JnJ’s August 2025 decision to terminate the license, as part of a broader strategic shift away from infectious diseases, this project aims to secure the continued clinical development of Mosnodenvir through transfer of data, materials, and know-how from JnJ to KULeuven, maintain IP, and find partners to continue clinical development.

title: Building an Integrated FAIR-Compliant Data Catalogue and Decision-Support Platform to Maximise Research and Public Health Impact
description: Despite generating large volumes of valuable research data, many research institutions in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) struggle to make these datasets discoverable, interoperable, and usable for policy and public health decision-making. Data generated through surveillance systems, clinical trials, laboratory platforms, and implementation research are often fragmented, inconsistently described, and poorly connected to routine health information systems, limiting their scientific and policy value. A key reason for this gap is the lack of institutional infrastructure needed to organise, discover, and integrate research data. Many institutions lack structured metadata standards, data catalogues, and interoperable systems that enable datasets to be easily identified, accessed, and securely linked. As a result, FAIR data principles remain difficult to implement in practice. This project will establish a foundational institutional data ecosystem at the KEMRI–Wellcome Trust Research Programme (KWTRP). It will develop a standards- based data catalogue, implement a data warehouse linking research, surveillance, and contextual datasets such as climate and geospatial data, and create decision-support dashboards translating integrated data into practical insights for researchers and health system stakeholders. The project will also generate practical lessons and reusable frameworks to support responsible data discovery, integration, and use across research institutions and health systems.

title: Support to Strengthen the CSIS Bipartisan Alliance for Global Health Security
description: We have identified two critical areas where additional support from the Wellcome Trust would permit us to start important new work, fill gaps, and extend and strengthen the Alliance. • A new opinion survey initiative focused on MAGA voters in red states. • A working group to address the urgent new crisis surrounding the biomedical research enterprise. Each area holds the promise of generating new ideas for action that may be advanced on a bipartisan basis in late 2026 and early 2027, on the assumption that the next electoral cycle is likely to bring positive changes in the configuration of power in Washington, D.C. In each area, we are seeking to navigate the current realities of the Trump administration and a deeply divided country with special care and caution: we are determined to keep open our engagement with serious individuals advancing defensible policies and initiatives, while ensuring we are not enabling or appearing to endorse behavior or initiatives that are inherently authoritarian. In both areas, the approach is intended to bring broad benefits that speak to the crisis in science and global health, and that speak to a broad spectrum of infectious diseases.
recipient: Center for Strategic and International Studies

title: Comparing Deliberative and Arts-based Approaches for Constructive Conversations on Genomics for Population Health
description: This pilot explores how different public engagement approaches can support constructive, ethical conversations about the use of genomics in population health. While genomics is expected to inform up to half of NHS healthcare decisions by 2035, public understanding remains uneven, particularly among marginalised communities and groups with lower trust in science. There is a need for methods that go beyond information provision to build trust, surface emotions, and support mutual learning between the public and researchers. The project will evaluate four engagement formats deployed in North East London in partnership with North Thames Genomic Medicine Service: two deliberative approaches (a full Citizens’ Jury/Panel and a streamlined innovative ‘Citizen Circles’ model) and two arts‑based approaches (Legislative Theatre and an innovative large‑scale Town Hall event). All will address themes around equity, data governance, trust, and future genomic applications. The methods vary in depth, scale and cost, enabling comparison of their ability to build trust, curiosity, mutual understanding and consensus. The project will assess outcomes and feasibility through mixed‑methods evaluation, including surveys and qualitative analysis. The findings will generate practical insights into the merits of different engagement models and their potential for wider adoption in genomics and other sensitive areas of science.

title: Innovative Financing to Support Infectious Disease Research & Development (R&D;): Mapping Models and the Ecosystem for South (SA) and Southeast Asia (SEA) - Phase II
description: In Phase 1, AVPN produced a comprehensive whitepaper mapping the innovative financing landscape for infectious disease (ID) R&D in South and Southeast Asia, with a focus on late-stage R&D and commercialization. Through desk research, expert committee consultations, and stakeholder interviews, we identified priority disease areas, financing gaps, and opportunities for sustainable capital mobilisation. The resulting whitepaper provides regionally grounded recommendations to strengthen infectious disease financing ecosystems. Phase 2 aims to translate these insights into actionable ecosystem engagement over 12 months. Using a structured Connect–Learn–Act–Lead approach, AVPN will drive systematic dissemination, strategic convenings, and cross- sector dialogue to advance pipeline visibility, early access pathways, and collaborative financing models. Engagements will be sequenced to move stakeholders from knowledge-sharing to validated priorities, partnership- building, and clear next steps for capital deployment. Key outputs will include prioritised innovation areas, validated R&D pipelines, access and translation roadmaps, and decision frameworks to inform future collaboration and investment. By strengthening alignment among funders, researchers, policymakers, and implementers, the programme seeks to accelerate equitable scale-up of breakthrough innovations across South and Southeast Asia. Leveraging its network of 700 funders across 44 markets, AVPN will serve as a trusted ecosystem backbone to enable sustainable, multi-stakeholder coordination in ID financing.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure for Climate and Health (DPI4CH) to advance climate health resilience
description: The World Health (WHO)-World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Climate and Health Joint Programme (Joint Programme Office), with partners, will advance digital public infrastructure (DPI) for trustworthy, integrated and interoperable climate and health data and information systems by extending the Digital Public Infrastructure for Climate and Health (DPI4CH) project through a new 12 month grant April 1, 2026 through March 31 2027. This extension builds on the existing partnerships with Digital Square at PATH and WHO’s Department for Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI (WHO Digital & Data). To empower health systems to anticipate and respond to climate threats, this extension operationalizes the Wellcome-Joint Programme Office’s vision to build a science-policy-implementation ecosystem where interoperability and collaboration is the default. Moving beyond the initial landscape identification, the primary purpose of this phase is to establish the normative foundation and institutional capacity required to turn climate science into actionable health decisions. By evolving the 'Global Goods' concept into active market horizon scan and analysis, as well as 'ground- truthing' technical guidance through in-country readiness assessments and local adaptation, this investment ensures that digital climate-health solutions are not just available, but can be scalable, standardized, and integrated as a sustainable core of national health and climate infrastructure.

title: Constructive Conversations Pilot Project: Mental Health, Artificial Intelligence and Religious Communities
description: This project pioneers and evaluates a new way of fostering constructive conversations between researchers and religious communities, to have positive impact on researchers while benefitting the religious communities and giving them a voice. We will adapt the Participatory Futures Dialogue (PFD) approach to cover sensitive scientific topics, with three modules: scientific information, societal issues, and religious issues. Multiple religious issues modules can be produced to enable interaction with different religious communities. This pilot will look at AI and mental health, engaging with UK Jewish and Christian communities. This approach is scalable to other scientific topics, regions and religions in future. We will examine the implications of emerging AI technologies for mental health, with particular attention to ethical, clinical and psychosocial dimensions as understood within religious contexts. Religious communities play a significant role in mental health and wellbeing support, yet remain underexplored in current AI and mental health research. Through constructive conversations with AI researchers, this project will investigate how faith communities understand and engage with both generic AI tools and AI-mediated mental health tools in pursuit of wellbeing, asking how theology shapes responses to automation, care and vulnerability, and how these perspectives can inform responsible, culturally sensitive deployment of AI.
recipient: The Faraday Institute for Science and Religion

title: A Multi‑Omics Profiling of Infectious Drivers of Miscarriage and Stillbirth in a High‑Burden Ugandan Population (OPIDMIS-Uganda)
description: Globally, 1 in 10 babies is born preterm or lost through miscarriage or stillbirth, a statistic that has remained unchanged for two decades and continues to impede progress in maternal and newborn health. In Uganda, the introduction of Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) systems has contributed to reducing stillbirths from 24 to 17 per 1,000 live births, yet persistently low reporting rates limit their full impact. The Iganga–Mayuge Health and Demographic Surveillance Site offers a rare opportunity: with over 41,000 registered pregnancies, very high pregnancy loss rates, reporting rate(86%), enabling a more complete understanding of these outcomes. While the infectious causes remain poorly characterised, epidemiological patterns strongly suggest an important role of zoonotic pathogens. Therefore our multidisciplinary team seeks to co‑develop a multi‑level research programme with affected communities to a) leverage multi- omics to improve evidence used by MPDSR as clinical support system and b) map the social complexities that shape pregnancy outcomes “social autopsy” to inform the creation of a parallel community-level support system. Together, these arms will generate multi-level datasets to underpin machine‑learning analyses to identify drivers of miscarriage and stillbirth and inform actionable interventions.
programme: Genomics in Context Awards: collaborative research at intersection of genomics

title: Tuning EARS for the Future: Reframing Engagement in (Genomic) Science
description: This project reorients public engagement away from a narrow fixation on stakeholders’ views and attitudes by developing a novel EARS framework to track the social distance between diverse publics and emerging scientific options. It combines qualitative and quantitative approaches to capture four interrelated dimensions of social distance—epistemic (E), affective (A), resource (R), and structural (S)—through which communities make sense of, and accommodate, technological interventions within their lived realities. Building on the team’s expertise in life-science engagement and policy deliberation, and its networks across genomic research and patient/user communities, the 12-month pilot will conduct expert consultations, four focus groups with patient and LGBTQ+ communities, and online Reciprocal Dialogue Workshops. The empirical focus is on direct-to-consumer genetic testing and in vitro gametogenesis (IVG), chosen for their contrasting socio-technical profiles. The project develops and calibrates a set of original, modular engagement tools comprising two interlocking components: a generative qualitative tool (the B/BQ LEGO Serious Play method) and a diagnostic quantitative tool (the EARS Compass). Designed to work in tandem, these tools translate complex social distances into actionable, comparable insights and are adaptable across different scientific and policy domains, making social distance empirically visible and trackable.

title: Union World Conference on Lung Health
description: The International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (The Union) hosts the annual World Conference on Lung Health (WCLH). WCLH is the world’s largest gathering of those working together to end the suffering caused by lung disease with a focus specifically on the challenges faced by low-and lower-middle income populations. Cutting edge science is a core element of the WCLH. Since 2018 we have offered a dedicated tract, TBScience, in the programme devoted to basic, clinical and translational science on tuberculosis. This track brings together scientists from microbiology, immunology, molecular biology, pharmacology, epidemiology and mathematical modelling to present and discuss recent findings on TB transmission, infection and disease. In the future the TBScience stream will be fully integrated into the WCLH foundational programming and will highlight scientific advances under the “Discovery Track” along side our other main tracts which focus on operational research, implementation science and advocacy. This proposal has two key goals 1\. To support the continued organisation of cutting-edge science content within WCLH for a 3 year period (in 2026 via TBScience and from 2027 onwards via the Discovery Track) 2\. To support attendance of key delegates from low- and middle-income countries to attend WCLH with scholarship funding
recipient: International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (The Union)

title: The multi-modal architecture of pre-eclampsia in Sub-Saharan Africa: advancing biological understanding for enhanced risk stratification and precision care
description: Pre-eclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal mortality in Sub- Saharan Africa (SSA), yet its underlying pathophysiology remains poorly understood. Consequently, no targeted treatments exist. Limited antenatal care, delayed diagnosis, and inequitable healthcare access further worsen outcomes. While epidemiological and heritability studies suggest a strong genetic component, adequately powered genomic studies are lacking. Despite the disproportionate burden, research has largely excluded women of African ancestry. Understanding the genetic basis of pre-eclampsia could uncover novel mechanisms, improving prevention, treatment, and risk stratification. However, genomic discovery studies must be integrated with scalable, affordable interventions for meaningful short-term clinical impact. This study will leverage CRADLE-SMART, a community-driven programme integrating a mobile-app- based clinical decision tool with novel point-of-care (POC) diagnostics, including the CRADLE Vital Signs Alert (Rapid), biomarker-based risk stratification, and AI-powered ultrasound. Specifically, it will: (i) Develop the CRADLE-SMART bundle as a risk stratification tool in Sub-Saharan Africa. (ii) Evaluate the predictive performance of the novel CRADLE-SMART risk stratification tool in Zambia and Sierra Leone. (iii) Investigate the genomic determinants of pre-eclampsia among women of African ancestry. Combining genomic research with practical, field-deployable diagnostics, this study aims to enhance biological understanding, improve risk stratification, and reduce maternal and neonatal mortality in SSA.

title: Understanding Acquired Epidermodysplasia Verruciformis in Young People Living with HIV in Zimbabwe
description: Perinatally-acquired HIV results in early-life immune dysregulation. Historically this led to high mortality rates in childhood. Following the widespread availability of antiretroviral therapy (ART), increasing numbers of people with perinatally-acquired HIV survive into adulthood. Despite effective viral suppression with ART, immune system abnormalities persist, predisposing individuals to a range of comorbidities. One such condition is acquired epidermodysplasia verruciformis (aEV), a disorder characterised by disseminated cutaneous infection with beta human papillomaviruses (HPV). While beta-HPVs are ubiquitous and typically asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals, some people with HIV can develop extensive and persistent flat warts and pityriasis versicolor-like lesions (aEV). Where the association with HIV is recognised, aEV is highly stigmatising. The associated HPV types, particularly HPV 5 and 8, are potentially oncogenic and there are emerging cases of skin cancer in young people with aEV. There are currently no clear diagnostic criteria and the epidemiology, risk factors, virological drivers, and quality of life impact of aEV in this population remain poorly understood. People with aEV are offered minimal information or support to help them navigate their condition. This study seeks to address these gaps. The findings will inform future research directions, guide clinical management strategies, and support the development of targeted interventions.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Clinical evolution and pathogenesis of VEXAS syndrome - towards improved understanding of haematoinflammatory disorders
description: VEXAS (Vacuoles, E1 ubiquitin activating enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic) syndrome, is a late-onset inflammatory disease, presenting with overlapping systemic inflammation and bone marrow failure. VEXAS' causative somatic mutations in UBA1 are found in hematopoietic stem cells (HPSCs) and lead to inactivation of UBA1, which is the E1 ubiquitin activating enzyme responsible for >90% initiation of ubiquitination, an essential cellular regulatory process. VEXAS, which has prevalence of 1:4,000 men aged over 50, mimics myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and several age-associated inflammatory diseases such as polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), Sweet's Syndrome and Polyarteritis Nodosa. This suggests that abnormalities in the ubiquitination pathway caused by UBA1 and related somatic mutations in HPSCs, could be driving factors in these and other age-related bone marrow failure and overlapping inflammatory conditions. My proposed study aims to characterise the clinical landscape of VEXAS syndrome; establishing its key features and unmet therapeutic needs following its discovery 6 years ago. Furthermore, I plan to characterise the role of selected UBA1 mutations on effector cell function and ubiquitination, in hope of providing novel insights into disease pathogenesis, possible future therapeutic targets, and informing future studies into age related inflammation and bone marrow failure.

title: Integrated nutritional care to improve outcomes amongst hospitalised adults with advanced HIV disease (IN-care)
description: Advanced HIV disease (AHD, defined as CD4 20% (3), and 60% of PLWH admitted to hospital are malnourished (5). Energy requirements for PLWH compared to people without HIV are approximately 10% higher when asymptomatic, and 20-50% higher if symptomatic (6), despite this there are currently no guidelines on nutritional support for hospitalised adults with AHD. The aim of my fellowship is to describe nutritional status amongst hospitalised adults with AHD, investigate for associations with mortality, and to co-develop and pilot a feasible and acceptable nutritional intervention to improve outcomes. Objectives: 1\. To understand and describe the current evidence in nutritional interventions for PLWH by conducting a systematic review. 2\. To conduct a cohort study of 250 hospitalised adults with AHD to describe the burden of severe malnutrition and to investigate for associations with mortality. 3\. To co-develop a feasible and acceptable nutritional-supplementation intervention. 4\. To pilot and evaluate the co-developed intervention amongst 60 hospitalised adults with AHD.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: UBUNTU-GENE: Co-creating Discovery Research on Heredity, Disability and Care in Africa
description: This transdisciplinary project investigates the convergence of African epistemologies regarding heredity, kinship, personhood, and care with genomic sciences, with the objective of formulating novel conceptual frameworks and research methodologies for disability studies. While genomics research typically adds ethical considerations after research questions are defined, we centre this study on the Ubuntu philosophy and African knowledge systems from the outset to discover what emerges when different ways of knowing heredity and disability encounter each other. Through co-collaboration between ethicists, cultural anthropologists, bioethicists, clinicians, disability studies scholars, and communities with lived experience in Uganda and Rwanda, we will explore three conceptual territories: (1) how Ubuntu ethics, which prioritise relational personhood and collective responsibility, challenge Western relational genomic frameworks; (2) how African disability ontologies offer alternatives to the medical model of disability that dominates genomics research; and (3) how kinship-based care systems might integrate genomic knowledge without displacing existing support structures. This project will generate theoretical frameworks for Ubuntu-based genomic governance, innovative methodologies for equitable transdisciplinary research, and a sustainable, Africa-centered research platform. Outputs include conceptual papers, guidelines, community resources, and a co-created research agenda for future genomics and disability research in Africa.
programme: Genomics in Context Awards: collaborative research at intersection of genomics

title: Improving the Early Identification and Intervention of Disability-Related Feeding Difficulties amongst Young Children in Uganda
description: **Research Goal:** To develop and evaluate a contextually relevant Integrated Clinical Care Pathway (ICCP) for early identification and intervention of disability-related feeding difficulties amongst young children (<3 years) with developmental disabilities in Uganda.  **Background:** Feeding difficulties affect up to 80% of children with developmental disabilities, contributing significantly to malnutrition and poor health outcomes, yet remain under-addressed in low-resource settings. Despite disproportionately affecting children in LMICs, there is limited guidance on identification and management approaches within healthcare systems.  **Methods:** This PhD research employs a participatory approach guided by implementation science frameworks. The research will be conducted across two government health centres and one specialist rehabilitation facility in western Uganda, enabling assessment across different healthcare contexts.  **Objectives:** (1) Conduct a scoping review of existing evidence on identification and intervention approaches; (2) Examine facilitators and barriers to accessing high-quality nutritional care through cross-sectional and qualitative assessment; (3) Co-design an ICCP through structured stakeholder workshops; and (4) Evaluate the ICCP's feasibility, acceptability and preliminary impact when implemented in government healthcare facilities.  This research addresses critical evidence gaps whilst developing a model for disability-inclusive healthcare that could be adapted across sub-Saharan Africa, ultimately improving nutritional outcomes for a frequently overlooked vulnerable population.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Pan-African Travel Bursaries for the 6th H3D Symposium
description: The 6th H3D Symposium, organised by the H3D Foundation, will take place from 13–16 October 2026 at the Arabella Hotel, Golf & Spa in the Western Cape, South Africa. Building on the success of previous meetings, the symposium is expected to convene over 300 delegates from academia, industry, and product development partnerships, including global leaders from organisations such as MMV, TB Alliance, DNDi, LifeArc, Novartis, leading universities, and African research centres. The programme will feature strategic perspectives on infectious disease drug discovery, advances in chemical biology and synthetic chemistry, disease biology to guide discovery, and emerging platforms and technologies that accelerate R&D, alongside poster sessions, workshops, and networking opportunities. The Holistic Drug Discovery and Development (H3D) Centre at the University of Cape Town has a strong history of innovation focused on improving treatment outcomes for African patients, advancing drug discovery technologies and strengthening African scientific leadership. We seek support for 15 travel bursaries for postgraduate students and postdoctoral fellows from low- and middle-income countries. These bursaries will enable early-career researchers to present their work, build international networks, and engage with global experts, fostering collaboration and empowering the next generation of scientists to address diseases that disproportionately affect African populations.

title: Characterizing human B-cell immune checkpoints to advance immunotherapy
description: B cells represent an attractive therapeutic target in autoimmunity, transplantation or cancer. However, the current B-cell-directed therapies rely mainly on non-selective pan-B-cell depletion with variable efficacy in different tissues and associated side effects, including severe infections. My preliminary data demonstrate that immune checkpoint molecules (ICMs)-key regulators of immune responses-are differentially expressed across human B-cell subsets and tissues. These findings open the opportunity for exploring B-cell heterogeneity, plasticity and avenues for more selective targeting. Using matched human tissue samples, state-of-art immuno-phenotyping technologies (including single-cell multi-omics, multi-parameter spectral flow cytometry, cytokines and antibody profiling), 3D immune organoid cultures (organ-on-chip) and multi-checkpoint CRISPR screens (Perturb-seq) and blocking antibodies, I will: (1) map baseline ICMs expression patterns across B-cell subsets in vivo, examining influences of tissue microenvironment, sex, and age to generate an integrated Human B-cell ICM Atlas; (2) characterize ICM expression dynamics during ex-vivo B-cell differentiation, expansion, and lymphoid follicle formation; (3) elucidate functional roles of ICMs in these biological processes. This work will deliver new insights into human B-cell biology necessary for developing more precise therapeutics with reduced toxicity, including advancement of future adoptive B-cell therapies. Additionally, it will illuminate potential mechanisms underlying autoimmune- like complications from checkpoint inhibitor therapies and inflammaging.

title: Neural Sheets: Engineering Next-Generation Human Brain Models via Apicobasal Polarity-Guided Directional Neurogenesis
description: Form dictates function – a fundamental biological principle underlying the complexity of multicellular life. Nowhere is this more evident than in the human brain, whose tightly orchestrated architecture enables cognition, perception, and consciousness. However, many features of human brain development – including cortical layering, grey/white matter, and gyrification – are not captured by current in vitro 2D/3D models, drastically limiting our ability to study human-specific neurodevelopment, function and disease. In Neural Sheets, I aim to radically advance our understanding of human brain development and overcome critical limitations of current in vitro models. This work will unfold across four integrated aims: 1\. Mechanism: I will investigate how a group of apical-inducing lipids repositions (neuro)epithelial polarity. 2\. Platform: I will engineer a scalable neuroepithelial platform (“Neural Sheets”) that will sustain organized progenitor sheets and enable directional, extended neurogenesis. 3\. Support Modules: I will develop a tissue grid perfusion stamper and scalable perfusion system for long-term proliferation and maturation to enable cortical layering and grey/white matter organization. 4\. Cortical phenotyping: I will perform connectivity mapping, physiology and transcriptomics and benchmark against human developmental cortex references. Neural Sheets will make polarity and shape programmable, enabling a ground-breaking new class of reproducible human brain models for mechanistic studies.

title: Pathogen Urbanism: Genomics, Social Interactions, and High-rise Urban Forms in Global South Cities
description: Rapid vertical densification has become a dominant organising logic in African cities, whilst urban governance, public health systems, and planning frameworks have not evolved at the same rate as this densification. Consequently, the material, environmental, and infrastructural conditions that shape pathogen circulation and exposure in dense vertical, urban settings remain poorly understood and weakly integrated into planning policy and practice. This proposal responds by linking genomics, social science, built- environment expertise, and community knowledge to examine pathogen exposure in rapidly densifying high-rise settlements in Nairobi. The study will: a) examine how everyday practices, mobility patterns, and climate stress in planned and unplanned dense vertical urban settlements in Kenya shape exposure to infectious disease, b) examine how urban forms, specifically materials, spatial layouts, microclimates, and incremental building practices, shape pathogen circulation and c) pilot a transdisciplinary, participatory proof-of- concept framework for studying pathogen exposure and circulation in dense high-rise settlements. The project will generate and engage through integrated methodological toolkits, open sampling protocols, and metagenomic datasets linking lived exposure intelligence with environmental genomics. Through advisory engagement and global convenings, it will also develop a strategic research agenda and shape follow-on multi-city studies on pathogen circulation in dense urban settlements.
programme: Genomics in Context Awards: collaborative research at intersection of genomics

title: Lancet Commission on the Future of Health in ASEAN
description: This Lancet commission will bring together health leaders from the 11 member countries of ASEAN to collectively examine the current state of health in the region, the many forces that are shaping it, and the domestic and regional policy responses to both longstanding and newly emerging health challenges affecting the citizens of ASEAN. The Commission will also put forward a vision for the future of health and health policy in the region. The final report, which will be launched in 2027 during the 60th anniversary of ASEAN, will be used as an advocacy tool for influencing policy reform and innovation both at national, regional, and even global levels.

title: Cartographies of Difference: Unsettling Race in the South African 110K Genome Project
description: The South African Human Genome Project (SA110K HGP) aims to sequence 110,000 genomes. While genomics research necessarily relies on population stratification to ensure analytic validity and clinical translation, its use raises profound ethical questions. Scientific classification is deeply entangled with colonial and Apartheid regimes that used racial categorisation to justify dispossession and discrimination. As the SA110K HGP moves from pilot to national scale, decisions must be made about how population categories are defined, used and communicated. This project convenes a transdisciplinary collaboration to examine the responsible use of population descriptors in the SA110K HGP. Bringing together diverse scholars and community partners, the project will surface conceptual and ethical concerns, articulate a forward-looking transdisciplinary research agenda, and develop an expanded public history resource on racial classification published through a leading South African people’s history platform. The research is organised into three workstreams: (1) historical analysis expanding an existing infographic on racial classification into an interactive public resource; (2) a sustained genomics dialogue bringing together a national community of practice to interrogate conceptual, technical and ethical assumptions underlying population classification in genomics; (3) structured community dialogues at six SA110K pilot sites exploring how population categories are understood and contested in everyday contexts.
programme: Genomics in Context Awards: collaborative research at intersection of genomics
