description: No description available

title: Research Project: The Socioeconomic Background of UK Postgraduates
description: Martingale Foundation finds, funds, and supports people from low-socioeconomic backgrounds to pursue postgraduate degrees at leading universities across the UK. As postgraduate qualifications become increasingly vital for academic and career advancement, our mission is to ensure that talented students facing financial barriers can access and thrive in postgraduate study. In collaboration with Wellcome, Royal Society and Pousaz Philanthropy, Martingale will address a critical evidence gap in access to postgraduate study for students from low-socioeconomic backgrounds. While there is a wealth of evidence on access to undergraduate education, research on postgraduate progression remains limited, with fragmented datasets and a lack of robust evidence. Martingale will work with Public First, a policy and strategy consultancy, to analyse HESA data, examining how factors including socioeconomic background, undergraduate institution and parental education, impact progression to postgraduate study. The report will set out a clear picture of the current postgraduate landscape, and make practical, evidence- based recommendations for government and key sector bodies, including universities, OfS, and UKRI. By providing clear evidence of current progression rates into postgraduate study, this study will inform national policy and encourage stakeholders at all levels to address current inequalities and ensure that all students, regardless of background, can pursue research.

title: IPPR Centre for Geopolitics and International Policy
description: The Centre for Geopolitics and International Policy’s mission is to enable the UK government to successfully navigate a ‘world between orders’ to deliver progressive outcomes – both domestically and internationally. The Centre will work across four strands; Global South, UK growth, geopolitics and progressive internationalism. In some areas the connection to Wellcome's priorities is direct – for example we plan to examine what health and science-based partnerships between the UK and the countries of the global south could look like, to the benefit of all. In some areas the connection is present but less direct – looking for example at how to build a City of London which mobilises finance needed to build the societies of the future. This could include unlocking finance for social goods internationally, such as R&D or health investments. Alongside our research, we will arrange convenings to sharpen our thinking and to influence relevant decision makers both during and after the research, as we did during the first phase of the programme.

title: Emergency support for the Discovery Research Platforms in Infection, University of Cape Town
description: The Discovery Research Platforms for Infectious Disease (CIDRI‑A) faces a funding shortfall following significant reductions in US grant funding, placing some early‑ and mid‑career researchers (ECR/MCR) at risk. In summer 2025, initial discussions took place regarding support for the platform; however, these were paused pending the outcome of the WT/Gates/SA‑MRC emergency fund. Interim, core CIDRI‑A PI have used existing funds to bridge staffing gaps whilst pursuing alternative sources of funding, to attempt recovery of some losses. Over time this requirement has reduced substantially and currently stands at either $36,601 (approximately £27k / R620k) to cover salaries only, or $115,891 (approximately £87k / R2m) including essential consumables. The reduction reflects combined factors, including the reinstatement of some NIH grants, support successfully secured from the SA‑MRC emergency fund, and individual ECR/MCR obtaining fellowships to support new research. The current request is therefore to provide targeted, one‑off bridging support for an ECR directly associated with the Platforms. This would enable them to complete data analysis, finalise projects, publish high‑quality outputs, and submit applications for further funding. Without short‑term support, there is a significant risk that valuable, high‑quality research will remain incomplete and unpublished, with negative consequences for both ECR/MCR progression and the wider research community.

title: Convening for Cholera Elimination through Research on Epidemiology and Transmission in Africa (CholERA) Proposal Development
description: Cholera continues to cause recurrent outbreaks across Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, and DRC, driven by interconnected transmission across shared lakes, river systems, and informal border crossings. Climate extremes, population mobility, limited access to water, sanitation and hygiene, and entrenched structural inequities sustain vulnerability in persistent hotspots. Despite decades of control efforts, existing surveillance systems do not adequately explain why outbreaks recur in the same locations or how transmission spreads across national borders. CholERA is a multi-country, transdisciplinary research programme investigating the primary drivers of cholera transmission across interconnected hotspots in eastern and southern Africa. The programme integrates epidemiology, genomic surveillance, climate and hydrometeorological analysis, human mobility, behavioural science, and structural assessment to generate a systems-level understanding of transmission pathways and vulnerability. This application seeks support for a two-day in-person convening in Nairobi, Kenya to bring together CholERA investigators to finalise a competitive proposal for submission to Wellcome. The convening will align methodologies, strengthen cross-border collaboration, agree governance and equity principles, and define clear pathways to policy impact aligned with national cholera control plans and the Global Task Force on Cholera Control 2030 roadmap. Keywords Cholera elimination; climate and health; cross-border transmission; epidemic preparedness; genomic surveillance; human mobility; WASH; sub-Saharan Africa

title: Understanding the Role of Respiratory Nurse Specialists (RNSs in Chronic Respiratory Condition (CRC) Management in Primary Care.
description: This PhD research will employ an exploratory convergent mixed methods design to address the research question: What is optimised respiratory care in primary and community settings, and what is the configuration and scope of the respiratory nurse specialist (RNS) role in relation to this? Qualitative semi- structured interviews with adults living with chronic respiratory disease, their carers, and healthcare professionals will explore stakeholder conceptualisations of optimised respiratory care and perceptions of the RNS role. In parallel, a quantitative survey will map current respiratory service provision in primary and community settings, including models of care and the configuration and scope of RNS roles. Qualitative and quantitative findings will be integrated to identify areas of alignment and divergence between stakeholder expectations and existing services. These data will be synthesised to develop an empirically grounded model of optimised respiratory care, which will be refined through engagement with key stakeholders to support implementation and identify strategic priorities for service and workforce development. Keywords Chronic respiratory disease; primary care; community care; respiratory nurse specialist; mixed methods

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs), metabolic health, and inequality: mechanisms in contemporary UK youth and lifetime economic consequences using LifeSim
description: Background: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are common and can shape health across the life course. While links between ACEs and adult metabolic dysfunction(e.g.,obesity, diabetes, or metabolic syndrome) are well established, young adulthood is an under-studied “turning point” when early risks may accelerate into long-term metabolic diseases. My systematic review found consistent evidence that ACE exposure is associated with higher BMI and emerging metabolic risk in young adults, with pathways through psychological distress and risk health behaviours. Approach: I will use UK longitudinal cohort data (primarily the Millennium Cohort Study) to estimate how ACEs relate to early metabolic risk and key mechanisms across adolescence and young adulthood. I will then integrate these estimates into the LifeSim - a well- established microsimulation model used in health economics to estimate life- course outcomes and policy impacts, providing monetary estimates of these impacts. The projected model outputs will be tested against real world evidence, including midlife patterns observed in other UK cohort data (i.e., BCS70). Impact: This project will quantify how much lifetime metabolic burden is already “locked in” by early adult risk due to ACE, identify actionable pathways for prevention, and provide policy-relevant scenario evidence on where early support could reduce long-term costs and inequalities.

title: Care pathways for perinatal mental illness: a mixed-methods study examining health inequalities and identifying opportunities for early detection
description: The case for detection and treatment of mental illness during the perinatal period (pregnancy, and up to two years after childbirth) has garnered widespread support in the UK’s political discourse and health service strategy. A recent expansion of specialist perinatal mental health services aimed to improve access to high-quality treatment, but these investments are undermined by two key problems: firstly, many women with perinatal mental illness do not access professional support; and secondly, there are inequalities in treatment access. The objective of this research is to provide an evidence base that could be used to implement targeted interventions to ensure access to care for perinatal mental illness is equitable (i.e. based on clinical need). To do this, the research aims to understand current care pathways for perinatal mental illness, and their determinants and outcomes. A mixed-methods approach employs retrospective cohort studies using routinely collected healthcare records alongside qualitative interviews with people who have experienced perinatal mental illness. The objective is to inform which settings (e.g. primary care or community outreach) and groups (e.g. those with low rates of healthcare use and poor outcomes) should be the focus of targeted interventions to improve service equity and accessibility.

title: Principles of deep networks and their relevance for the neural circuit mechanisms underlying learning
description: How the brain learns remains much of a mystery. We are often surprised by our rapid learning on some tasks and inability on others, the diversity across individuals and the seemingly unpredictable course of learning trajectories. Remarkably, the advent of deep learning has revealed that artificial neural networks (ANNs) can flexibly learn complex tasks and share many similarities with the brain. As a growing community of theorists uncover the principles governing learning in ANNs, this presents a unique opportunity to investigate whether similar principles underlie learning in the brain. Here, I propose to experimentally test deep learning as a framework with which to model, measure and make predictions about neural learning mechanisms. To do so, I have developed behavioural tasks for rodents that probe key learning phenomena: long-term learning through stages, the transfer or forgetting of previous knowledge in continual learning and the learning of non-linear computations. I aim to apply large-scale recording techniques to measure the neuronal teaching signals and changes in activity throughout learning, and compare these to predictions from deep learning models. This work has the potential to transform our understanding of learning in the brain by constructing a formal framework to describe learning across neural circuits.

title: Understanding the role of the tumour suppressor Adenomatous Polyposis Coli in Paediatric Craniopharyngioma
description: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas are a type of brain tumour, arising from the progenitor stem cells of the pituitary gland, with an incidence of 1.7-2.1 cases per million per year. These lesions erode into the surround pituitary tissue resulting in debilitating and life threatening endocrinopathies as well as a profound impact on a child's well being through hypothalamic dysfunction (obesity, adipsia, sleep-wake cycle alteration) and progressive blindness. These lesions are driven by mutations in multiple components in the Wnt-B- catenin pathway, with my PI Dr Gaston-Massuet having carried out earlier instrumental work in understanding how these tumours progress overtime and the molecular biology using murine models. Next generation sequencing of human tumour samples has demonstrated several mutations beyond the original CTNNB1 finding, in particular APC mutations- adenomatous polyposis coli. The benefit of studying this cohort of mutations is that the B-Catenin produced would be degradable and may be responsive to medications which target B-catenin degradation- we would be keen to test two novel therapeutics in this regard. In summary the key steps are 1. Modelling tumour initiation and progression in murine models of APC mutations using LOX-CRE systems, 2. Genotype-phenotype correlation studies (300 samples) to guide clinicians on care and 3. Testing therapeutics.

title: Neuro-Skeletal Mechanisms for Osteoarthritis onset
description: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent cause of chronic pain and disability and currently lacks effective disease-modifying therapies. The most predominant symptom of OA is pain. Emerging evidence implicates altered sensory innervation of subchondral bone as a key contributor to OA pain. However, the mechanisms involved in sensory nerve growth within bone in OA remains vaguely understood. My PhD will address neuro-skeletal communication, specifically the predisposition to abnormal sensory innervation in the joints preceding cartilage degeneration, and identification of markers for patient stratification during early stages of OA. I aim to: (1)Define the temporal relationship between neuronal sprouting, and OA development using in vivo and in vitro analyses using genetically modified zebrafish and bone cell culture and advanced imaging; (2)Identify shared causal genetic variants and molecular pathways linking pain susceptibility to OA pathogenesis performing genome-wide colocalization analysis of pain and OA GWAS; (3)To detect pain-associated biomarkers predictive of OA through integrating UKBiobank proteomic and clinical data and using machine learning approaches. Together, my research aims to elucidate early neuro-skeletal mechanisms underlying OA onset, propose causal mechanisms leading to therapeutic targets for disease modification and pain management, and discover biomarkers to enable early diagnosis and patient stratification.

title: Sensory trauma and the school-to-prison pipeline: Changing health and education trajectories through participatory action research.
description: The school-to-prison pipeline refers to the link between negative school outcomes (e.g. school absence/exclusion) and involvement in the criminal justice system. Neurodivergent children experience school absence, exclusion and imprisonment at disproportionately higher rates–particularly when also racially minoritised or from low-income families. Most exclusions are for “disruptive behaviour”; this focus on risk rather than vulnerability means behaviour is met with exclusion/criminalisation rather than being recognised as an unmet mental health need. However, recent research suggests “challenging behaviour” in neurodivergent populations may be coping mechanisms or responses to sensory stress. Through participatory action research, this study will investigate the role of sensory stress in the school-to-prison pipeline. We will use a range of qualitative and quantitative methods (e.g. interviews, rating scales, heart-rate monitoring, and sound/light level meters) to explore sensory experiences in mainstream school, alternative provision and secure custody settings. We will test whether factors (e.g. classroom behaviour, school avoidance) linked to negative outcomes (e.g. school nonattendance, exclusion, custody) are underpinned by sensory stress and intersecting identity categories. We aim to inform school- and custody-based interventions that promote better mental health, educational and justice outcomes.

title: Evidence of AI in Health (EVAH) Initiative - J-PAL and APHRC
description: Under the Real World Evidence Platform (RWEP), J-PAL will design and deliver a competitive funding process for randomized evaluations in low- and lower- middle income countries that: 1) examines whether clinical AI tools improve real-world health outcomes; 2) tests innovations that increase effective AI tool adoption, use, and integration into health systems; and 3) advances methodological innovations to ensure evaluations keep pace with AI development. J-PAL will manage the portfolio for project success. J-PAL will develop a rigorous, policy-relevant evaluation pipeline by cultivating research partnerships through matchmaking and project development, two evaluation incubator workshops, and a regional scholars program. J-PAL will enable RWEP evidence use nationally and regionally through partnerships integrating evidence into partners’ initiatives, scaling support, and evidence synthesis and dissemination. Within Africa, the African Population and Health Research Center (APHRC) will be a close partner for advancing RWEP’s goals. We describe expected areas for collaboration below, and activities that APHRC will lead independently including i) developing an atlas of AI tools in Africa, ii) conducting regulatory scoping to document policies and frameworks on AI governance, adoption and evaluation, iii) additional evaluation capacity building for African researchers, and iv) evidence dissemination at institutional and continental levels.
recipient: African Population and Health Research Centre

title: Exploring inequalities in pathways to mental health care and the long-term outcomes of NHS Talking Therapies
description: People from minoritised ethnic groups experience multiple barriers in access to psychological therapies across primary and secondary care, have worse health outcomes, and are more likely to come in contact with mental health services via acute, crisis and involuntary routes. I plan to use novel data science methods (natural language processing and national data linkages) to study inequalities in pathways to mental health care for people from minoritised ethnic groups taking an intersectional approach. I will embed the perspectives of people with lived experience and wider stakeholders by establishing an overarching steering group and facilitating co-production workshops with individuals from Patient and Carer Race Equality groups and NHS Race and Health Observatory to explore bottlenecks in the care system, including disparities in the quality of assessments in those accessing NHS Talking Therapies (“NHSTT”, previously known as Improving Access to Psychological Therapies), the impact of service changes due to COVID-19, namely remote therapy delivery, and the effect of NHSTT treatment on subsequent mental health service use. Better co-produced understanding of inequalities at different stages in the pathway to mental health care will help identify where resources should be targeted for optimal outcomes and improve the effectiveness of the system.

title: Arbovirus Vector Genomic Surveillance Platform (ArVGen): Building a platform to enable the genomic surveillance of arbovirus vectors at scale to address a major global health challenge
description: The overarching goal of this proposal is to build a foundational arbovirus vector genomic data platform with an open, community driven, accessible, scalable and expandable resource of vector variation and associated detailed metadata. This resource will accelerate a technological step-change to enable the use of arbovirus vector genomic data for public health surveillance, including viral transmission, for the first time, and enable data-driven, pre- emptive, selection and targeting of precision public health interventions and outbreak prediction. The proposal has four key aims: Aim 1 - Bridge key technological and technical gaps that currently limit the generation of high- resolution and informative genomic data at scale for arbovirus vectors by establishing protocols for high throughput Aedes genomics. Aim 2 - Create a cloud data resource and cloud-native analytics platform to accelerate arbovirus vector surveillance and locally led data use. Aim 3 - Develop a gold standard methodology for detection of key arboviruses/within-strain variants in mosquitoes, and a module for hosting virus data alongside WGS variation data in the surveillance platform to enable disease transmission associations to be explored. Aim 4 - Generate a global baseline data resource for Aedes aegypti genomic surveillance, including ~5,000 novel WGS samples.

title: Psychosis and the Question of Belonging in Racialised Worlds
description: In white-majority societies, racial minorities are disproportionately affected by psychosis. Epidemiological research highlighted the role of adverse social conditions in these disparities. Yet the lived racial dimension of psychosis — how it unsettles identity and interpersonal relations — remains overlooked. This conceptual gap carries clinical consequences. Justified wariness towards white-majority institutions is often misinterpreted as paranoia. Clinicians report difficulty addressing racial issues in practice, leaving patients to navigate racial and mental health stigma with limited support. This project redresses this gap by focusing on belonging as a neglected but crucial aspect of racialisation, where identity and trust become vulnerable. Drawing on phenomenological psychiatry, migration studies, psychosocial research, and first-person and community perspectives, it develops a novel framework of racialised dwelling to articulate the experiential nature of belonging among racial minorities, and how this can become destabilising in psychosis. The project asks: (1) How is belonging sustained by racial minorities in white- majority contexts? (2) How can racialised dwelling account for lived racial identity and racialised distress? (3) How can racialised dwelling explain the experiential link between racialisation and psychosis? By answering these questions, the project clarifies an overlooked association between racism and psychosis and offers conceptual foundations for future clinical and qualitative research.

title: The forgotten groups in global Hepatitis B strategy
description: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) affects 254 million people worldwide, and 4.5 million women living with surface antigen-positive (HBsAg-positive) HBV infection give birth annually. Approximately 90% of infants born to these mothers do not become infected. These HBsAg-exposed uninfected(HBEU) infants are typically excluded from HBV research and policy, but preliminary data from a Zimbabwean cohort suggests HBEU infants have increased morbidity compared to unexposed children. Women with Occult HBV infection(OBI) are also neglected in global health policies. In OBI, conventional assays fail to detect HBsAg, but DNA is positive. Data suggest a 6-12% OBI prevalence in high HBV-endemic countries, but the prevalence and impact of OBI in most settings is unknown. Together, OBI and HBsAg-positive infection means HBV-infection may be as common as HIV but is much more overlooked. Sub-Saharan Africa is estimated to have the highest global OBI prevalence rate but constitutes

title: Fluorescent virus-like particles for investigating humoral responses to SARS- CoV-2 and other respiratory viruses.
description: SARS-CoV-2 Spike mediates viral entry by shifting between pre- and post-fusion conformations. Pre- and post-fusion Spike is present on the virus, but it remains unclear whether post-fusion Spike is an immune decoy or site of vulnerability. I will screen plasma responses and isolate mAbs against post- fusion Spike. I will examine these mAbs in neutralisation and effector function assays, and investigate the conformational landscape of infected cells with super-resolution microscopy. Waning plasma neutralising antibodies and emerging VOCs increase BTI risk. It is important to generate durable broadly cross-reactive MBC responses, which rapidly reactivate and produce antibodies upon re-exposure. Multiplex staining using molecular barcodes allows in-depth analysis of rare antigen specific B-cells. However, the number of Spike variants studied using this method is often limited. I will incorporate molecular barcodes into fVLPs and integrate them with a custom scRNA-seq platform. This will enable high-throughput analysis of Spike specific MBC breadth across donors with diverse exposure histories, alongside mAb isolation and functional characterisation. The platform will be expanded to investigate additional viral families beyond coronaviruses, forming the basis of a multi-virus deep repertoire analysis approach. Overall, this work will establish fVLPs as a novel approach to investigate humoral responses against viral fusion glycoproteins.

title: Estimation-Driven Adaptive Trials: A Framework for Balancing Design Efficiency with Reliable Estimation to Improve Clinical and Health Economic Decision- Making
description: Adaptive clinical trials are changing how we evaluate new treatments by allowing trial modifications based on accumulating data. Group sequential designs, for example, can stop a trial early if results suggest benefit or harm, improving efficiency and reducing patient exposure to ineffective treatments. However, these modifications affect the accuracy and uncertainty quantification of treatment effect estimates. Inflated or deflated estimates are then fed into benefit-risk assessment or cost-effectiveness models that often do not account for them, making treatments seem more (or less) beneficial than they actually are. As a result, healthcare systems may approve interventions that offer less value to patients than expected, or fail to adopt genuinely beneficial treatments. Current adaptive designs largely focus on controlling error rates, without explicitly incorporating estimation reliability as a design objective. Moreover, adaptive decisions and interim analyses are often incompletely reported, limiting transparency and making it difficult for downstream users to account for their impact on estimation. This project addresses both gaps, developing frequentist and Bayesian design strategies that balance estimation reliability with trial efficiency and promoting transparency and awareness of how adaptive features affect trial results. This work will ultimately improve the reliability and interpretability of evidence for clinical and policy decision-making.

title: Developing a programme theory for the implementation of pharmacogenomic panel testing into cancer treatment pathways
description: In this fellowship I will develop a programme theory for how a multi-gene inherited pharmacogenomic panel-test intervention could improve outcomes for people undergoing systemic anti-cancer treatment (SACT) for solid tumours. I will partner with stakeholders to design a pharmacogenomic testing pathway. I will use real world prescribing data and quantitative research methods to examine the potential value of pharmacogenomic panel testing to inform prescribing of SACT and medicines used in the management of toxicities. I will assess the feasibility of offering testing within SACT prescribing pathways, and of collecting patient-relevant outcome data and evaluating clinical and cost-effectiveness of the proposed pathway. I will consider whether there are patient characteristics associated with increased utility of testing. I will use qualitative methods to understand the views of patients and cancer care professionals towards introducing a pharmacogenomic panel-test within SACT prescribing pathways, whether for curative, life-extending or palliative intent, and which factors might contribute to successful implementation. Each work package will contribute to the development of the programme theory, which will articulate the key components of this complex intervention. The developed programme theory will support the ability to design a future definitive pharmacogenomic panel interventional study that will permit robust evaluation.

title: The intersectionality of sex and ethnicity on primary care management of symptoms of suspected colorectal cancer
description: Colorectal cancer (CRC), the second leading cause of all UK cancer-related deaths has worse outcomes when diagnostic delays are over two weeks. Ethnic minorities face delays of up to three weeks longer than white counterparts. Suboptimal referrals may contribute to females having longer referral times and worse survival than males. Urgent primary care referrals for diagnosis depend on symptoms or faecal immunochemical test(FIT) results. Identifying variations in management could inform interventions. Aim: To explore the inequalities associated with the sex-ethnicity intersectionality on primary care management and outcomes in people with suspected CRC. Methods: Work package(WP)1 (systematic review) will identify factors affecting timeliness of FIT and referrals in primary care patients with suspected CRC symptoms across sex and ethnicities. WP2 will analyse CPRD-Aurum, HES and ONS data to investigate sex and ethnic differences in tests, treatments and alternate diagnoses for suspected CRC symptoms. WP3 will investigate if sex and ethnicity are associated with (a)time to FIT (b)time to referral and (c)death. WP4, will collate WP1-3 findings through focus group discussions with stakeholders. Findings will inform a consensus panel to guide recommendations. Impact: This will provide critical evidence on CRC detection across sex and ethnicities, informing intervention development and influencing policy.

title: Research to progress scaled deployment of Wolbachia replacement methods for arbovirus control
description: This proposal outlines a project focusing on the development and field testing of cold adult transport of mosquitos as well as an automated Aerial Release Mechanism in Brazil that will be integrated with a selected Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle platform. The project will facilitate development and assessment of new WMP distribution and release technology aimed at enhancing scalability and efficiency of the World Mosquito Program’s Wolbachia replacement method. The project will leverage a broad collaboration with Wolbito do Brasil SA, with a view to scaling the Wolbachia replacement technology across Brazil, supporting the current national Ministry of Health rollout strategy. Distribution and release methods developed in the project will be suitable for other country projects, contributing to global scaled deployments of Wolbachia mosquitoes. The technology development will emphasise integration across the value chain, including distribution, cold chain transport, automated release engineering, and the sharing of production and field data analytics for optimisation and increased productivity.

title: Development of next-generation CAR-T cells for enhanced efficacy and reduced toxicity in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL)
description: Background: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) has dismal outcomes in relapsed/refractory disease. Whilst CAR-T therapy revolutionised B-ALL treatment, translating this to T-ALL is challenging. Targeting pan-T antigens causes fratricide during manufacture and life-threatening T-cell aplasia. Anti-CD7 CAR-T trials show 80-100% initial responses but frequent antigen- negative relapses, serving merely as bridge-to-transplant with ~20% mortality. I have focused on T-lymphoblast restricted antigens to overcome these challenges, demonstrating CD21 expression on ~50%of T-ALL but less than 10% normal T cells. However, these targets face limitations including heterogeneous expression and potential for antigen-negative relapse. Aims: I will develop next-generation CAR-T therapies through three approaches: discovering novel T-lymphoblast-restricted antigens via proteomics; engineering CAR-T cells co-targeting multiple antigens to maximise patient coverage and prevent escape; and exploring asparaginase combination, exploiting T-ALL's asparagine synthetase deficiency whilst sparing normal T-cells. Methods: Cell-surface capture proteomics on primary T-ALL samples will identify novel targets. Multi-antigen CAR-T cells will be developed using co-transduction approaches and tested against engineered lines and primary samples. Asparaginase combinations will be characterised in vitro and validated using xenograft models. Impact: This research will establish personalised CAR-T therapy pathways, transforming treatment from bridge-to- transplant into standalone curative therapy, potentially revolutionising outcomes for this neglected disease.

title: Africa-led Human Mucosal Immunology Platform to Advance Rational Development of TB Vaccines and Immunotherapies (writing retreat)
description: This is a writing retreat for proposal entitled Africa-led Human Mucosal Immunology Platform to Advance Rational Development of TB Vaccines and Immunotherapies. The overal aim of the program is to generate a comprehensive understanding of human airway mucosal immunity and the mediators influencing immune protection against Mtb, thereby informing the design and evaluation of TB vaccines in high-burden settings. We will draw on our unique cohorts established at each site (MLW, AHRI, UCT and SUN) and shared expertise in immune profiling of human airways to identify the mucosal responses required for TB immunity and establish assays to measure candidate CoP in accessible samples.

title: Profiling peripheral blood immunophenotypes to identify predictive biomarkers and associated immunobiology of response to advanced therapies in Crohn's disease
description: Inflammatory bowel disease is a relapsing-remitting condition of the gastrointestinal tract, characterised by aberrant intestinal mucosal immune responses. Treatment non-response is a key unmet need in Crohn’s disease (CD). Notably, patients with CD have significantly higher rates of surgery and lower patient-reported quality of life compared to those with ulcerative colitis. Despite expanding therapeutic choices, the chance of any given treatment inducing remission is less than 50% with no current means of selecting the right drug, for the right patient. This study aims to identify and functionally validate pre-treatment peripheral blood immunophenotypes associated with treatment (non)response in patients with moderate to severe CD. Blood samples will be collected prior to commencement of biologic or small molecule therapies. Derivative peripheral blood mononuclear cells and plasma will be used to undertake single cell RNA sequencing and proteomic analyses, respectively. These data will inform the design and development of a full- colour flow cytometry panel, to further interrogate disease immunobiology and putative biomarkers of treatment outcomes. This precision medicine research has the potential to improve patient outcomes by informing personalised selection of biologic or small molecule therapies most likely to benefit an individual with CD and by providing mechanistic insight into treatment resistance.

title: Eco-Evolutionary Approach to Isolate, Evolve, and Characterize Broad-Host- Range Bacteriophages to Inform Solutions for Antimicrobial Resistance
description: This project will develop an eco-evolutionary framework for discovering, evolving, and characterizing bacteriophages (phages) capable of infecting a wide range of clinically relevant bacteria bearing antibiotic resistance plasmids. By focusing on plasmid-dependent phages (PDPs), which target the conjugative plasmids responsible for disseminating antibiotic resistance genes, we seek to reduce the spread of multidrug resistance at its source. Starting from phage-rich environmental samples (wastewater, rivers), we will build an isolation pipeline that depletes somatic phages and enriches for PDPs by sequential exposure to diverse plasmid-bearing hosts. We will then systematically broaden host range using stepwise experimental evolution guided by evolutionary distance metrics derived from protein-structure prediction and protein language model embeddings of plasmid-encoded pilus proteins and phage receptor-binding proteins. Phage infectivity dynamics will be quantified using high-throughput assays, and deep sequencing will identify genetic changes underpinning expanded infectivity. Finally, long-term coevolution in continuous culture will test how broadened-host-range PDPs and multiple distinct bacterial species adapt reciprocally, and whether outcomes converge (e.g. predictable receptor-binding modifications) or diverge (host-specific trajectories). Ultimately, this work aims to deepen mechanistic insight into phage-bacteria coevolution and inform phage-based interventions that could limit the spread of antibiotic resistance. Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; plasmid-dependent phages; conjugative plasmids; experimental evolution

title: Liverpool City Region R&D; impact series
description: Aid Alliance proposes a Liverpool City Region R&D impact series, a programme of events connecting local MPs, the Metro Mayor and civic leaders with universities and employers driving health and life sciences research across the region. The aim is to show how R&D delivers visible local benefits: creating good jobs, attracting investment, and building civic pride in the region’s contribution to global progress. The series will be led by Lou Harbour, Aid Alliance’s North West Field Organiser, who combines hands-on experience in global health research with a deep understanding of the region’s political landscape. Her background at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine and service as the Labour Deputy Leader of Knowsley Council in Liverpool make her uniquely placed to convene partners across science, policy and civic life.

title: Quantifying the reassortment potential of influenza viruses for pandemic risk prediction
description: Influenza A virus (IAV) reassortment – the exchange of genes between segmented coinfecting viruses – is a major driver of viral evolution and pandemic emergence. However, we are currently unable to predict which IAV pairs will produce compatible reassortant genotypes or which genotypes pose the greatest risk of emergence. In this fellowship, I will dissect the biological and evolutionary barriers that govern viral reassortment, using biosafe single- cycle infectious IAVs (sciIAVs) and a novel application of single-cell sequencing for the identification of individual viral genotypes in mixed populations. I hypothesise that reassortment is shaped by complex interactions of evolutionary, functional, and mechanistic constraints whose influence varies across viral lineages. Defining these interactions will explain why some coinfecting IAVs readily generate reassortants while others do not. To investigate this, I will quantify reassortment across a phylogenetically diverse panel of human, avian, and swine sciIAVs, and characterise reassortant phenotypes to link genotype to function. I will use these data to develop machine-learning models that predict reassortment compatibility and the pandemic risk of specific strains. These models will be embedded within IAV risk-assessment platforms at UKHSA and APHA to enable real-time prioritisation of high-risk IAVs before novel reassortants arise, transforming pandemic preparedness from reactive to predictive.

title: Engineering Immune Clearance with Conditionally Lethal Chemical Tools to Fight Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria
description: Antibiotic resistance is a growing threat with a global impact which necessitates the discovery of novel antibiotics with alternative mechanisms of action. One of the developing methods of antibiotic research explores the discovery of conditionally lethal drugs that can only kill bacteria in the presence of a specific immune response. Many of these methods are host- directed therapies using a drug to target host proteins to modulate the immune response to kill resistant bacteria. However, there are limited bacteria- directed strategies where the drug targets bacteria to increase the effect of immune attack. An immune response that may be enhanced by the latter strategy is oxidative stress as the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) can damage bacterial DNA, proteins or lipids. Bacteria have various repair mechanisms that can effectively defend against oxidative stress. To address this question, a new antibiotic strategy will be explored to identify conditionally lethal tools that target resistant bacteria to increase clearance only in the presence of ROS. Identifying the targets of these compounds and their mechanism of action using medicinal chemistry and chemical biology techniques could further aid the development of novel antibiotics against the most resistant bacterial pathogens in the world.

title: Deciphering desmoplakin biology in rare inherited cardiocutaneous syndromes
description: Desmoplakin (DSP) is an essential desmosomal protein expressed as two major isoforms, DSP-I and DSP-II. Germline variants in DSP cause DSP cardiocutaneous disease, a rare and poorly understood disorder characterised by variable arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and palmoplantar keratoderma. The isoform- specific functions of DSP and the molecular mechanisms underlying disease development remain unclear, although emerging evidence suggests roles for altered cell signalling and immune or inflammatory pathways. This study aims to define the distinct biological functions of DSP-I and DSP-II and to identify the molecular mechanisms underpinning disease development. To achieve this, two novel mouse models will be used: Dsp I/II +/- mice, modelling the common human haploinsufficient genotype, and Dsp I -/- mice, enabling investigation of DSP-I–specific functions. Dsp I/II +/- mice will undergo exercise to test the hypothesis that mechanical stress triggers or exacerbates disease. Phosphoproteomics will identify dysregulated signalling pathways, while spatial transcriptomics will characterise regional gene expression changes in weight-bearing (stressed) versus non-weight-bearing areas of the paw. Epidermal ultrastructure will be assessed by electron microscopy. Key findings will be validated using a human palm-derived keratinocyte line and palmoplantar skin biopsies from patients and controls. This work will advance understanding of DSP biology, elucidate disease mechanisms, and identify potential therapeutic targets.

title: Individual Responsiveness to Exercise to Improve Health Outcomes in Women and Ethnically Minoritised Groups
description: This project will investigate individualised cardiometabolic responses to exercise, with a view to supporting personalised type 2 diabetes (T2D) prevention. Specifically recruiting women, including those from ethnically minoritised groups, to contribute to addressing the underrepresentation of diversity in research. While women are often described as relatively “protected” from cardiometabolic disease, this perspective may obscure important physiological differences and delay targeted intervention, especially given the disproportionate burden of gestational diabetes and subsequent T2D risk. Two stages of research are proposed. First, a systematic review considering women with overweight and/or obesity and the impact of exercise-only interventions on cardiometabolic risk markers. This will inform intervention and outcome selection for the second stage of the research and identify whether heterogeneity in response is present. Second, a replicated crossover study will examine intra-individual variability in response to a short-term exercise intervention in premenopausal women with overweight and obesity. The primary outcome will be continuous metabolic syndrome severity z-score, enabling detection of subtle changes in preclinical risk. Secondary outcomes include individual metabolic markers and cardiorespiratory fitness. This work aims to advance precision medicine by distinguishing true physiological variability in response to exercise from day-to-day biological variation and measurement error.

title: The role of type I interferons in human macrophage response to Listeria Monocytogenes Infection
description: Research in mice has indicated that type I interferon (IFN-I) has a deleterious role during Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) infection. Susceptibility to disease mediated by IFN-I has been demonstrated both in vivo and in vitro in mice, but this phenomenon has not yet been investigated in humans, therefore its clinical relevance is uncertain. I hypothesise IFN-I impairs the human host responses to Lm infection by inducing macrophage cell death and crosstalk with critical antibacterial cytokine signalling pathways. I have generated pilot data using human macrophages, derived from gene edited induced-pluripotent stem cells and from circulating human monocytes, suggesting that loss of IFN-I signalling confers resistance to Lm-induced cell death, supporting my hypothesis. This proposal builds on these pilot data to dissect potential molecular mechanisms underlying susceptibility to Lm infection in human macrophages. Completion of this project would provide novel insight into pathogenesis of Lm, with potential relevance to other intracellular bacteria and may identify targets for host-directed therapeutic development. These data might also support the concept that a host immune pathway, which has evolved to combat viruses, can be exploited by bacteria.

title: Integrated Climate, Food Systems, Nutrition and Health Research in LMICs: barriers, enablers and opportunities
description: Climate change and environmental degradation are shaping food systems, nutrition and health outcomes, especially in LMICs, while global food systems and diets are contributing to worsening planetary health. Despite growing recognition of these interconnections, research that empirically links these themes remains underdeveloped along many pathways and methodologically fragmented. We will produce an evidence-based needs assessment of the global research ecosystem at the climate–food systems–nutrition–health intersection, with a deliberate focus on LMIC researchers and institutions and their collaborators. We will identify and critically analyse the conceptual, data, capacity and structural barriers that currently limit generation of high- quality interdisciplinary research, alongside opportunities to catalyse research development. Using a mixed qualitative approach, we will (i) map data landscapes, availability and analytic capacities through desk review, and (ii) conduct expert consultation through semi-structured interviews with funders, reviewers and researchers, including applicants to climate–food–health research calls. The project will generate actionable recommendations to inform funders, policymakers and research leaders on how to align investments, strengthen enabling environments and promote interdisciplinary research. Outputs will include a peer-reviewed publication, validation exercise and stakeholder convenings to support a step-change in the generation of policy- relevant evidence linking climate change, food systems, nutrition and health.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: The spectrum of early Tuberculosis treatment responses: evaluating associations with post-treatment outcomes
description: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant global health concern with an estimated 1.25 million deaths and 10.8 million incident cases in 2023. Programmatic outcome definitions focus primarily on mortality and cure, rather than long-term wellbeing. Estimates of residual post-TB lung damage range from 18-80%, nutritional recovery post TB is slow and in many cases incomplete, and studies reviewing quality of life, report improvement on treatment but no complete resolution to pre-TB levels. This fellowship aims to improve the understanding of the spectrum of TB severity at presentation and how this relates to treatment response in individuals diagnosed with TB to identify prognostic factors associated with post-TB morbidity and develop a standardised method of TB severity scoring. This will be achieved through a 9-month observational longitudinal cohort study of a people with newly diagnosed TB in Zimbabwe, with close observation of respiratory status, immune activation, nutritional markers, disease burden, and mental health early in disease. Immune activation will be measured through measuring a panel of matrix metalloproteinase levels in plasma and sputum. Outcomes will focus on treatment failure, quality of life, nutritional deficiency and lung damage at 9 months. Key words: Tuberculosis, matrix metalloproteinases (MMP), post-TB morbidity, post-TB lung disease

title: AI for Scientific Discovery
description: I develop AI systems that discover mechanistic, closed-form laws from large biological datasets. Rather than fitting black-box deep networks, I use large language models to propose, test and refine compact equations whose parameters are interpretable and experimentally perturbable. In my rotation, I built an AI equation discovery agent and applied it to large-scale two-photon recordings from mouse primary visual cortex during finely sampled drifting- grating stimulation. The agent discovered a simple tuning law with a parameter controlling peak smoothness which had not been spotted by human scientists; fitting this law reconciled classical single-cell tuning models with the empirically observed high-dimensional geometry of population responses, suggesting that the model was capable of generalising to different scales. In my PhD I will generalise this framework into a reusable AI Science Agent for neuroscience and optical biology, linking discovered equations to analytically tractable circuit models and testing their causal predictions using optogenetic and genetic perturbations during optical recordings. Keywords: interpretable AI, equation discovery, population coding, visual cortex, two- photon imaging, optogenetics.

title: A Burundian Health Intelligence Platform (BHIP): Leveraging technologies to track and improve maternal and neonatal outcomes in a very low-income setting
description: I demonstrated in my DPhil that the Burundi’s health information system for maternal and newborn health (MNH) remains poor; records are missing or likely inaccurate. Plus, only women who contact health facilities are captured, leaving significant community-level events and outcomes unrecorded. To transform routine health surveillance in Burundi, one of the world’s poorest countries, I propose designing and testing how a Health Data Intelligence System (HDIS), focused on MNH, could be implemented leveraging on proven digital technologies to capture and integrate community health worker and facility data and on evolving large language models (LLM) that, for example, enable obstetric risk stratification and other forms of patient and provider decision support. Operationally, CHWs will record antenatal and postnatal information into a smartphone App (CHW MNH App), while facility personnel will access a web platform to add peri-partum information. These will stream into existing facility information systems; OpenClinic and DHIS2. A pilot implementation articulated in a ‘Programme Theory’ will generate learning for scalability and transferability while producing actionable MNH data useful for building and testing a ‘data to decision-making pipeline’. This research will foster local data governance, create and operationalise a data protection policy, and strengthen South-South and South-North partnerships

title: A pilot randomized controlled trial of Tirzepatide in people living with type-2 diabetes and stage B heart failure
description: The 2015 national diabetes audit identified heart failure (HF) as the most common and deadliest cardiovascular complication of T2DM. HF continues to have high morbidity and mortality, representing an urgent unmet clinical need. Consequently, early detection, prevention and treatment of HF in T2DM is a priority of the NHS and major international cardiology and diabetes societies. Those with T2DM are now classified as at risk or Stage A HF, and those with asymptomatic structural and/or functional cardiac alterations as Stage B HF (SBHF). We hypothesise that a 24-week treatment of Tirzepatide in those with SBHF will lead to significant weight loss and reverse remodelling of cardiac structural and functional changes. We anticipate clinically meaningful improvements in cardiac outcomes (LV mass and GLS), exploratory markers (NT- proBNP and hsCRP), functional capacity (Peak Vo2) and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L). Thus, building evidence for the use of Tirzepatide as part of an early preventive treatment for HF in those with T2DM. Additionally, we will assess whether a 6-month delay in treatment affects outcomes by initiating Tirzepatide in the control arm after 24 weeks. Finally, to support sustained weight loss for significant reverse remodelling, treatment in the intervention group will continue until week 52.

title: CREATE PhD Programme
description: Respiratory viruses can increase bacterial colonisation, density, and secretion from the upper respiratory tract (URT), yet these interactions remain poorly understood—particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Characterising these relationships is pivotal in formulating measures to mitigate secondary bacterial infections and bacterial transmission. To address these key knowledge gaps this study investigates the impact of respiratory viruses on the colonisation and transmission dynamics of Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes in Gambian households. Using an existing longitudinal household dataset (TransVir), which includes over 14,000 oral/nasal swabs collected weekly from 349 participants across 52 households, I will: 1.​ Determine the impact of respiratory viruses on URT carriage and density of S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, and S. pyogenes using qPCR-based bacterial quantification. 2.​ Assess how respiratory viral infections influence household transmission of these bacteria using hidden Markov models. 3.​ Characterise virus-induced changes in the URT microbiome through metagenomic sequencing, evaluating shifts in microbial composition and strain-level dynamics. My preliminary analyses indicate that respiratory viruses such as RSV and rhinovirus increase pneumococcal colonisation risk, but SARS-CoV-2 does not. These findings will enhance understanding of viral-bacterial interactions and aims to inform viral and bacterial vaccination strategies and viral pandemic responses in LMICs.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Midlands Mental Health and Neurosciences PhD
description: Eleanor (she/her) is a dramatherapist, conducting her Doctoral Fellowship at Warwick Medical School, supported through the MHNDTP. Eleanor’s project, PAINT, aims to understand what the intervention components and mechanisms of action of arts psychotherapies used in NHS adolescent services are, what the outcomes of these interventions are, and which measures are currently used for evaluation. PAINT will demonstrate how components, mechanisms, and outcomes can be linked in a logic model to enable systematic and consistent evaluations. The study uses mixed methods, including interviews, co-design workshops, and practice observations. Eleanor is passionate about PAINT, to increase understanding of arts psychotherapies interventions for stakeholders at all levels, to offer clearer expectations for interventions and to empower patients to make informed decisions about their treatment. Research into the arts psychotherapies aims to offer diversified and patient centred provisions, and decrease health inequities Stakeholders, including members of the public, patients and parents/carers, and clinicians, will be involved at all stages of PAINT. Key words: Mental Health; Youth Mental Health; CAMHS; NHS; Psychological Interventions; Arts Psychotherapies; Dramatherapy; Art Therapy; Music Therapy

title: Psychological difficulties in survivors of subarachnoid haemorrhage: Exploring the role of glymphatic disturbance using advanced MRI
description: Patients who suffer aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) often have residual cognitive and mood disorders. The mechanism of how the haemorrhage relates to theses outcomes is not clearly understood with patients often having normal structural imaging. Recently the glymphatic system has been discovered as system of peri-arterial spaces that connect to the subarachnoid space. It has been proposed that subarachnoid haemorrhage can disrupt the normal function of the glymphatic system with blood products causing direct blockage. I will attempt to use new MRI markers of glymphatic dysregulation such as DTI-ALPS (diffusion imaging) and BOLD-CSF coupling (fMRI) to investigate if psychological symptoms after SAH are related to glymphatic disturbance. Participants will be recruited through Nottingham regional neurovascular and neurointerventional service. At 3 months they will undergo addition research sequences to their clinical MRI follow up and questionaire evaluation. The questionnaires will be the MoCA, HADS, FSS, MFS and SAHOT to assess cognition, anxiety ,depression , fatigue and impact on their lives. The tests will be repeated at 9 months to assess longitudinal the effects where we would expect improvement due to glymphatic improvement following blood product breakdown.

title: Personality disorders in youth: descriptive epidemiology and patient experience within services
description: Personality disorders (PD) are common mental health conditions associated with functional impairment, self-harm, and high service use. Although PD symptoms typically emerge during adolescence, diagnosis and intervention frequently occur in early adulthood, following prolonged periods of unmet need. This project aims to improve understanding of how young people come to receive a PD diagnosis in early adulthood and how clinical, social, and service-related factors shape their trajectories and experiences. Using a mixed-methods approach, the project will address three research questions. First, it will characterise the sociodemographic, clinical, educational, occupational, and service-use profiles of young people diagnosed with PD in early adulthood. Second, it will examine which adolescent factors predict later PD diagnosis and distinguish these from predictors of other psychiatric diagnoses using comparative analyses. Third, it will explore the views and experiences of young people, carers, and professionals within healthcare services. The research will combine a systematic review with quantitative analyses of anonymised electronic health records and linked administrative data, alongside qualitative interviews and focus groups. By integrating epidemiological evidence with lived experience perspectives, this project will inform earlier identification and developmentally appropriate service pathways for young people at risk of PD.

title: Funding for Global Health Partnerships (formerly THET) to provide the secretariat to the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Global Health & Security.
description: GHP is seeking £10,000 from Wellcome to support its role as secretariat for the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Global Health and Security. This contribution will strengthen how UK parliament engages with global health, ensuring parliamentarians have consistent access to expert insight, including LMIC perspectives, on the most pressing global health challenges. The APPG provides a cross-party forum for policymakers to examine the UK’s role in global health and security. As secretariat, GHP convenes experts, produces accessible briefings and reports, and ensures diverse perspectives inform parliamentary debate. Wellcome’s support will enable at least four meetings each year on priority global health themes, establish an Advisory Group and produce high-quality briefing materials for parliamentarians. To improve external understanding of the UK’s role in global health, GHP will also strengthen communications through dedicated website and social media channels. This work directly supports the promotion of themes central to Wellcome’s global health strategy, ensuring they receive sustained cross-party attention in parliament. This includes the Future of Global Health Initiatives process, antimicrobial resistance, mental health, global health equity, pandemic preparedness and climate health threats. Through this partnership, Wellcome can help create a more informed and effective policy environment for advancing Global Health and Security.

title: Optical Biology PhD Application
description: Astrocytes are increasingly recognised as active regulators of neural circuit function – from modulation of the Node of Ranvier and synapses to influencing behavioural states. Astrocytes have also been shown to be molecularly diverse, but how this heterogeneity relates to local circuit function and behaviour is poorly understood. Are distinct populations of astrocytes in different brain regions uniquely specialised and wired to shape different aspects of sensory processing and adaptive behaviour? My PhD project will address this question using larval zebrafish - an excellent model that through optical and genetic accessibility permits brain-wide, non-invasive, in vivo interrogation of circuits in behaving animals. My project will first link astrocytic molecular diversity to functional activity whilst animals are engaged in acute and adaptive behavioural paradigms. Building on this, I will selectively manipulate discrete radial astrocyte populations to assess their causal contributions to behaviour and dissect the mechanisms through which they exert behaviourally relevant effects on specific circuits. This project will reveal the functional significance of astrocyte heterogeneity in the vertebrate brain in the context of sensory processing and behavioural adaptations, while establishing a foundation for future studies into how distinct populations may be differentially involved in pathology and regeneration.

title: Understanding the epithelial-stromal crosstalk driving imperfect healing in biliary fibrosis
description: Fibrosis is the common pathological outcome of many chronic inflammatory diseases and a major global cause of mortality, yet the early events that determine whether tissue injury resolves or progresses to irreversible scarring remain poorly understood in humans. A major barrier to defining these mechanisms, particularly in internal organs, is the difficulty of obtaining tissue samples across the temporal spectrum of healing. To address this, I have curated a unique collection of archived human bile duct specimens of regenerative and fibrotic healing at different time points. The aim of this project is to define the early cellular and molecular mechanisms that determine regenerative versus fibrotic healing in the bile duct. I will achieve this by: (1) generating a single-nuclei transcriptomic atlas of human bile duct healing to identify repair trajectories across disease stages; (2) developing a 3D bioengineered bile duct to interrogate epithelial-stromal pathways in a scalable in vitro model; (3) testing whether early pathogenic pathways can be therapeutically modulated to prevent fibrosis in a porcine model of biliary fibrosis. By using biliary fibrosis as an archetype, this work aims to identify broader mechanisms of fibrotic healing and inform future disease-modifying therapeutics in the bile duct and other organs.

title: Understanding the experiences of parents whose children have anxiety and/or low mood: using qualitative and quantitative methods to generate new theory
description: We know that your child experiencing anxiety or low mood has a significant impact on parents’ wellbeing. Parents have to manage highly stressful situations like their child self-harming, feeling suicidal, struggling to attend school and arguments at home. Studies show this group of parents experience higher levels of shame, stigma, anxiety, and stress than other parents. However, at present, there is a lack of clarity on what good support aimed at improving wellbeing of parents in this situation would look like. Support options for parents often focus on improving their child’s wellbeing, or are more generally targeted at parents’ pre-existing mental health needs. Researchers have highlighted a lack of evidence-base regarding what specific mechanisms maintain higher distress for parents when they are parenting a child with mental health difficulties. Without understanding this, what targeted support for parents in this unique situation would involve, and how existing approaches may need to be adapted to be effective. I will look to meet this gap, using interviews and daily surveys (ecological momentary assessment) to identify key maintenance processes and develop a model of distress. Finally, I will explore the impact of potential intervention elements on parents’ distress, using a single-case experimental design.

title: Evaluation of a multianalyte biosensor monitoring system for predicting clinical and neurological deterioration during severe acute respiratory infection in South Africa
description: Pneumonia, influenza and tuberculosis are consistently in the top five causes of death in South Africa, with an estimated in-hospital mortality of 7-12%. Recognising the deteriorating patient is challenging in South Africa where nurse:patient ratios can be 1:18 and laboratory testing is limited due to cost. During severe acute respiratory infection, mortality can be predicted by infection markers, and I have shown that brain injury biomarkers predict functional outcomes. I aim to build on our low-cost continuous biosensor monitoring system optimised for the low-resource setting. Through three work packages, I will: \- Conduct a mixed-methods biosensor evaluation, validating a biosensing patch and point-of-care device for infection and brain injury biomarkers (lactate, CRP, IL-6, Tau, and Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein) in the clinical setting, and evaluating the sociotechnical system using patient journey modelling and focus groups. \- Describe the profile of infection and brain injury biomarkers during severe acute respiratory infection. \- Develop and validate algorithms to predict clinical deterioration by NEW2 score, and neurological deterioration by Glasgow Coma Scale, and engineer software to display results. Short term, this will provide an early warning system for deterioration, and in the longer term, may create a platform for personalised care.

title: Optimising evidence-based intervention for children and young people with Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake disorder
description: Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) is characterised by a clinically significant restriction or avoidance of food, driven by sensory sensitivities, low interest in food, and/or fear of the consequences of eating (APA, 2013). Despite increasing recognition, ARFID remains under-researched, with limited evidence-based interventions (Haidar et al., 2025). This research therefore aims to develop, refine, and evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of a modular intervention for children and young people with ARFID. Modular interventions are flexible and customisable, comprising interchangeable components that can be tailored to individual needs, maintaining factors, and symptom profiles. Initially a systematic review exploring components, delivery requirements and outcomes of therapeutic interventions for children and young people with Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder will be conducted. This will be followed by the development and iterative refinement of a modular intervention using a Plan Do Study Act methodology. Stakeholder feedback and clinical data will be used to optimise content and delivery. The final phase of this study will be a single-arm case- series study to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the refined modular intervention across 2 clinical services. Findings will inform future trials and provide the beginning of an evidence-based pathway for scalable ARFID intervention development.

title: Building a Global Knowledge & Connection Platform for Mental Health Innovators
description: Thank you for the invitation to apply for a Wellcome Discretionary Award. This proposal aims to expand Hemingway from an emerging community and publication into a global knowledge and connection infrastructure for mental health innovators. Hemingway already brings together people across research, clinical practice, industry, lived-experience and policy. But they still lack a reliable way to learn from each other in real time, access diverse perspectives, and build on emerging evidence rather than working in isolation. These gaps slow the development and spread of approaches that could meaningfully improve population mental health. The project delivers three major enhancements: Hemingway Sessions: Weekly, structured discussions where practitioners, researchers, and lived-experience contributors share insight on topics such as clinical models, safety, implementation, and evaluation. Hemingway Chapters: Local groups in global hubs that strengthen collaboration, peer support, and the practical exchange of experience. Hemingway Guides: Co- created, high-quality resources that translate collective insight into practical frameworks to support better decisions and avoid common pitfalls. Topics include care model design, business model design, user engagement, fundraising, etc. Together, these activities will create a more connected and better-informed community of innovators. By doing so, promising ideas will develop more efficiently and reach the people who need them.

title: Capturing Hidden Regulatory Mechanism of Human Membrane Proteins via Soft- landing Mass Spectrometry-Guided Cryo-EM
description: Membrane proteins function as dynamic conformational ensembles shaped by lipid composition, ligand occupancy, and intrinsically disordered cytoplasmic regions (IDRs). Conventional single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo- EM) primarily resolves dominant conformations from solution-averaged populations, leaving low-abundance regulatory states structurally inaccessible. This limits mechanistic understanding of membrane protein regulation and disease-associated conformational variation. This programme establishes a state-resolved structural framework integrating native mass spectrometry (native MS) with cryo-EM using electrospray ion beam deposition (ESIBD)-based soft-landing. By mass-selecting defined ligand- and lipid-bound charge states prior to vitrification and exploiting reduced dielectric screening in the gas phase, the approach shifts conformational equilibria to stabilise regulatory regions under-represented in solution. Mass-defined populations are then structurally characterised by cryo-EM to test whether electrostatic and compositional modulation enables visualisation of otherwise obscured conformations. The research progresses from bacterial membrane proteins to regulatory IDRs in human transporters, culminating in analysis of ligand- and lipid-associated states in the disease-relevant solute carrier SLC45A4. This work moves structural biology from passive ensemble observation toward controlled state enrichment. The programme will define how lipid environment, ligand binding, and electrostatic interactions reshape conformational equilibria in membrane proteins, establishing a platform for resolving regulatory heterogeneity across transporters and ion channels.

title: Support for IPCC's 7th assessment report meetings
description: I will serve as a Lead Author for Chapter 5 (Enablers and barriers) of the Working Group III Contribution to the Seventh Assessment Report. In my role, I will be responsible for several sections of the chapter. I will be liaising with the Health chapter in WGII, and have been asked to be a Contributing Author to the Africa regional chapter in WGII. title: Investigating Visual Pathway Defects in Albinism through Precision Medicine and Advanced Imaging Techniques
description: Albinism is an inherited condition characterized by hypopigmentation, visual impairment, and nystagmus, with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 12,000 in European populations. Beyond visual challenges, people with albinism (PwA) often experience stigma and psychosocial difficulties, which can negatively affect wellbeing. Emerging evidence suggests a potential genetic predisposition to mental health conditions in PwA, possibly linked to dopamine system dysregulation. There is a critical gap in UK-based studies exploring psychological impacts and support needs for PwA. This project aims to address this gap through three integrated components: Systematic review to synthesize current evidence on wellbeing and quality of life (QoL) in PwA. Quantitative analysis using UK Biobank data to conduct a phenome-wide association study (PHeWAS) of genetic variants linked to albinism, focusing on neuropsychiatric and QoL phenotypes. Qualitative interviews with UK adults with albinism to explore lived experiences, coping strategies, and sources of support. Findings will inform evidence-based interventions to improve psychological wellbeing and QoL in PwA, with future research exploring causal mechanisms through Mendelian Randomisation.

title: Towards Tourettic Futures
description: Tourette Syndrome (TS) has gained unprecedented visibility across academic and public discourse, yet critical scholarship remains dominated by biomedical and deficit-based frameworks. This project makes a decisive intervention by situating TS within critical disability and neurodiversity scholarship, reframing the tourettic not as pathology but as lived, cultural, and political formation. Using interviews, digital ethnography, and participatory creative methods (zine-making and movement workshops), the project investigates how tourettic experience is shaped through digital technologies, from online diagnosis and platformed visibility to the formation of transnational communities of care. Implementing embodied and creative methods to translate findings across cultural divides and foreground tourettic experiences, this research centres the systemically excluded g lobal majority ethnicity, queer, and trans tourettic communities’ experiences, alongside the insights they offer. Through integrating a mixed methodological approach, the project develops the first sustained, interdisciplinary framework for Tourettic Studies. It delivers new forms of evidence for arts, humanities and health, demonstrating how tourettic ways of moving, sensing, and communicating can generate alternative epistemologies of health and difference. In doing so, the project shifts TS research beyond restrictive diagnostic framings and establishes the tourettic as a vital site of knowledge production, cultural creativity and collective hopeful future for tourettic people.

title: SPARK-PMDD: Studying Psychological Changes and Inflammatory Markers in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
description: Background: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe reproductive mood disorder with distressing symptoms that emerge monthly in the week or two before menstruation. For people with PMDD, cyclical symptoms cause a great deal of difficulties at home, work, and/or school. Previous research from our team has shown elevated inflammatory levels in people with depression and postpartum depression. This study aims to understand whether severity of PMDD symptoms is linked to variation in inflammatory levels across the menstrual cycle. Approach: We will recruit people with and without PMDD and ask them to complete daily questionnaires about their PMDD symptoms, and other psychological processes. Blood samples will be collected at 2 timepoints during their menstrual cycle to measure inflammation levels in their bodies. At these times, participants will also be asked to provide detailed information about thought processes like self-criticism, body image, rumination (repetitive distressing thoughts), and suicidality (thoughts, plans, behaviours related to suicide). Additionally, we will gather participants’ opinions on biological and psychological treatments for PMDD and their lived experiences with the disorder. Impact: There are currently limited available treatments for PMDD. With this data, we will provide a better understanding of ways to improve treatment for this underrecognised disorder.

title: The use of rapid infection diagnostics to optimise antibiotic use for patients with multimorbidity in Scotland
description: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a large threat to global health. Broad spectrum antibiotics are often used empirically, in lieu of access to reliable laboratory diagnostic tests, which creates a perpetuating cycle of inappropriate antibiotic use driving the emergence of antibiotic resistance. It is likely that patients with multimorbidity are more at risk of antibiotic resistance, because of their repeated health care exposures and due to multiple complex presentations, which may mimic infection. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and biomarkers, e.g. procalcitonin, for infection have the potential reduce unnecessary exposure to antimicrobials, but there is limited understanding of their impact in patients with multimorbidity. The aim is to understand the association between RDTs and antibiotic use for patients with multimorbidity and how this may differ in remote versus urban areas in Scotland. Methods include a systematic literature review assessing the impact of rapid diagnostic tests on antibiotic use in patients with multimorbidity; mapping of RDT use in NHS Health boards in Scotland; population-based statistical analysis of healthcare datasets, and a multi-site ethnographic study of the RDT system, process and healthcare worker experiences and practices affecting patients with multimorbidity across different healthcare organisational settings, including remote and urban locations in Scotland.

title: Determinants of fungal asthma in children
description: Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterised by wheeze, shortness of breath and cough. In the UK, 1.1 million children suffer from asthma and children with severe asthma are more likely to experience progressive respiratory deterioration into adulthood. Mould exposure and fungal sensitisation are linked to more severe asthma in adults, but not much is known how this affects asthma severity in childhood. The aim of my project is to identify environmental and genetic risk factors driving asthma in childhood, to focus on mould exposure as an important and under-assessed specific risk factor and to obtain a better insight into the immunopathology of fungal asthma in childhood.
