I will investigate the environmental, genetic and clinical factors contributing to severe asthma in childhood using Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) data, including mould exposure and fungal sensitisation. I will also examine immune responses in children with asthma by measuring inflammatory markers in blood and respiratory samples. This research will enhance our understanding of severe asthma in children and the impact of mould exposure and sensitisation, advance my own research skills, and integrate multi-domain approaches. It may help identify new management strategies and prognostic markers for fungal asthma.

title: Instrumentalised Disability: Gendered Pathways to Health Injustice in China's one-child generation
description: This project investigates a hidden phenomenon – instrumentalised disability – as a biosocial process through which children’s bodies, health statuses and diagnoses were strategically mobilised under a restrictive regime, with lasting health consequences. Empirically grounded in China’s one-child policy, which permitted additional births in cases of disability, it introduces a critical gender lens to reveal how son preference systematically shaped which child’s disability was mobilised as a familial resource. Building on critical disability studies, this project analyses instrumentalised disability as multiple practices emerging from triadic negotiations among families, communities and local bureaucrats. These practices, including induced impairment, neglected treatable conditions, coerced performance and administrative manipulation, are analysed as variations of a process shaped by scarcity, documentation and moral evaluations. The research examines three interrelated domains: (1) family strategies that recalibrated children’s bodily worth amid conflicting patriarchal fertility norms and state regulation; (2) community moral economies that normalised concealment; (3) everyday bureaucratic collusion that enabled disability claims. Using life- course narrative interviews and trauma-informed methods, the project traces the long-impacts of this gendered instrumentalization on health and personhood. Drawing on critical disability studies and bio-legitimacy approaches, it develops a transferable framework for similar forms of stratified health injustice in other resource-constrained policy contexts.

title: The Development of a Novel Robotic and Surgical Navigation System for Veterinary Surgery
description: Key Words -- Robotics, Orthopaedics, Veterinary Surgery, Surgical Accuracy, Computer Aided Orthopaedic Surgery The aim of this project is to develop a novel surgical robotic system for use by veterinary surgeons to increase surgical accuracy and reduce complications. The benefits of robotic assisted surgery have been documented in the human literature as reduced post operative pain and increased functionality post surgery. These benefits are directly transferable to veterinary patients but as of yet a cost reasonable robotic system does not exist nor is one validated for veterinary patients. We aim to use virtual guides as a mechanism of robotic control that can be applied to a generic robotic arm and infra red camera system to provide a financially reasonable alternative which is still highly accurate and repeatable. The key goals of this research will be to validate this mechanism of control for a variety of surgical procedures and evaluate its performance compared to physical guides and current established gold standards in veterinary and human orthopaedic surgery.

title: A NEW FUND FOR SCIENTIFIC SOFTWARE
description: Scientific software is essential for AI-driven scientific discovery, yet the open-source ecosystem supporting AI applications in science is underfunded. As scientific workflows increasingly adopt AI, the underlying software and its communities must evolve. Although various funders (philanthropic, public, and industry) are investing in open-source software to facilitate this shift, they currently lack an effective coordination mechanism. This proposal aims to establish a new fund that will enable multiple funders to direct resources toward software advancing AI in science. The fund will serve as a central coordination hub, maximizing the visibility, impact, and sustainability of the funding. While this proposal focuses on a single fund, it will lay the groundwork for a shared infrastructure, allowing for the creation of a portfolio of funds to support multi-funder opportunities across diverse areas of software and science. The proposed fund will be established in partnership with the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and will be hosted by the grantee, Renaissance Philanthropy.

title: Characterising the role of brainstem mechanisms in consciousness, neural inertia and anaesthetic sensitivity
description: Understanding the neural mechanisms of consciousness remains a major challenge in neuroscience and medicine, with implications for anaesthesia, sleep disorders, coma, and delirium. Using 7-Tesla fMRI to resolve activity within individual brainstem nuclei, and leveraging anaesthesia and sleep as model systems, this work aims to clarify how neurochemical arousal networks mediate a) consciousness, b) neural inertia, and c) anaesthetic sensitivity. Because these arousal nuclei release specific neurotransmitters, the findings have significant therapeutic potential. a) Consciousness depends critically on the meso-pontine brainstem, as stroke in this region causes irreversible coma. While cell-specific lesions in this region do not induce coma, specific pharmacological modulation can produce sedation and this reduces delirium compared to traditional anaesthesia. Mapping these pathways may inform strategies to prevent delirium and accelerate recovery from coma. b) Neural inertia—the brain’s resistance to state transitions—underlies anaesthetic hysteresis, where loss and recovery of consciousness occur at different drug concentrations. Identifying mechanisms specific to recovery of consciousness could help prevent anaesthetic awareness and improve coma outcomes. c) Heightened anaesthetic sensitivity, reflected by greater behavioural impairment at a given drug level, is linked to postoperative delirium. Understanding its neural basis could reveal targets for perioperative neuroprotection and personalised anaesthetic care.

title: Pneumococcal Vaccine Responses in Small Vulnerable Newborns
description: Childhood mortality has shown an impressive 59% decline between 1990 to 2022; unfortunately, this reduction has not been equal. Low-incomes countries, and sub-Saharan Africa in particular, now account for the majority of global child deaths; currently the under-5 mortality rate per 1000 births in Africa is ten times that in Europe. In conjunction, the recent Lancet Small Vulnerable Newborn (SVN) Series highlighted key underlying risk factors for infant mortality, with 25% of live births carrying one or more vulnerabilities: low birthweight, small for gestational age, and/or prematurity. The gap in improving infant mortality between high- and low-income countries demonstrates the inequity faced by this population and the need to increase research around SVNs to inform new evidence-based interventions. Globally, SVNs have the most to gain from interventions to reduce infant mortality, such as vaccination, however they are drastically under-represented in vaccine efficacy trials and particularly in newer vaccines, there is little evidence of their efficacy in this population. Pneumococcal disease remains one of the most prevalent causes for pneumonia globally, despite the introduction of PCV13 across many countries. This project will characterise the response to PCV13 in SVNs, considering immunogenicity and B cell recruitment, durability of protection and mucosal immunity.

title: Remembering the cold – integrating engrams and metabolism
description: Environmental thermal challenges require the brain to coordinate both autonomic and behavioural responses to maintain physiological homeostasis. How and whether thermal experiences are encoded as memories remains unknown. This proposal aims to uncover the mechanistic basis of “cold memory” in thermoregulation, and the reciprocal relationship between cold experience and memory engrams. Using advanced methods, including engram labelling, optogenetics, chemogenetics, calcium imaging, and transcriptomics, we will define the molecular and circuit mechanisms governing the storage and activation of cold sensitive engrams. By integrating molecular, physiological, and behavioural approaches, we will generate a detailed, multi-level understanding of how cold memories are formed and utilized to drive adaptive behavioural and metabolic responses. The results will provide the first fundamental insights into how memory influences metabolic physiological adaptation, with implications for neurological and metabolic disorders, including conditions characterized by impaired thermoregulation.

title: Co-designing communication strategies of type 2 diabetes complication risks
description: People of South Asian and Black ethnicity are disproportionately affected by type 2 diabetes (T2D) complications, and under-represented in research. Therefore, how people with T2D perceive complication risks and healthcare professionals (HCP) communicate these to different ethnic groups, is important for T2D care. Aim: co-design acceptable approaches for communicating risk of T2D complications, underpinned by prediction models, for people from South Asian and Black ethnicities and HCP. Methods: WP1- Systematic review to explore existing communicating risk models of T2D complications. WP2- Prediction modelling of leading complication risks using a large, diverse Northeast London (NEL) T2D cohort. WP3- Semi-structured interviews with people with T2D across NEL, to identify perceptions of complication risks and barriers/ facilitators to communication. WP4- Complementary HCP interviews will explore their experiences of risk communication and inform effective approaches. WP5- Four workshops (people with T2D/ HCP/ stakeholders) will co- design acceptable communication approaches, tailored for different ethnic groups. Prototype materials will be produced, ready for feasibility testing. Impact: People with T2D and community organisations in an advisory group will guide research, outreach activities, dissemination and clinical integration. I will provide best-practice communication principles, utilising robust estimates for T2D complications, for HCP and tailored for South Asian/ Black ethnic groups.
recipient: City St George's, University of London

title: Targeting adrenal stem cells by gene therapy to rescue adrenal insufficiency in Familial Glucocorticoid Deficiency type 2
description: Familial Glucocorticoid Deficiency (FGD) is a rare autosomal recessive disease characterised by isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. The condition is fatal unless treated, due to adrenal crisis in the neonatal period. 20% of cases are due to mutations in melanocortin 2 receptor accessory protein (MRAP), termed FGD type 2 (FGD2). Treatment is life-long glucocorticoid replacement which is associated with morbidity and mortality, due to over- or under-replacement and inability to replicate physiology. Gene therapy offers a curative promise for genetic diseases. Our research group has generated a novel FGD mouse model lacking MRAP expression, recapitulating human FGD2. Our study aims to target the adrenal progenitor cell niche in MRAP-knockout (Mrap-/-) animals using Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) to restore MRAP expression. By targeting these, we aim to repopulate the adrenal gland throughout a lifetime. Our aims are to (1) identify the optimal AAV serotype to transduce adrenal progenitor cells and therefore build our gene therapy construct, (2) use this to determine replacement of MRAP in adrenal progenitor cells lacking MRAP, (3) administer the gene therapy to Mrap -/- mice models and assess efficacy, safety and longevity of rescue. The project will provide proof-of-concept data for translational studies in FGD and other forms of adrenal insufficiency.

title: The UNITE study: UNderstanding and Improving how the limitations of blood TEsts are discussed in primary care – a participatory ethnographic study to inform clinical practice
description: Almost half of all NHS blood tests are carried out in primary care and testing rates have tripled since 2000. Blood tests are valuable but are often over- ordered, leading to high costs, increased workload, and potential harm to patients. Examining what happens in clinical consultations where blood tests are discussed is key to understanding the rise in testing and ensuring blood tests are used wisely. This project will use ethnographic and participatory methods to understand and improve how the limitations of blood tests are discussed in primary care settings. The research will inform strategies to promote the judicious use of blood tests. There are four work packages: \- WP1: Meta-ethnography synthesising existing qualitative literature on blood testing communication. \- WP2: Ethnographic observation of interactions about blood testing in two GP practices. \- WP3: Video-reflexive ethnography workshops with primary care staff to identify and resolve challenges around blood test communication. \- WP4: Forum Theatre workshops to explore new ways to communicate about the limitations of blood tests. Study findings will be used to co-produce a workshop resource (for clinicians) and an online resource (for patients/the public), both aimed at improving how blood tests are discussed in primary care.

title: Optimising Cardiovascular Risk Prediction in the Type 2 Diabetes UK Population: Enhancing Resource Allocation and Informing National Health Recommendations
description: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a growing public health challenge in the UK, with increasing incidence, particularly among people under 40 years of age. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) represents the main source of morbidity and mortality in individuals with T2D, placing substantial burdens on patients, families, and healthcare systems. However, existing CVD risk prediction models for people with T2D are often unreliable therefore limits their ability to identify individuals at high risk of potentially preventable cardiovascular events. The aim of this project is to improve the prediction of preventable CVD among people with T2D. The research method will be conducted in four phases. Phase 1 involves a PROSPERO-registered systematic review to critically evaluate existing CVD risk prediction models used in T2D populations. Phase 2 focuses on the development of a new risk prediction model using 10 years of follow-up data from 3,057 participants in the ADDITION-Europe trial, incorporating both traditional cardiovascular and T2D-specific risk factors. Phase 3 will externally validate the model using UK-wide T2D datasets to assess its generalisability and performance. Finally, Phase 4 will explore preferences of primary care practitioners and patients through a survey, ensuring the model’s design and functionality support effective implementation in clinical practice.

title: Neutrophil-fibroblast interactions – how do they alter the tumour microenvironment and influence disease progression in non-small cell lung cancer?
description: In cancer, there is an ecosystem of cells and other factors around the tumour cells, known as the tumour microenvironment. Non-cancerous cells in the tumour microenvironment include neutrophils, a common type of immune cell, and fibroblasts, which provide the environment for cells to live in. Such non- cancerous cells interact with cancer cells and can affect cancer progression, but the exact effect of each cell type is not fully understood. I will investigate changes which occur in neutrophils and fibroblasts when they enter the tumour microenvironment. I will focus on the thousands of proteins found in these cells and look at changes to protein production and exchange. I will do this by isolating these cells and growing them with and without cancer cells to determine how their proteins change in different conditions which will reflect the tumour microenvironment. I am particularly interested in looking at a group of neutrophils that might help create an ‘anti-cancer’ environment to see if I can find ways to help create more of these cells. I will test these within established cancer tissue databases to see how the presence and behaviour of these ‘anti-cancer’ neutrophils relates to growth and spread of lung cancers.

title: COMPASS- Cancer Outcomes in Multimorbidity: Pathway and System Study
description: Multimorbidity is common at cancer diagnosis and can influence screening uptake, route to diagnosis, treatment decisions, and survival. Understanding how the presence, type, and complexity of long-term conditions shape cancer diagnostic journeys can identify patients at risk of delay, reveal mechanisms such as symptom masking or competing priorities, and inform interventions to shorten diagnostic intervals. The overarching aim of this PhD is to investigate how multimorbidity, measured in multiple ways, impacts cancer diagnostic pathways and outcomes. This PhD will use a multi-methods design. A systematic review will describe and analyse the current literature exploring the impact of pre-existing long-term conditions on diagnostic route and timeliness in people diagnosed with one of the four most common cancers in the UK (breast, prostate, lung and colorectal). Quantitative analyses of linked routine health data will then focus on pathways for bowel cancer, evaluating how individual and multiple conditions impact screening uptake, primary care clinical activity, diagnostic route and timeliness, stage at diagnosis, and survival. Finally, qualitative interviews with primary care professionals will explore how pre-existing conditions influence the management of suspected bowel cancer and identify strategies to improve detection in patients with multiple and complex health needs.

title: Lyophilization process development for PanChol
description: We created a single-dose oral live-attenuated cholera vaccine (PanChol) that has the potential to circumvent the limitations of current killed vaccines. The Wellcome Trust funded a Phase I first-in-human study to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of PanChol in healthy volunteers in Massachusetts, USA. This study was carried out using GMP-manufactured frozen PanChol cells. The results of this study are extremely promising. No dose-limiting side effects were observed and all volunteers, regardless of dose, developed robust vibriocidal antibody responses. Given the encouraging results in this trial, further development of PanChol is warranted. Our overarching goal in PanChol development is to enable real-world deployment of this vaccine in LMIC. A key next step to meet our goal is to create a new formulation of PanChol that will be feasible for storage and distribution in LMIC and that can be manufactured at scale at low cost. Here, we propose to develop a manufacturing process for a lyophilized presentation of PanChol. The key deliverable of the work is development and process engineering of a lyophilized form of PanChol stable at 2-8° for >2 years. The proposed process development is part of the critical path for developing a globally scalable product.

title: Transitioning Health Policy Watch to a Sustainable Global Public Good
description: Health Policy Watch (HPW) aims to consolidate its transition to a sustainable, globally relevant public-interest news platform. The funding will strengthen institutional stability by expanding our donor base; securing predictable support for senior editors and core editorial functions; and extending our network of Global South journalists who connect lived realities with global policy debates. HPW provides open-access, interdisciplinary reporting that links complex health challenges—climate change, infectious diseases, AMR, NCDs, mental health, and emergency preparedness—with political, financial, and governance decisions. This proposal includes: engaging a development director to implement strategies for structured donor diversification and enhanced reader support of the open-access model; gradual expansion of our network: and enhanced mentoring and training of reporters in under-represented regions. Wellcome’s partnership will ensure succession and building upon more than CHF 600,000 invested since 2020. At a time of geopolitical uncertainty and rising global health misinformation and disinformation, and rapid advances in generative AI—where information increasingly circulates through AI-mediated systems—independent, evidence-based journalism is essential to foster informed, democratic debate. This grant will enable HPW to remain a trusted, representative media institution and strengthen its long-term resilience—expanding evidence-based reporting, elevating Global South voices, and reinforcing global health decision-making through timely, accessible, and impactful journalism.

title: Testing the Ecophenotype Hypothesis in Conduct Disorder: Clinical, Neurocognitive, and Neurostructural Correlates of Childhood Maltreatment
description: Keywords: conduct disorder, childhood maltreatment, children, ecophenotype hypothesis, developmental psychopathology Conduct disorder (CD) is a highly heterogeneous, severe psychiatric condition characterised by persistent antisocial and aggressive behaviour in children and adolescents. Despite a global prevalence of 3% and significant co-morbidity, CD remains under- researched. Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a well-established risk factor for CD. Moreover, the ecophenotype hypothesis proposes that environmental exposures such as CM may shape distinct clinical subtypes within a diagnostic category. A systematic review and meta-analysis will be conducted to explore the association between CM and CD. Following this, to test the ecophenotype hypothesis, the project will draw on assessment datasets from the large (N = 11,875) longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (ABCD Study®). We aim to characterise clinical (symptom severity and functional impairment), neurostructural (grey and white matter), and neurocognitive correlates in youth with CD and a history of CM relative to three comparison groups: maltreated youth without CD, non-maltreated youth with CD and typically developing controls. The project will advance understanding of how CM shapes the clinical, neurocognitive, and neurostructural profiles of CD. Furthermore, findings may inform more refined subgroup models of CD to support the development of tailored interventions across psychiatry, education and forensic services.

title: The impact of post TB lung disease in the migrant population in Leicester
description: This research aims to address the significant burden of post-tuberculosis lung disease (PTBLD) among migrant populations in Leicestershire, a group disproportionately affected by TB and related health inequalities. While TB treatment is often considered curative, evidence shows survivors face long- term complications, including impaired lung function, psychological distress, and reduced quality of life. Mortality post-TB may be up to three times higher than the general population, yet UK-specific data on PTBLD are lacking. This project will quantify medium- to long-term health and economic impacts of PTBLD in Leicester’s migrant community and evaluate a culturally adapted pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programme. The research plan includes: (1) a systematic review of exercise-based interventions; (2) a prospective cohort study assessing functional and psychological outcomes; (3) refinement of PR through stakeholder engagement; and (4) a feasibility trial incorporating measures of muscle quality and cost-effectiveness. Expected outcomes include improved understanding of PTBLD burden, development of tailored interventions, and evidence to inform NHS strategies to reduce health inequalities. Keywords: tuberculosis, post-TB lung disease, pulmonary rehabilitation, migrant health, health inequalities, respiratory outcomes, cost-effectiveness.

title: Biological Embodiments of Societal Complexities: Sociocultural Determinants of Human Skeletal Health
description: What is the social skeleton? This project investigates how social factors influence human health and biology, and how they are “embodied” in the human skeleton. Using a holistic interdisciplinary approach, it combines skeletal biology with the humanities and social sciences to examine how social variables such as childhood living conditions, social status in adulthood, ethnocultural identity, and social age impact skeletal aging, growth, and pathology. By focusing on an exceptionally well-documented late 19th-century Austrian anatomical collection—comprising skeletal remains of more than 700 individuals of known identity—this research uses genealogical data (in order to illuminate the social environment and documented lives of these individuals, as well as of their parents and grandparents) to explore how life course and intergenerational social conditions affect health outcomes. It applies social theoretical frameworks and uses a long-term contextualised historical perspective to explore patterns through the Social Determinants of Health (SDoH) and the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) frameworks. This historical perspective will illuminate the sociocultural mechanisms that drive chronic health disparities faced by vulnerable communities today. Furthermore, the project integrates art as a conceptual tool for communicating the research questions, reflecting on the scientific findings and their wider significance.

title: Centromere Dynamics: Bridging Fundamental Mechanisms and Agricultural Innovation
description: Cell division is fundamental to cellular life, requiring precision to produce healthy, viable daughter cells. Errors in this process can result in aneuploidy, developmental abnormalities, cancer, or cell death. Central to this process is the segregation of genetic material, mediated by a specialised protein complex at a chromosome locus called the centromere. Advances in long- read sequencing have enabled the complete assembly of centromeres, revealing that, despite conserved function, the DNA sequences vary widely in size and structure. Understanding how genetic and epigenetic factors shape centromere formation and dynamics is a critical question in biology and the focus of this proposal. This research leverages Arabidopsis thaliana functional genomics, live-cell imaging, quantitative proteomics, and long-read sequencing to investigate how centromere fidelity is regulated by the genome and chromatin environment. In Work Packages 1 and 2, we will identify genetic, protein, and chromatin factors contributing to centromere formation and fidelity. In Work Package 3, we will remodel centromeres to functionally influence chromosome inheritance, enabling applications in crop breeding. These insights will transform our understanding of this fundamental biological process, provide practical applications in crop breeding, which can be used to address global challenges in food supply, enhance food security, and promote human well- being.

title: Understanding the heterogeneity and evolutionary dynamics of Barrett’s oesophagus to predict cancer risk
description: Many cancers evolve over years, offering a window to uncover the cellular and molecular changes that precede diagnosis, yet many are still detected at advanced stages. The precancerous lesion Barrett’s oesophagus (BO) provides a compelling model for studying these early events. While the driver gene landscape has been elucidated for this disease, little is known about why only a minority of BO patients progress while most remain indolent. We hypothesise that a biology-informed approach capturing dynamic molecular and cellular changes over time could transform current understanding and practice. We will leverage a comprehensive, longitudinal bioresource of BO progressors and non- progressors collected over 30 years, integrate cutting-edge single-cell and spatially resolved omics, and employ newly established multi-disease-stage organoid models to dissect the key events driving progression (or indolence). Our interdisciplinary team will investigate: (i) which cells are roots of progression at each disease stage; (ii) the timing, ordering and consequences of mutations; and (iii) how highly mutated BO reshapes its microenvironmental niche and evades immune surveillance. These data will feed into (iv) an integrative, dynamic statistical model incorporating time-dependent clinical, pathological and molecular variables to predict individual cancer risk.

title: Development of an Embryonic Chick Model for In Vivo Study of Human Congenital Cataracts
description: Congenital cataracts are the leading cause of childhood blindness, resulting from disorganisation of lens fibres and protein accumulation that disrupts lens transparency. The mechanistic basis for most genetic variants remains unclear. My project aims to use a chick embryo model to understand how mutations affect lens formation and function. My project has two aims: 1\. To test if pathogenic human genetic variants cause congenital cataract when introduced into the chicken lens. I will perform microinjection of mutated gene constructs into the embryo to determine if their expression results in abnormal lens structure and refractive properties. In parallel, I will generate a stable gene-edited chicken line with an allele associated with early-onset human cataracts. 2\. To identify the changes in gene expression, protein abundance and activities, and the metabolic effects that occur when cataracts develop using the chicken embryo model system. This could reveal common pathways and targets that could be used to explore new diagnostic and treatment strategies. The combination of both genetic approaches will allow in-depth characterisation and comparisons of the effects of the introduced mutations using a biomedically-relevant, reproducible and scalable model system. The outcome of this work could lead to improved non-surgical treatments for children with cataracts.

title: Co-produced solutions for low use of public access defibrillators following Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) in deprived urban communities in Scotland.
description: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a leading cause of sudden death and a significant public health challenge (1). In Scotland, national strategies have improved bystander response (2,3), with CPR rates rising from 41% to 66% (2015–2023) and better survival outcomes (4,5). However, use of public access defibrillators (PADs), which can improve survival by three to five times, remains low at 9.8% (5). Data from The Circuit (6) and PADmap (7) reveal disparities in PAD access and usage. Fewer than 5% of OHCAs occur within 200 meters of a PAD (8). SIMD 1 (9) communities face the highest OHCA burden and poorest outcomes (10). While PAD availability is similar across deprivation levels, bystander use is much lower in SIMD 1 (6.2%) than SIMD 5 (10.3%) (5). Barriers include poor PAD visibility, inconsistent maintenance, low health literacy, and cultural concerns such as fear of harm and legal ambiguity (11–18). This research will identify social, cultural, behavioural, and knowledge barriers to PAD use in SIMD 1 areas through literature and lived experience. Findings will inform a formative evaluation of a community co- designed intervention to improve PAD maintenance and use and contribute to national OHCA policy.

title: Systemic immune adaptation to menstruation: Defining the role of bone marrow in endometrial repair
description: Each month, the lining of the uterus is shed during menstruation and then rapidly restored. This repair is fast and scarless, which is unusual compared to healing elsewhere in the body. Immune cells called monocytes, made in the bone marrow, travel through the blood to the uterus and help with this process. However, we still do not understand how the body coordinates this response or what happens when it goes wrong. In this project, I will use a laboratory mouse model that closely mimics menstruation in humans to study how the bone marrow responds. I will investigate whether specific signals, such as a molecule called G-CSF, prompt the bone marrow to release immune cells. I will also test how inflammation affects this process and whether blocking or enhancing these signals changes healing. To understand how these findings apply to people, I will study blood samples from women across different stages of the menstrual cycle. This research could change how we think about menstruation. Instead of seeing it as a process limited to the uterus, we may begin to understand it as a coordinated response involving the whole immune system. This could help improve treatments for reproductive, inflammatory and immune-related conditions.

title: Developing a deep learning-based model to predict rehabilitation outcomes in underserved groups living with multiple long-term conditions
description: This project aims to develop a deep learning–based model to predict successful completion of exercise-based rehabilitation amongst people living with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC). MLTC are increasingly prevalent among ethnic minority and socioeconomically disadvantaged populations, experiencing reduced quality of life, lower physical function, and higher healthcare utilisation. Although rehabilitation improves outcomes across many long-term conditions, adherence is low and early drop out is common. The research will begin by establishing a consensus-based definition of rehabilitation "completion". This definition will be used alongside real-world datasets from exercise-based rehabilitation programmes, to identify subgroups of participants based on demographic, socioeconomic, clinical and functional factors that associate with completion. This large dataset will be used to develop and train a deep learning model capable of identifying individuals at risk of non-completion. Following this, the views and experiences of people with MLTC who were deemed "non-completers" of exercise rehabilitation will be explored using qualitative interviews. This will identify personal, social and service level barriers and facilitators to programme completion, aiming to guide the development of personalised support strategies to improve adherence and promote equity in rehabilitation services. Keywords: multiple long-term conditions, rehabilitation, deep learning, health inequalities, adherence, prediction.

title: The MARIA Study: Multimorbidity, Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Associations
description: Background: Multimorbidity is associated with premature death, increased likelihood of hospitalisation, and poor quality of life. The COVID-19 pandemic showed a close relationship between infection, morbidity and poor patient outcomes, and as a result those most at-risk of deterioration were prioritised for shielding, vaccination and treatment. However, the relationship between multimorbidity, bacterial infection and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is poorly understood. Aim: To undertake foundational work investigating the relationship between multimorbidity, bacterial infection and AMR to inform strategies to improve patient outcomes and care. Approach: We will synthesise existing evidence on the epidemiology and burden of infection in multimorbidity through a systematic literature review (SLR) and meta-analysis. Using linked NHS datasets, we will undertake a retrospective cohort study to investigate whether bacterial infection leads to worse patient outcomes and more AMR in patients with multimorbidity, and to test whether acute bacterial infection is an indication of deterioration in multimorbidity. Genomic sequencing will be applied to characterise resistant infections and infer how they are transmitted. Expected outputs: Using the results from our SLR and cohort study we will develop a clinical risk stratification tool to identify patients at greatest risk of deterioration.

title: Intradermal BCG Controlled Human Infection Model in the UK and Malawi: Evaluating the Influence of Environmental Mycobacteria Sensitisation on BCG Clearance and Immune Response
description: Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading infectious killer worldwide. BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) is the only effective TB vaccine. BCG gives variable protection against tuberculous lung disease with ~80% protection in the UK but none to adults in equatorial countries, such as Malawi. Cost inhibits the development of novel effective vaccines which are urgently needed. A TB controlled human infection model (CHIM) would be a cost-effective tool for down-selecting novel vaccines, however, infecting humans with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) is unethical. A safe intradermal CHIM has been developed using BCG as a surrogate for M. tb infection which is being established in Blantyre, Malawi. BCG CHIM offers the opportunity to study why BCG is less effective in Malawi than in the UK. One theory is that repeated exposure to environmental non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) living in the tropical climate attenuates the protective efficacy of BCG. This study will recruit BCG-vaccinated Malawians with a range of NTM sensitisation to undergo intradermal BCG CHIM and compare against UK cohorts using stored samples. We hypothesise that high levels of NTM sensitisation will be associated with lower antimycobacterial immunity. Further Malawian BCG CHIM data will develop the platform for vaccine down-selection in a setting with urgent need.

title: Exploring postnatal care experiences of adolescent mothers: A grounded theory study in Ghana
description: Adolescent childbearing carries significant health risks, including maternal and neonatal complications. Ten percent of global births are to women aged under 20 with 90%occurring in LMICs. The risk of maternal mortality and neonatal deaths during the postnatal period is higher in LMICs including Ghana and many deaths could be prevented with enhanced care. Approximately 70,000 adolescent mothers die annually from complications which oftern occur in the postnatal period. Addressing poor outcomes requires strategies for providing quality maternity care for young mothers and babies, including the often- overlooked postnatal period. Whilst previous research has focused on reducing adolescent pregnancies, this study aims to develop a theoretically-informed intervention in Ghanain Ghana to improve postnatal care for adolescent mothers. This study will be conducted in three phases. Firstly, existing literature on adolescent postnatal care in LMICs and interventions will be reviewed. In the second phase, a grounded theory methodology will be used to conduct interviews and observations with adolescent mothers, health workers, and other individuals identified as being involved in the care process to explore the related social processes and influences. Finally, findings will be used to inform a consensus process to co-produce a protocol tailored to the needs of adolescent mothers in Ghana.

title: Multimorbidity in children and young people with intellectual disabilities
description: People with intellectual disabilities experience earlier onset and higher prevalence of multimorbidity compared to the general population and their life expectancy is, on average, 20 years shorter. This project aims to investigate the accrual of multiple long-term conditions in children and young people with intellectual disabilities, and the impact of multimorbidity on health and education outcomes for this population. A systematic literature review of multimorbidity in children and young people with intellectual disabilities will be completed. Large, routinely collected, linked electronic health and education datasets will be used for subsequent objectives. Trajectory of accumulation of long-term conditions in children and young people with intellectual disabilities will be modelled. Hospitalisations and premature mortality will then be compared between children and young people with and without intellectual disabilities and with and without multimorbidity. The impact of multimorbidity on outcomes such as school attendance and post-school destination for children and young people with intellectual disabilities will also be investigated. These studies will help to understand how multimorbidity develops in children and young people with intellectual disabilities and how it affects their health and education / participation outcomes. This will help to identify priorities for targeted intervention and prevention.

title: Complex Connections: Simulating Interventions for Multimorbidity Prevention and Levelling-up Equity (SIMPLE)
description: Multimorbidity, defined as living with two or more chronic health conditions, is becoming more common globally, and is strongly linked to deprivation. It is associated with poorer quality of life, higher healthcare usage, and worsening of health inequalities. To tackle this, “place-based” public health interventions that focus on improving the areas that people live in, for example, better housing, green space availability and access to transport, are becoming more popular. However, we do not fully understand how effective these interventions are in preventing or slowing down the development of multimorbidity, and/or whether they reduce or widen health inequalities. The SIMPLE project aims to develop a computer simulation, known as an Agent-Based Model (ABM), that mimics how people in Scotland develop multimorbidity over time, factoring in individual and group behaviours and interactions, health status, and the environments they live in. By simulating the effects of various public health interventions, the model will help predict what works, for whom, and where, and whether these actions make health inequalities better or worse. The SIMPLE project will provide new tools and insights for public health professionals and policy-makers to plan fairer, more efficient strategies to reduce the rising burden of multimorbidity in Scotland.

title: Mapping the Evolution of Louse-Borne Bacteria Using Genomic Time Series
description: Louse-borne diseases are an under-recognised burden, disproportionately affecting populations facing health inequalities, and are expected to increase as human displacement intensifies. Three bacterial pathogens transmitted by human lice, Borrelia recurrentis, Bartonella quintana, and Rickettsia prowazekii, have caused outbreaks throughout history, yet the correlates and drivers of their evolution remain poorly understood. Each of these species represents a separate evolutionary shift from tick- or flea-borne ancestors to strictly louse-borne transmission. This transition has been accompanied by increased virulence, epidemic potential, and substantial genome reduction. However, the genomic features underlying these changes are largely unknown and cannot be recovered from limited contemporary genomic datasets. My Wellcome ECA combines contemporary, historical and ancient pathogen genomes, including material recovered from archaeological remains and archival collections, to reconstruct how and when these bacterial pathogens adapted to lice. Using a pan-genomic, time-calibrated evolutionary framework across genomic time series, I will identify the genes and functional pathways that were lost or gained during this transition and place these changes within their historical context. By analysing each genus independently and comparatively, my work will identify convergent evolutionary pathways, providing insight into the genomic processes that have shaped the emergence, spread and epidemic potential of these louse-borne diseases.

title: From Soft Tissue to Stone: Investigating the Interplay between Systemic Inflammation, Cellular Crosstalk and the Hyaluronan Matrix in Chronic Kidney Disease-associated Vascular Calcification.
description: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Standard CVD treatments are less effective in patients with CKD; this is partly due to the prominence of a different pathophysiological process, vascular calcification (VC). VC is an active, highly-regulated process underpinned by osteogenic transdifferentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). The mechanisms driving VSMC-osteogenic transdifferentiation remain poorly understood, and no targeted VC therapies exist. Approach/Expected Impact: I will use single- nucleus RNA sequencing to define the transcriptomic heterogeneity of VSMCs and other key cell types in human arterial tissue with and without calcification. I will spatially validate these findings and use bioinformatics approaches to establish the roles of key cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. We have recently shown hyaluronan (HA), a matrix glycosaminoglycan, to be significantly altered during VSMC osteogenic transdifferentiation; I will identify target HA-associated pathways in the snRNA-seq data which I will validate in an in vitro model of VC. Generating this novel understanding of the fundamental cellular contributors, mediators and pathways in CKD- associated VC will help identify new therapeutic targets.

title: Co-Creating and Scaling a Tailored, Lay-Delivered Group Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (G-CBT) Intervention for Depression Among Young People Living with HIV (YPLHIV) in Cameroon: A Hybrid Implementation-Effectiveness Study
description: This proposal, led by the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) Cameroon in collaboration with the National AIDS Control Commission (NACC), the Directorate of Health Promotion, and an association of lived-experience experts, aims to adapt and scale a lay-delivered Group Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (G-CBT) model to strengthen the management of depression among young people living with HIV (YPLHIV, aged 15–24 years) in Cameroon. The project will unfold in two linked phases. The Foundation Phase will establish coordination structures, assess evidence and site readiness, and co-create and culturally adapt the G-CBT model with youth and lived-experience experts. This phase will culminate in an implementation package—comprising an intervention manual, facilitator training curriculum, supervision and fidelity-monitoring tools, and a finalized protocol to guide the Impact Phase. The Impact Phase will assess the clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and scalability of the adapted model through a Hybrid Type II cluster-randomised trial, guided by RE-AIM and CFIR frameworks. Expected outcomes include improved depression management, better ART adherence and retention, and enhanced psychosocial wellbeing. The project will yield a validated implementation toolkit, a costed scale-up model, and policy-ready evidence to integrate depression care into youth-friendly HIV services in Cameroon. Keywords: Depression, Adolescents, HIV, Mental Health, G-CBT, Implementation Research, Cameroon
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: Mapping Population Variability in the Human Brain
description: Brain imaging provides some of the most versatile and powerful tools in neuroscience. With the advent of population-level imaging, we can now study how the human brain relates to cognition, lifestyle, genetics, and disease. However, an outstanding challenge is how to create a valid basis for comparison across thousands of unique brains. Currently, analysis centres on either reducing population data to an over-simplistic population-average atlas, or analysing individuals in isolation, untethered from a biological reference to other subjects. Instead, we need to place individuals within the context of a far more complete description of the population. This requires a true "like-with-like" comparison that accounts for the unique structural folds, connections, and functional regions of each individual’s brain. To meet this challenge, we propose the Large Adaptive Neuroimage Atlas (LANA), a foundation model of population-level imaging data, along with a new platform to build and utilise this atlas. This transformative approach will allow small, focused studies to leverage big data, drive personalised therapeutic predictions, and enable the first high-resolution whole-genome-to-brain translation. We will create an accessible software platform to maximise LANA's impact, allowing researchers globally to discover complex links between the brain, genes, lifestyle, and disease.

title: The impact of rurality and deprivation on mental health problems, access to services and outcomes in young people
description: Background: Mental health (MH) problems are common and can have lasting impacts on young people (YP). their families, as well as wider economic impacts for society. Despite its importance, there is an absence of systematic research investigating the MH needs of YP living in rural and deprived communities in the UK. Approach: This proposal uses a mixed-methods approach to develop our understanding of the impact of rurality and deprivation on the MH of YP. In addition to examining linked, multinational, administrative healthcare data (Study 1) and longitudinal cohort study data (study 2), this Fellowship also includes complementary quantitative and qualitative studies (Studies 3 and 4). This approach will enable us to triangulate findings and provide a clearer understanding of the epidemiology and causal pathways to MH problems, service use and outcomes in this substantially under-researched population. Expected impact: This research will answer important questions on the impact of rurality and deprivation on the MH of YP. Outputs will address significant evidence gaps and the findings and recommendations will help to identify areas for further research and improve service planning and targeting of resources.

title: Germline susceptibility and immunometabolic pathways contributing to treatment-related neurotoxicity and neurocognitive outcomes in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
description: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the most common childhood cancer. Treatment-related neurological toxicity remains a substantial and potentially preventable burden. Approximately 10% of children experience acute central nervous system events, and up to 40% develop long-term neurocognitive impairment which impacts functional outcomes and quality of life. This project will investigate germline susceptibility and biological mechanisms underlying neurological sequelae in childhood ALL survivors. Aim 1 will use genome-wide association studies to identify germline variants associated with acute neurotoxicity and long-term cognitive outcomes. Polygenic risk scores will be integrated with treatment and environmental exposures to develop multivariable risk prediction models. Aim 2 will apply Mendelian randomization to explore the causal role of immune, inflammatory, and metabolic biomarkers in these outcomes. Aim 3 will analyse existing MRI data from ALL survivors and matched controls to map region-specific brain vulnerabilities. A feasibility pilot study using diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance spectroscopy will characterise persistent in vivo markers of chemotherapy-related neuroinflammation. Integrated analysis of germline genetics, causal biomarker pathways, and advanced neuroimaging across international cohorts will provide insight into the factors driving individual variation in treatment-related neurological toxicity. Findings have the potential to inform risk stratification and supportive care strategies within emerging treatment protocols.

title: A Physiotherapy-Led Service for Postnatal Women with Vaginal Prolapse
description: Vaginal prolapse is a bulge or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina. Up to 43% of women report severe symptoms at one year after childbirth. A prolapse can stop women doing normal activities and can interfere with emptying the bladder or bowel and can affect a woman’s sex life. Women with a prolapse are five times more likely to have postnatal depression. There are however problems for postnatal women: 1) Poorly designed care pathways can result in multiple trips to the doctor before being referred for pelvic floor muscle exercise, and again for a pessary. This causes frustration, delays treatment and wastes appointments. 2) Postnatal women with prolapse are not always offered a pessary. Interviews and a survey showed 82% of GPs will not offer a pessary. This is because a pessary is more often used to treat prolapse in older women and GPs lack training in fitting pessaries. A service designed by and for women with prolapse could provide more treatment options and allow women to make better-informed choices. This research aims to improve health outcomes for postnatal women by testing if a new service for postnatal women with prolapse is feasible and acceptable to women.

title: Innovating with Care: A Comparative Ethnography of Lived Experiences with Assistive Technologies and Evolving Practices of Care
description: Neurodegenerative disorders (ND) are progressive conditions impairing motor function and affecting life quality. As global populations age, their prevalence is rising, intensifying pressures on healthcare systems and caregivers. Assistive technologies (AT) are promoted as tools to help tackle these needs by enhancing care practices, yet limited user involvement and engagement in innovation processes often result in technologies that are neither inclusive nor useful. This research aims to understand the impact of AT on health and care provision by examining how notions of care are, or might be, embedded in technology development. It does so by drawing on multi-sited comparative ethnographic case studies in Japan, South Korea, Italy and the UK—four ageing countries where AT development is a strategic priority. Through an engaged research approach, it will involve technology developers and people with lived experiences of ND, ageing and care. It investigates how cultural values, care practices, and sociotechnical infrastructures shape AT design and use. It aims to: 1) advance theory and concepts in Science and Technology Studies on how care is embedded within technological innovation; 2) inform country-specific frameworks of responsible innovation by developing conceptual toolkits and methodologies to offer guidance for user engagement relevant to developers and policymakers.

title: Bicarbonate transport and intracellular pH homeostasis as a checkpoint for T‑cell function in acidic tissues
description: T cells must function in tissues where extracellular pH (pHe) becomes acidic in infection, inflammation and tumours – an environment that suppresses effector function even when antigen recognition is intact. As activation- driven glycolysis generates intracellular acid load, maintaining intracellular pH (pHi) may be a key bottleneck for tissue immunity. This programme will test whether sodium-coupled bicarbonate co-transporters (SLC4A7/NBCn1 and SLC4A10/NBCn2), acting with lactate/proton export and carbonic anhydrases, form an “immune acid-tolerance module” that sustains pH homeostasis, metabolism and effector programmes in human T cell subsets adapted to harsh environments, such as mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) and tissue- resident T cells. I will: (i) define causal transport mechanisms using live- cell pH imaging, genetic and pharmacological perturbation, and single-cell multi-omics under controlled acid stress; (ii) map acidic immune niches in human tissues and derive transferable pH-adaptation signatures using spatial transcriptomics and computational inference; and (iii) test proof-of-concept engineering strategies to enhance pH resilience in tissue-relevant models, including organoids and CAR-T systems. Outputs will include validated assays, an atlas of acidic immune niches, and prioritised targets for tuning immunity in acidic microenvironments. Keywords: intracellular pH, bicarbonate transport, SLC4A7, SLC4A10, MAIT cells, acid-base physiology, tissue immunity, spatial transcriptomics.

title: Pamoja Furaha: Integrating Group Interpersonal Therapy into maternal-child health services for perinatal adolescents in Kenya
description: Adolescent pregnancy rates remain high in Kenya, at approximately 20% of adolescents age 14-19. This group has disproportionately high risk of developing perinatal (pregnancy through first year after delivery) depression. We aim to develop and evaluate a perinatal depression treatment for adolescent girls age 14-19, integrated into maternal-child health services in Western Kenya. Our proposed intervention, Pamoja Furaha, includes (1) universal depression screening, (2) lay-delivered group interpersonal therapy, (3) measurement-based care, and (4) a bundle of implementation strategies to facilitate successful real-world implementation. Our team is comprised of Kenyan researchers in maternal-child health and mental health, a representative from Kenya’s national Ministry of Health, and experts in perinatal psychiatry, epidemiology and implementation science in the US. Foundation Phase: We will hold participatory workshops with national and county Ministries of Health, healthcare facility leadership, and lived experience experts, to formalize partnerships, agree on shared goals and priorities, and co-develop implementation strategies. Impact Phase: We will conduct an effectiveness-implementation hybrid cluster-randomized trial in 20 maternal-child health facilities in Homa Bay County. This low cost scalable package could extend across maternal-child health clinics throughout Kenya to improve mental health of adolescents and their infants.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: RISE (Regional Implementation and Scale-up of Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions)
description: We propose to scale-up WHO–UNICEF endorsed Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions-EASE programme across Pakistan’s four provincial tertiary child and adolescent mental health(CAMH) facilities. Building on strong efficacy evidence from two RCTs(Pakistan and Jordan), we will evaluate EASE’s real- world clinical, implementation and cost-effectiveness compared with Enhanced Treatment as Usual using a Hybrid-Type-I trial design. EASE will be delivered by supervised postgraduate psychiatry and psychology residents, enabling rapid CAMH workforce expansion by integration in established and structured training, supervision and delivery pathways. Alongside the trial, to ensure integration and scale-up, co-designed by our Lived-Experience (LE) experts we will a)nationally, establish a government-endorsed Hub of Excellence for CAMH to coordinate scale-up; b)regionally, host a Collaborative Learning Group and Regional Fellowship Programme in eight CAMHSAN countries (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka); and c)globally, co-develop a digital learning and knowledge-exchange hub using The Global Health Network(TGHN)’s Pathway to Impact framework to facilitate scale- up of CAMH psychotherapies and build scalable, youth-centred implementation capacity. LE youth will be embedded and co-lead governance, evaluation, and implementation, ensuring RISE delivers scalable, sustainable early intervention systems across Pakistan and South Asia. Keywords: EASE, active ingredients, implementation, (cost)-effectiveness evaluation, LE experts, task-shifting, regional and global scaling.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: SLFN11 in replication stress tolerance in cancer and therapy resistance
description: SLFN11 is silenced in ~50% of all cancers and is the strongest predictor of chemotherapy resistance. Since replication stress-inducing agents activate SLFN11 as a tRNA nuclease triggering translation shutdown and p53-independent apoptosis, we hypothesize that loss of this safeguarding mechanism confers replication stress tolerance and the emergence of therapy-resistance. Insights into the repertoire of SLFN11’s cellular functions, how it is activated by replication stress but constrained during normal DNA replication, why it is silenced in treatment naïve cancers and its role during tumour evolution and are currently unknown. We recently: 1) established that SLFN11 senses and is activated by unprotected ssDNA following RPA exhaustion, 2) discovered NSUN2 and FAM122A as co-factors that cooperate with SLFN11 to eliminate cells with heightened replication stress, 3) uncovered a non-canonical function of SLFN11 and NSUN2 independent of the SLFN11 tRNA nuclease activity and translation shutdown, and 4) implicated SLFN11 loss as a key determinant in the survival of ATRX deficient cells during telomere crisis and ALT establishment. Based on these discoveries, we propose a multi-disciplinary strategy using genetics, proteomics, biochemistry and biophysical approaches to interrogate the function(s) and regulation of SLFN11 in replication stress tolerance, with implications for cancer development and therapy resistance.

title: Safeguarding against division-induced damage in complex tissues
description: Pioneering work from myself and others has provided growing evidence that dividing cells are an underappreciated weak-point in proliferative tissues. This is because division temporary disrupts cytoskeletal structure, cell shape and adhesion, generating challenges when cells divide in multicellular contexts. Therefore, specific mechanisms are required to safeguard tissue architecture during proliferative growth, with severe consequences if these mechanisms fail. Critically, the nature of these challenges depends on the architecture and complexity of the tissue. As such, I have developed live imaging protocols to study cell division in 2 complex dynamic tissues, each with distinct architectures: 1) budding tissue growth, using the genetically tractable Drosophila air sac primordium and 2) vertebrate angiogenesis, using zebrafish intersegmental vessels. My key goals are to identify factors that play protective roles during/immediately after cell division, thereby unraveling the core mechanisms that safeguard complex tissue architectures against division-induced damage. Parallel investigations, in the above complementary systems, will determine if mechanisms are conserved across tissues and identify which architectural features are particulary susceptible to division-induced damage. Longer-term, this work will be relevant to several disease states, including the loss of tissue organisation/integrity seen during tumour initiation, cell dispersal during metastasis and vascular diseases associated with excessive division.

title: Temporary Childbirth Migration and Reproductive Justice: Reconceptualising Continuity of Maternal and Child Healthcare in Rural India
description: In many South-Asian societies, including India, pregnant women often relocate to their natal homes during the third trimester of pregnancy and stay for several months post-childbirth. While this practice often provides the much- needed care, rest and emotional support for mother and child(ren); it can potentially hinder service provision continuity during a critical monitoring and intervention period. This study examines how temporary childbirth migration(TCM) shapes maternal and child healthcare (MCH)service-provision in two Jammu- Kashmir rural districts. Employing a participatory qualitative longitudinal design, the study follows 40 pregnant women from late pregnancy through six-months postpartum to document changing expectations, experiences of care, and pathways of healthcare access across natal and marital settings. Rooted in reproductive-justice framework, the research adopts a polyvocal methodology that pairs women’s narratives with interviews from key care-givers and stakeholders to understand the differences in healthcare across natal/marital households; the socio-economic,and cultural-costs of postnatal care;and variations in duration of stay, and rest afforded to women depending upon the gender of the newborn. By situating TCM at the intersection of gender,kinship,and health- systems-the fellowship will generate transferable insights to inform equitable health-system responses that strengthen healthcare continuity for migrants and improve overall MCH outcomes in resource-constrained settings.

title: Mesoscale MRI in the living brain with simultaneous multi-contrast encoding
description: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a crucial tool for examining the living brain in health and disease non-invasively. However, we cannot achieve the kind of spatial resolution which is available with microscopes: neuroimaging data typically has voxel dimensions of approximately one millimetre, and anything much smaller than this is difficult to resolve - let alone quantify accurately - due to motion during acquisition. This misses important opportunities for capturing early changes in neurodegenerative diseases (e.g. Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s), where pathology is evident in sub-millimetre nuclei tens of years before symptoms emerge. In this proposal, I put forward a series of technical developments in the way that we can acquire and reconstruct images from MRI scanners. They take advantage of signals that are usually ignored or discarded during the acquisition process, and with an understanding of the underlying physics, turn them into free additional sources of information about tissue microstructure and brain motion. I plan to exploit this additional information to develop new approaches which make MRI more efficient and motion-robust, before applying these in some of the world’s most powerful systems. With this, I aim to extend the achievable spatial resolution of quantitative MRI in the living brain to the limits of feasibility.

title: EPIC – start-up funding
description: The EPIC project is being submitted as an application for a Wellcome discretionary award. It aims to (a) assess the prevalence of resistance to drugs used in rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) regimens in 6 key countries across South America, Africa and Asia, to (b) investigate why people fail RR- TB treatment and why drug-resistance may thereby emerge, and (c) to investigate the clinical implications of mutations in genes associated with phenotypic resistance to drugs in RR-TB regimens. EPIC is an ambitious project and the start-up funds are being requested to pay the salary of an experienced research co-ordinator at OUCRU, Vietnam, from January 2026 until EPIC is funded. They will navigate the EPIC project through the process of obtaining permissions and thereby bring the start-date of recruitment in Vietnam forwards significantly. The current source of their salary expires at the end of December. Secondly, the start-up funds would pay for the EPIC PI to visit Vietnam for in-person meetings with the local hospital and the National TB Programme that are essential to align with stake holders in Vietnam.

title: The hidden code in the coding sequence: how embedded features impact protein function
description: The redundancy in the genetic code, with 61 codons encoding only 20 amino acids, means that multiple coding-sequences can encode the same protein and not all mutations result in altered amino acid sequences. While these “synonymous” mutations have long been overlooked, emerging evidence shows that this redundancy carries hidden regulatory information that can influence ribosome speed and, in turn, protein expression and function. Understanding this “hidden-layer” of regulation is critical for identifying disease- associated synonymous mutations and for improving mRNA therapeutic design. For example, current mRNA therapies utilise optimal codons, as these are most efficiently translated by ribosomes, but my data suggests non-optimal codons impart important regulatory information that controls co-translational processes. Here, reporter assays, advanced microscopy and transcriptome-wide approaches will be used to investigate how codon optimality shapes protein function. Novel assays to quantify co-translational complex assembly will reveal critical sequence elements and regulatory factors. Live-cell imaging will demonstrate how mRNAs that encode interacting proteins find each other within the cell, and the consequence of specific synonymous mutations on protein function will be investigated. Finally, how ribosome speed influences the fate of nascent proteins will be examined, using direct RNA-sequencing to understand how RNA modifications regulate this process.

title: PATHS – Psychedelics as Therapeutics: Harm Reduction and Safety
description: We are world leaders in researching substance use development, psychedelic pharmacology, and drug stigma, but we do not yet know precisely how millions of vulnerable people worldwide are using psychedelics as medicines outside formal medical systems — nor how to make this safer. This is urgent: individuals experiencing mental health crises are using psychedelics in unregulated settings lacking therapeutic support and safeguards, facing risks from uncertain supply, criminal networks, exploitation, and poorly-processed difficult experiences. Marginalised populations bear disproportionate risks. For many, the choice is understood as ‘legally dead or illegally alive’. This UK-focused discovery programme, through unprecedented partnerships with hard- to-reach communities — cluster headache patients, police using psychedelics for occupational trauma, festival crisis intervention providers — will investigate emergent, informal therapeutic psychedelic use outside legal and medical jurisdictions during the critical transitional period before anticipated approval. We will deliver a paradigmatic step-change in psychedelic harm reduction scholarship by shifting focus from institutional clinical trials to lay therapeutic practices. We will discover what harms users encounter, and evaluate which community-led innovations work or fail. Understanding these practices and consolidating fragmented grassroots knowledge will have transformative potential for the lives, health, and wellbeing of those driven to engage in therapeutic psychedelic use.

title: Mechanisms and impact of antifungal and dual-purpose effectors delivered by the Type VI secretion system
description: Microorganisms live in polymicrobial communities shaped by competitive interactions between their members. These interactions are key determinants of human microbiota composition and health. Many bacteria use Type VI secretion systems (T6SSs) to deliver antibacterial effectors (toxins) into competitor bacterial cells. We revealed previously that T6SSs also deploy specific antifungal effectors against fungal competitors. Subsequent work has shown that T6SS-mediated antifungal activity is widespread, that antifungal effectors display novel antifungal biology, and that some function as ‘dual- purpose’ effectors which also target other kingdoms. However, few antifungal effectors have been characterised and large knowledge gaps remain regarding delivery, spectrum-of-activity and real-life-impact. Here, we will use our cross-disciplinary expertise to elucidate the mechanisms and impact of antifungal and dual-purpose T6SS effectors, from molecular detail to complex microbial communities. Specifically, we will: expand the repertoire of antifungal and dual-purpose T6SS effectors and determine the spectrum-of-T6SS- activity against fungal and other eukaryotic microbes; define the mode-of- action and determinants of fungal compatibility for these effectors; and determine potential contributions of antifungal T6SSs and effectors to complex polymicrobial communities and future translational applications. Fungal pathogens represent a critical global-healthcare challenge. Elucidating how T6SSs operate as biological antifungal weapons and shape health-relevant microbial communities should inform future antifungal strategies.

title: Sensitising brain MRI to cell type and shape
description: We propose to sensitise brain MRI to cell type numbers and shapes or morphologies. The goal in each case is to achieve cell specificity. We will do so by (1) enhancing diffusion MRS to provide tissue microstructure intracellularly to distinguish between neuronal, astrocyte, and microglia morphology, by (2) combining high resolution diffusion and quantitative MRI with 2D and 3D microscopy and spatial transcriptomics to generate models that can predict cell distribution, and by (3) developing novel molecular MRI contrasts that provide cell or molecule specific signatures read out through the widely used BOLD signal. Each of these three classes of methods will be important on their own, but it is in their integration that we expect to achieve cellular specificity and spatial resolution in vivo. At the end of the eight year project we will have significantly advanced our ability to use MRI as a cell-specific readout of brain architecture and provided key insights into how variation in the cellular architecture of the brain leads to variation in risk and resilience in mental health.

title: Disentangling the diverse forms of collective protein homeostasis in neuronal condensates
description: This project will interrogate interstasis, a mechanism for collective dosage regulation of co-condensing proteins that contain specific types of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Interstasis involves a collective feedback loop, where mRNAs that encode for the co-condensing proteins are captured into the same condensate as these proteins. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrated how interstasis at nuclear speckles collectively regulates the proteins with mix-charged IDRs by capturing their own mRNAs into speckles. Here we will assess whether similar feedback loops regulate additional types of IDR-containing proteins in various condensates. We will identify key RNA- binding proteins and RNA signatures that are important for each type of interstasis. Ultimately, we will determine the biological roles of interstasis in the context of various physiological shifts, stress responses and aging. We’ll use small molecule screening to determine the cellular pathways that can modulate interstatic mechanisms, and will thereby study the crosstalk between RNA and protein-mediated proteostatic pathways. Finally, we will combine genetic and environmental variation in neurons to assess the functions of interstasis in protection from stress and aging, and to demonstrate its physiologic roles in protein homeostasis.

title: Evidence of AI in Health (EVAH) Initiative - J-PAL and APHRC
description: Under the Real World Evidence Platform (RWEP), J-PAL will design and deliver a competitive funding process for randomized evaluations in low- and lower- middle income countries that: 1) examines whether clinical AI tools improve real-world health outcomes; 2) tests innovations that increase effective AI tool adoption, use, and integration into health systems; and 3) advances methodological innovations to ensure evaluations keep pace with AI development. J-PAL will manage the portfolio for project success. J-PAL will develop a rigorous, policy-relevant evaluation pipeline by cultivating research partnerships through matchmaking and project development, two evaluation incubator workshops, and a regional scholars program. J-PAL will enable RWEP evidence use nationally and regionally through partnerships integrating evidence into partners’ initiatives, scaling support, and evidence synthesis and dissemination. Within Africa, the African Population and Health Research Center (APHRC) will be a close partner for advancing RWEP’s goals. We describe expected areas for collaboration below, and activities that APHRC will lead independently including i) developing an atlas of AI tools in Africa, ii) conducting regulatory scoping to document policies and frameworks on AI governance, adoption and evaluation, iii) additional evaluation capacity building for African researchers, and iv) evidence dissemination at institutional and continental levels.

title: Novel peptide sequences for co-translational separation of a polyprotein
description: 2A peptides mediate co-translational separation of a polyprotein via a mechanism known as "ribosome skipping" or "StopGo". These ~30 amino acid peptides, with a common C-terminal motif (D/G/C/N)(V/I)ExNPGP, adopt a specific conformation within the translating ribosome that prevents peptide bond formation between the C-terminal glycine-proline, but instead releases the nascent peptide and, additionally, allows translation to continue with near-100% efficiency. 2A is widely used in research and biotechnology but, since its discovery some three decades ago, no other groups of peptides with this activity have been found, until now. We recently identified seven new classes of peptide with StopGo activity but radically different sequence motifs. We aim to characterise the occurrence, function and mechanism of action of the new peptides using bioinformatics, molecular biology and cryoEM. This will provide extraordinary new insights into nascent-peptide-mediated mechanisms of ribosome manipulation, and elucidate the general principals that define the specific activity of StopGo peptides. From a biotechnological perspective, it is critical to have alternatives to traditional 2A peptides, as the N- and C-terminal fragments that remain appended to target proteins can interfere with protein function, stability or localisation. Our research will provide a vastly increased repertoire of StopGo peptides from which to select.

title: Redefining how flaviviruses build infectious virions
description: Flaviviruses including dengue (DENV) and Zika (ZIKV) pose escalating global health threats, yet how infectious virions form within host cells remains poorly understood. While the canonical model depicts sequential assembly along the secretory pathway, our recent discoveries challenge this linear model, revealing that flaviviruses generate specialised "morphogenesis hubs"‒distinct ER/ERGIC-derived compartments enriched in GTPases, membrane-shaping proteins, and lipid-transfer machinery that recruit cholesteryl-ester-enriched lipid droplets (CE-LDs). We propose that these hubs couple lipid metabolism with virion assembly and are the predominant sites of infectious particle formation. This proposal employs spatial proteomics (LOPIT-DC), cryo-electron tomography, live-imaging, and targeted lipidomics across physiologically relevant iPSC-derived cells to: (1) resolve the molecular composition and assembly dynamics of morphogenesis hubs; (2) dissect how remodelled lipid droplets supply envelope lipids to morphogenesis hubs, driving virion infectivity; and (3) define viral adaptations in structural proteins (prM/E, capsid) and 3'UTR motifs that optimise hub exploitation, enhancing epidemic fitness. By reframing infectious virion formation as hub-centric morphogenesis, this work will expose druggable virus-host interfaces with broad-spectrum antiviral potential while illuminating fundamental mechanisms of inter-organelle lipid transport and virus-induced compartment biogenesis. Beyond flaviviruses, this framework provides a roadmap for dissecting virion biogenesis across diverse membrane-remodelling viruses including coronaviruses and alphaviruses.

title: Defining T and B-cell correlates of viral control for tissue-optimised, vaccine-guided immunotherapy
