description: Sustained adaptive immune control of hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a crucial unmet therapeutic goal and an informative paradigm for overcoming constraints imposed by high antigen load and the tolerogenic liver niche. Research from our lab and others is defining targets to recapitulate spontaneous HBV ‘functional cure’. We hypothesise that consolidating molecular correlates from unique ‘HBV controller’ blood and liver samples will refine selection for mechanistic testing, applying a novel strategy of vaccine-guided, tissue- adapted and antigen-specific immunotherapy. We aim to: (1) Discover functionally-relevant T and B-cell correlates of control in acute and chronic- resolving HBV, exploring distinct liver-compartmentalised contributions; (2) Dissect defective T-B-cell cross-talk in infection, and in lymphoid tissue responses to existing therapeutic vaccines, to direct coordinated immune boosting; (3) Design and refine a novel immunotherapeutic approach using antibody-signposted lipid nanoparticles to co-deliver mRNAs for costimulants and HBV antigens to professional antigen-presenting-cells; we will test the capacity to achieve immunogenic T and B-cell lymphoid priming, and for intravenous boosting to amplify and re-programme intrahepatic responses for long-lived immunosurveillance. This programme will discover functional components of HBV adaptive immune control and test their recapitulation with vaccine-immunogen-guided, tissue-optimised immunotherapy. Conceptual advances will be of broad relevance to hepatotropic pathogens and tumours.

title: DHIS2: Digital infrastructure empowering the health sector to use climate information for decision making in LMICs
description: We leverage DHIS2 systems in low- and middle-income countries and open-source climate-health and predictive modeling tools to strengthen the use of climate services by the health sector for climate resilience and adaptation. We do this through supporting locally owned digital infrastructure, participatory action research, designing with users, and capacity building within countries, coupled with global sharing of knowledge and reusable solutions. The HISP Centre at University of Oslo works hand-in-hand with 23 local HISP groups based in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Europe and government partners to accelerate the effective use of climate services. Guided by national health adaptation plans, our project empowers national health sector decision-makers to enhance early warning systems for climate-sensitive infectious diseases; incorporate predictive modeling into routine climate-health decision making; mitigate health impacts of extreme weather events on vulnerable communities; prepare for climate impacts on food security and nutrition; and facilitate climate vulnerability assessments for improved health infrastructure, planning and resource prioritization. Strategic local and global partnerships seek to fill gaps in climate health data and digital modeling infrastructure, expand the flexibility of DHIS2 tools to support a wide range of climate and health needs, and help bring targeted interventions to scale within and across countries.

title: The Role of Public R&D; Funding in Driving Innovation and Access - supporting the Pandemic Agreement
description: The adoption of the WHO Pandemic Agreement represents a major milestone in strengthening global pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response. Article 9 of the Agreement focuses on research and development (R&D), aiming to ensure that countries are better equipped to respond rapidly and equitably to future health emergencies. Article 9.5, a binding provision, establishes a principle that public R&D funding should be conditional on access, affordability, transparency, and knowledge sharing. This project, led by the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi), seeks to support the operationalisation of Article 9.5 by working with public R&D funders and governments to translate these principles into practical policy and funding models. Drawing on DNDi’s two decades of experience in needs-driven innovation and equitable access, the initiative will help ensure that public investments in health R&D deliver meaningful public health benefits, particularly for low- and middle-income countries. The programme includes three workstreams: (1) convening a collaborative group of public R&D funders; (2) mapping and analysing existing practices to build an evidence base; (3) developing and promoting high-level principles and model policies. Keywords: public R&D funding, equitable access, Pandemic Agreement, Article 9.5, global health, research policy, access conditions, health equity

title: Teacher-Delivered Short-Term Group-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Programme to Tackle Depression in Adolescents in West Africa (Ghana, Nigeria & Sierra Leone)
description: Adolescent depression poses a substantial public health burden in West Africa. This study aims to scale up a school-based, teacher-delivered group Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (group-CBT) programme for adolescents (aged 13–18) with early-stage depression (PHQ-9 ≥ 10), building on interventions that have been developed and evaluated for efficacy by the Centre for Child and Adolescent Mental Health (CCAMH), University of Ibadan. The implementation of the intervention in Ghana, Nigeria, and Sierra Leone will be led by CCAMH alumni who set up pioneering CAMH services in these countries. Teachers will be trained to deliver manualized, five-session group-CBT programme focusing on psychoeducation, behavioural activation, cognitive restructuring, spiritual integration, and relaxation techniques. This is a hybrid effectiveness–implementation study. The foundation phase will focus on co- adapting the intervention using the ADAPT-ITT framework and engaging stakeholders, including implementation partners and persons with lived experiences, to foster sustainable partnerships and strengthen capacity for the subsequent impact phase. Multisectoral implementation partnerships and economic evaluation models will be developed. The impact phase features a cluster-randomized controlled trial to assess clinical effectiveness, cost- effectiveness, fidelity, acceptability and appropriateness. This study will provide a scalable, evidence-based model to tackle adolescent depression in West Africa.
recipient: College of Medicine, University of Ibadan
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: ACCELERATING POLICY ACTION FOR A FUTURE WITH SUSTAINABLE ACCESS AND USE OF ANTIMICROBIALS FOR ALL
description: In support of its ultimate objective–sustainable access and use of antimicrobials for all–the AMR Policy Accelerator (the Accelerator) is guided by two key aims: 1) To strengthen antimicrobial resistance (AMR) global governance structures that integrate equity and intersectoral/One Health principles and accelerate AMR action globally. 2) To advance evidence-informed AMR policy decisions at the national level with a focus on the context- specific needs of low and middle-income countries. By combining rigorous interdisciplinary policy research, open access policymaking tools and training, and an external communications structure that ensures timely and effective reach to the right audience at the right time, the Accelerator gives decision makers the resources they need to develop and implement evidence- informed policies to address AMR. Since 2022, the Accelerator’s work has gained significant national and global traction, and this momentum will be amplified through continued research and strategic collaboration in the coming years. The Accelerator will support the establishment of a robust Independent Panel for Evidence for Action against AMR (IPEA) as an integral part of a nimble and effective global governance system for implementing the Global Action Plan and advancing the 2024 United Nations Political Declaration on AMR.

title: Decoding early life exposure and immunity to Streptococcus pyogenes
description: Streptococcus pyogenes (Strep A) causes 500,000 deaths annually, largely through immune sequelae leading to Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). Vaccine development is hindered by limited understanding of natural immunity and correlates of protection. How infant exposure patterns common in LMICs (skin infections, high antigenic diversity, intense early-life exposure) shape protective and maladaptive immunity remains unclear. We will address three fundamental questions: What antibody responses correlate with protection against Strep A skin and pharyngeal events? Why does intense early-life exposure in high-burden settings fail to generate early protective immunity? Does priming for RHD begin in infancy, and which exposure patterns drive these pathological immune profiles? We will leverage multiple well-characterised cohorts and establish a new birth cohort in The Gambia with an embedded azithromycin intervention altering early colonisation, to define how distinct exposure profiles shape immune development. Whole-proteome multiplex serology combined with statistical and machine-learning approaches will reconstruct individual immune trajectories, identify early biomarkers linked to RHD risk, and map how cumulative Strep A exposures shape protective and pathological immunity. Our programme will transform understanding of early-life Strep A immunity in high-burden settings, generating insight to inform vaccination and prevention strategies against RHD worldwide.

title: Decoding adaptive-like γδ T-cell recognition in human herpesvirus infection
description: Our work has revised understanding of human γδ T-cells, establishing that in addition to innate-like subsets, the compartment unexpectedly includes a major adaptive-like component. Adaptive-like γδ T-cells are an evolutionarily ancient, MHC-unrestricted arm that acts as ‘Nature’s CAR-T-cells’, driving protection against pathogens and tumours. However, an understanding of how changes denoting infection and cancer are ‘encoded’ in antigenic ligands, and how such alterations are ‘deciphered’ by the γδ-TCR - a holy grail in the field - is currently lacking. This proposal focusses a multidisciplinary collaborative team on tackling this challenge, exploiting Cytomegalovirus and Epstein Barr Virus as human models of microbial stress. Leveraging virology, γδ T-cell immunobiology, ligand identification, and molecular skillsets, we will define how γδ-TCRs sense virally-induced signatures of ‘altered-self’ and how this relates to γδ TCR-mediated recognition of ‘transformed-self’. Our programme will profoundly shift current paradigms of γδ T-cell immunobiology, establishing adaptive subsets as sophisticated sensors of stress-induced ligand alterations. Collectively, it will reveal new molecular targets, uncover distinct principles of TCR/ligand recognition, and define novel antigen-specific γδ-TCR clonotypes. In doing so, the outcomes will create a platform for development of new classes of γδ-TCR-based biotherapeutics and engineered cellular therapies with broad applicability for infection and cancer.

title: Validating novel, selective CaV2.3 inhibitors as oral, small molecule therapies for posttraumatic stress disorder
description: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a prevalent mental health condition with significant unmet medical need. Over 5% of trauma-exposed adults worldwide develop PTSD during their lifetimes, with those exposed to certain types of trauma such as combat and assault carrying a particularly high burden. The few approved drug treatments (e.g. paroxetine and sertraline) have limited efficacy and significant side effects. A recently published multi-ancestry meta-analysis of genetic data from >1 million individuals exposed to trauma reported significant risk of PTSD associated with the CACNA1E gene which encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel (CaV2.3) with high expression in brain areas (hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex) involved in memory, emotional regulation, and stress response. Genome-wide analyses of transcription indicated that the highest risk alleles are linked to significantly higher expression of CACNA1E, suggesting that inhibition of CaV2.3 function has potential therapeutic benefit. Lario Therapeutics has developed first-in-class, small molecule inhibitors of CaV2.3 which are potent, selective, and brain-penetrant. This collaborative proposal aims to validate CaV2.3 as a target for PTSD and to test potential CaV2.3-targeted therapeutics in mouse models of PTSD including stress-induced alterations in anxiety, fear conditioning and in paradigms showing learned flexibility of instinctual fear behaviours.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: Addressing everyday ethical tensions in global mental health task-sharing
description: Global Mental Health task-sharing (GMH-TS) involves redistributing tasks from mental health specialists to community-based health workers, or to lay “helpers”. It is heralded globally as a flagship innovation that increases access to effective and contextually appropriate mental healthcare. In everyday practice GMH-TS generates ethical tensions embedded in the epistemic, relational, and moral demands of delivering mental healthcare in local communities. These ethical tensions both motivate the unique strengths of GMH- TS, whilst raising potential distress and harms for those engaging with this form of care. Currently, GMH-TS lacks robust empirical and conceptual understandings, and practice-based approaches, to recognise and respond to such ethical tensions. I will address this through empirical bioethics research co-developed with collaborators in Pakistan and Ethiopia. Ethnographic and qualitative research will explore the ethical tensions arising in three diverse GMH-TS case studies: (1) individual manualised psychosocial support intervention, (2) expert-by-experience peer-support groups, and (3) religious and traditional healer collaborative care with specialists. Research will examine the ethical values GMH-TS embodies and invokes, the ‘goods’ it offers, and the suffering it provokes. This study will transform our understanding and practice of GMH-TS by generating significant theoretical advances, and developing practice-based resources for responding to the ethical tensions GMH-TS creates.

title: Scaling delivery of Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) and the NETFacts community model for young survivors of gender-based violence in Guinea
description: The adolescent mental health burden is increasing, particularly among survivors of gender-based violence (GBV), who face a higher risk of Post- Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). In Guinea, where 48% of people are under 18, GBV is pervasive and existing support focuses on physical health. Our previous work revealed major gaps in mental health care due to a lack of trained professionals. Addressing this will enable early intervention, which is critical to improve long-term mental health outcomes for young people. The proposed solution is training local practitioners in Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET), a scalable trauma-focused treatment effective in low-resource settings, and its community-based variant, NETfacts. NETfacts offers individual treatment with community reconciliation, reducing stigma and improving long-term outcomes. This study will test if NET/NETfacts provides an effective, low-cost, scalable intervention for young GBV survivors in Guinea. Our partnership—UCL, UNFPA, CJFLG, Guinean Health Ministry, vivo (NETfacts developers) and Universities of Conakry and Konstanz —will develop and evaluate this approach. During the Foundation Phase, the team, youth with lived experience, and stakeholders will co-design the adapted intervention for Guinea, the implementation and scale-up plan using UNFPA/CJFLG’s networks and a robust methodology to assess effectiveness and economic feasibility.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: Towards a Scalable Early Intervention System for Youth Depression and Anxiety in Indonesia.
description: This Foundation Award will establish research and delivery infrastructure for a scalable, culturally adapted early intervention programme for adolescent depression and anxiety in Indonesia. Co-led with young people and lived experience contributors, the programme prioritises inclusive design, creative engagement, and community-based delivery. This preparatory work will enable a future impact study to expand early access to Behavioural Activation (BA)—a WHO-recommended psychological intervention that targets inactivity and avoidance, core mechanisms of depression and anxiety. BA’s simplicity, adaptability, and strong evidence base make it well-suited for delivery by trained lay health workers in low-resource settings, ensuring feasibility and sustainability. Three work packages will guide this foundation programme: WP1 (Empower) will build inclusive research capacity through training, translated resources, and digital tools to support meaningful participation. WP2 (Prepare) will co-develop youth-informed research infrastructure using creative methods and plan stigma-reduction strategies. WP3 (Develop) will strengthen strategic partnerships and collaborative governance. We will also identify culturally relevant, age-appropriate screening tools for early detection of depression and anxiety, ensuring practicality in low-resource contexts. Lived experience leadership will shape all stages, with arts-based activities—such as youth-led films, exhibitions, and plans for a co-created serial drama—amplifying youth voices, reducing stigma, and promoting help- seeking.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: Cluster-randomised hybrid type 2 effectiveness-implementation trial and economic evaluation of a school-based problem-solving intervention for adolescent depression and anxiety: Co-design and trial preparation in Rajasthan, India
description: Adolescent depression and anxiety are prevalent in India but effective early interventions are scarce. Problem-solving is a common component of evidence- based programmes for both conditions, teaching individuals to identify tractable stressors, generate solutions, and test chosen options. Prior research in New Delhi showed that “Step 1,” a low-cost, school-based problem- solving intervention, reduced mental health symptoms, including internalising difficulties, up to 12-month follow-up. This proposal’s Foundation Phase will adapt Step 1 for secondary schools in Rajasthan, India’s largest state. Intervention materials, supervision and training will be updated for local relevance. We will also co-design a foundational implementation support package, build local partnerships, and finalise a trial protocol to enable rigorous evaluation of experimental implementation strategies. The Impact Phase will test two discrete implementation strategies using a type 2 hybrid effectiveness–implementation trial with a 2×2 factorial design. One comparison will examine the original multi-session programme against a single-session version that has potential to increase efficiency and reach. The other will compare delivery by external lay counsellors versus delivery by existing school staff to assess outcomes across workforce models. Findings will establish scalable, sustainable approaches for delivering Step 1 and inform broader implementation of early mental health interventions across India and beyond.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: Molecular annotation of the Drosophila connectome by optimised expansion microscopy
description: Our recent collaborative work has produced connectomes (synaptic resolution wiring diagrams) for the Drosophila central nervous system – the first for an animal that can walk (or fly) with complex visual, motor and cognitive behaviour. We have also identified over 11,400 cell types within these electron microscopy (EM) connectomes, defining their conserved neural circuit architecture. However, only a few hundred of these cell types have been molecularly characterised as far as the genes they express. Moreover, the precise positioning along neurites of key signalling molecules such as gap junctions, fast acting neurotransmitters and neuropeptides and their receptors is a crucial determinant of circuit function, but this information is largely unknown. We propose to optimise new expansion microscopy methods that use total protein staining to label neuronal ultrastructure with EM-like contrast in samples physically expanded up to 30x. This super-resolution approach will allow key signalling proteins and RNA transcripts to be localised within individual neurons and to obtain the complete morphology of all neurons within a brain. In Drosophila, neuronal morphologies can be directly matched across brains so this will enable molecular annotation of the connectome. We will focus on Drosophila but the pipeline will be applicable in other species.

title: From Pigment To Pattern: Mechanisms Shaping Foveal Specialisation
description: No treatments exist for disorders that arrest foveal development, leaving many children partially sighted or registered blind. This arrest, termed foveal hypoplasia (FH), is most common in pigmentation disorders like albinism. The mechanistic link between melanin synthesis and foveal specialisation remains unclear, preventing therapeutic development. I hypothesise that disrupted L-DOPA/GPR143 signalling and subsequent downstream pathways drive FH pathogenesis. To address this, I have developed zebrafish models that faithfully recapitulate human foveal architecture. This programme will dissect FH mechanisms in vivo using novel FH zebrafish models. Using single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial multi-omics, I will map cell-type-specific transcriptional changes and metabolic gradients within developing foveal tissue, defining the signalling hierarchy governing foveal specialisation. Through targeted pharmacological screening of identified pathway nodes, I will determine critical developmental windows for intervention. Bespoke ultra-high- resolution retinal imaging will enable unprecedented cellular-level phenotyping of human FH patients, directly translating mechanistic insights from models to patients. This integrated programme, combining genetic models, multi-omics approaches, and advanced clinical imaging, will establish the molecular logic underpinning foveal development and identify actionable targets for early-life intervention in children with FH.

title: A lost generation? Scaling iPDT to transform mental health outcomes for young people (age 16-25) in the UK
description: NHS-Talking Therapies (NHS-TT) is among the largest mental health service providers in the UK, receiving 1.82 million referrals in 2023/24. Yet the 16–25-year-old group has the poorest outcomes of all those referred to NHS-TT. Our vision is to improve engagement and outcomes for young people aged 16-25 seeking help with low mood. We aim for a stepped change in reach, impact, equity and sustainability by integrating an evidence-based, scalable digital intervention, designed by and for young people, into NHS-TT. During the Foundation Phase we will partner with key stakeholders, including young people, researchers, NHS services, policymakers, technology and implementation scientists to understand and plan how to embed internet-based psychodynamic therapy (iPDT), an evidence-based, guided self-help programme, into NHS-TT. The aim is to overcome barriers to young people receiving effective help. Working with our partners we will plan the Impact Phase to: (1) evaluate whether iPDT leads to higher levels of engagement, retention and impact in young people referred to NHS-TT services, (2) collect data to determine iPDT’s economic impact, including reduced onward referrals to higher-cost services, and (3) develop detailed plans for implementation and scalability. This project is a real-world transformation initiative with a clear route to sustained impact.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: eLife Pathways: Building a collaborative open science ecosystem with integrated technology and services
description: The promise of open science publishing to revolutionise scholarly communication is hindered by significant technology, knowledge and expertise gaps. While the research community is eager for more open, transparent, and efficient ways to share research, there are a lack of suitable alternatives to the traditional, journal-centric publishing system, which stifles innovation and perpetuates inequitable knowledge sharing and participation. A major part of this problem is the lack of coordination among scholarly open-source infrastructure providers, which is preventing the building of foundational, robust infrastructure that benefits the entire scholarly community. To address this shortfall eLife proposes to establish a new independent initiative called eLife Pathways, to focus on building a diverse and inclusive publishing ecosystem for all. By strengthening existing and establishing new collaborations, we will serve the community to co-create a scholarly communication ecosystem where research is assessed responsibly, knowledge is shared equitably, and innovation thrives. We will deliver (i) community- validated enhancements to our existing software connecting it with key open- source infrastructures to accelerate adoption and improve ecosystem interoperability, (ii) co-develop an open-source tool that enables any journal in the world to produce high-quality, standards-compliant JATS XML and (iii) provide technology and expert support to advance critical community projects.

title: Structural and mechanistic basis of tunnelling nanotube mediated intercellular mitochondrial transfer
description: Biological tissues have traditionally been viewed as assemblies of autonomous cells but emerging evidence shows that fundamental organelles can be dynamically shared between cells, reshaping tissues into integrated, responsive systems rather than isolated cellular units. In particular, intercellular mitochondrial transfer (IMT) has been shown to occur both physiologically during development and pathologically in cancer. One of the major pathways by which this happens is via tunnelling nanotubes (TNTs), long actin-based cellular protrusions that connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. Despite the widespread implications of TNT-mediated IMT, the structural and mechanistic basis of this phenomenon is largely uncharacterised, creating a major bottleneck in the field. I will address these gaps in knowledge by firstly using cryo-FIB milling and cryo-ET to investigate the architecture of the mitochondrial transport machinery in TNTs and the structural basis of cell-TNT junctions. Secondly, I will leverage an IMT assay I developed to identify the signalling pathways that induce TNT-mediated IMT. Finally, I will characterise the in vivo functions of TNT-mediated IMT during zebrafish development. Together, this project will establish the fundamental principles of TNT-mediated IMT, changing our understanding of cells as autonomous units and laying the groundwork for therapeutic exploitation of this phenomenon.

title: Scaling up Problem Management Plus to Young Adults experiencing marginalization in Lebanon and Palestine – a initiative by and for young adults
description: Our proposal focuses on young adults-YA (18-30 years old) with symptoms of anxiety or depression, living in contexts of war, uncertainty, displacement in Lebanon and Palestine. YA exhibit higher rates of mental health distress than younger peers but are rarely the focus of interventions. Contexts of war/uncertainty/displacement increase distress. Yet, there are not enough licensed mental health providers to meet needs. We want to implement Problem Management Plus (PM+), an early-intervention community-based psychological intervention. PM+ works to decrease anxiety and depression by using strategies like problem-solving, stress management, taking action, and strengthening social support. A unique aspect of our application: YA without current distress will be trained to give PM+ to their peers. Our implementation partners include government mental health programs, a UN agency, NGOs that provide mental health programs, and Justice for Mental Health, a lived/living experience NGO in Lebanon. We will use the Foundation phase to include a Palestinian lived experience organization. This range of implementation partners will help us understand what works best to scale-up PM+. Plans for meaningful involvement of persons with lived experience will be developed by lived experience NGOs. The Foundation phase builds trusting relationships amongst the whole team and co-designs the impact phase.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: i3c BRIC-RCB PhD Program in Biosciences
description: i3c BRIC-RCB PhD Program is an innovative initiative,offering cohesive, interdisciplinary research training designed to train the next-generation of bioscience leaders. This program replaces the conventional single-student- supervisor-laboratory PhD training to a team-based, inter-institutional research model. It aims to develop a cohort of highly skilled, competitive and driven researchers, adept at tackling both current and futuristic scientific challenges. A key highlight of the program is an enriching ‘on field immersion’ offering experiential learning. After six months of coursework and advanced instrumentation training at RCB, students spend three months in the field, often in rural or underserved settings. This training bridges the gap between lab research and real-world problems. By engaging directly with grassroots communities and societal issues, scholars gain a deeper understanding of scientific challenges and are inspired to use their research to create impactful solutions. Proposal seeks grant in aid for logistics and travel support during immersion training for the entire annual cohort of 250+ students of iBRIC+. A nominal support to immersion partners is proposed to acknowledge and support their role in delivering this critical on-field experience.This discretionary award will thus fund the immersion training for all PhD scholars, enabling equitable access to high-quality experiential learning across the iBRIC+ network.

title: Improving mental health among UK adolescents through a school-based sleep intervention
description: This project will prepare to test the efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and scalable delivery of a sleep intervention to treat adolescent depression and anxiety by building on an established, evidence-based sleep programme, utilising existing school mental health delivery structures, and by strengthening links with implementing partners. The sleep need in young people with mental health problems is high, unmet, and likely to impact on ability to benefit from other interventions. Sleep interventions have proven efficacy to improve symptoms of anxiety and depression alongside broader positive impacts on mental health and functioning. We will address the key knowledge gap of how to implement a sleep intervention across Mental Health Support Teams in Schools (MHSTs) in the UK. We have 3 objectives: 1) To create a sustainable partnership between researchers, stakeholders, and implementation partners. 2) To generate study protocols for the intervention and trial design, as well as co-designing effective recruitment, measurement, and data collection processes. 3) To prepare for a cluster-randomised controlled trial of a Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) programme “The Better Sleep Programme” on depression and anxiety in MHSTs. These foundational activities will establish a sustainable school-based model for improving mental health, designed and fit for future scale-up.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: Support for Global Health Advocates advocacy during France’s 2026 G7 presidency
description: The proposal has two objectives: 1) Building momentum on health in the lead up and during the French Presidency of the G7; 2) Amplifying supportive voices including from Africa to influence the G7 negotiations. Proposal outputs include: 1) Development of advocacy materials, including case studies and policy briefs; 2) Collaborative campaigns between French and African civil society organizations (CSOs); 3) Strategic engagement with French policymakers—across government, parliament, and embassies—leveraging key moments such as the French G7 Presidency, the One Health Presidential Summit, and the Africa-France Summit. Expected outcomes: \- Health is well featured within key political events led by France during the French G7 Presidency (including the One Health Presidential Summit and the Africa-France Summit); \- Evidence is developed and disseminated to key decision makers on the links between health and other issues (including climate, infectious diseases, and global health architecture); \- Civil society, notably African CSOs, and key advocacy targets (though leaders) are mobilized to raise compelling messages toward French authorities.

title: Y-MIND Africa: A Multi-Country Hybrid Type 2 Implementation-Effectiveness Stepped-Wedge Trial of a Scalable Psychological Intervention for Depression Among Adolescents and Young People.
description: Depression and anxiety often begin during the teenage years, especially around age 15. While effective and affordable treatments exist, many young people in low- and middle-income countries still struggle to access the support they need. The Y-MIND intervention helps adolescents/young people aged 15-24 years re-engage in meaningful activities and build problem-solving skills. It is delivered by trained lay counselors making it accessible through trusted community spaces. From the outset, adolescents/young people in Ghana and Zimbabwe helped shape the Y-MIND intervention – identifying what matters to them, ensuring the language felt real, and making activities practical and relevant to their daily lives. Adolescents/young people who participated in the early stages of Y-MIND have voiced their strong support for bringing this program to others like them. Together, we now plan to expand Y-MIND to four countries across West (Ghana, Burkina Faso), East (Kenya), and Southern Africa (Zimbabwe), in both English- and French-speaking communities. Through the INDEPTH Network – comprising health research centres that operate Health and Demographic Surveillance Systems across Africa, Asia and Oceania, we will partner with schools, communities, and adolescents/young people to test real- world delivery models, assess costs and resources, and co-design a sustainable scale-up plan rooted in equity and youth leadership.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: Targeted Pathogen Degradation and its Synergy with Antiviral Immunity
description: TRIM21 is an intracellular antibody receptor and E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediates the rapid degradation of antibody-bound pathogens, thereby preventing infection. By recognising antibodies, TRIM21 can target an exceptionally broad range of substrates, including viral capsids and proteopathic aggregates. This proposal seeks to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying TRIM21’s ability to degrade such diverse targets, determine how degradation synergises with the wider immune response against different viruses and develop degrader- based tools for studying host-pathogen biology. In Aim 1, we will determine how TRIM21 selects between proteasomal and autophagic degradation pathways, challenging the prevailing assumption that these systems operate independently. Aim 2 will investigate how TRIM21’s unique catalytic mechanism—substrate caging and proximity-induced activation—enables ubiquitination of structurally diverse molecules. Aim 3 will examine how degradation pathway choice influences TRIM21’s coordination with innate immune sensing and adaptive responses during infection in mouse models. Finally, Aim 4 will develop antibody-independent TRIM21-based degraders, including chimeric bioPROTACs and small-molecule ‘VIRTACs’, to explore targeted pathogen degradation as both a discovery tool and potential antiviral strategy. Together, these studies will define how TRIM21 orchestrates intracellular antibody immunity, reveal how degradation pathway selection shapes immune outcomes, and establish a foundation for TRIM21-inspired degraders.

title: Transforming Early Psychosis Care through Supported Employment and Education in Peru
description: Supported employment and education can transform early psychosis care by helping young people recover through work and study. This project will launch Peru’s first national implementation of the Individual Placement and Support (IPS) model for youth with early psychosis. The Foundation Phase (Year 1) will build a multi-sector partnership across health, labour, and education to co- adapt IPS—an evidence-based model that integrates vocational and educational recovery into mental health care. Co-designed with young people, caregivers, employers, lived-experience leaders, and policymakers, this phase will ensure cultural and contextual fit, and sustainability. It will: (1) establish governance through a Steering Committee and Youth Lived-Experience Advisory Panel; (2) deliver IPS co-adaptation workshops and develop Spanish manuals and training materials; (3) create an employer and education engagement framework and inclusion toolkit; and (4) design a hybrid effectiveness–implementation trial protocol, public and patient involvement plans, and dissemination strategies. The Impact Phase (Years 2–6) will evaluate IPS within Peru’s community mental-health network, assessing effects on education, employment, functioning, and recovery, and examining implementation feasibility and cost- effectiveness. Findings will guide a national scale-up roadmap co-produced with government and lived-experience partners, including validated implementation tools, and financing mechanisms. Keywords: Early psychosis; Supported employment; Early intervention services; Lived experience co- production.
programme: Directed call - Mental Health – Psychosocial Foundation Phase

title: The cognitive mapping of uncertainty by integrated neuromodulation in the hippocampus
description: In a constantly changing environment, the brain must store and update information in a way that depends on uncertainty. The hippocampus is central to this continual process but relies on inputs that signpost new information and regulate the extent to which it is incorporated in future estimates. Our central hypothesis proposes that this signposting is performed by functionally overlapping neuromodulator systems interacting in an integrated fashion to signal different types of error and uncertainty. This signal enables appropriate updating of memories stored in the hippocampus providing realistic expectations on which to base decision making in uncertain situations, a fundamental process whose disruption is a core feature of multiple psychiatric disorders. To test these models, we will measure where and when neuromodulation by acetylcholine, dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin occurs in the hippocampus during spatial navigation tasks in mice designed to manipulate the type and degree of error and uncertainty. These findings will inform a novel theoretical framework which will be iteratively refined by experiments to selectively manipulate neuromodulator release and downstream targets, providing mechanisms for how neuromodulators integrate to modify observable hippocampal representations of space. Ultimately this project will fundamentally reappraise the principles of neuromodulation and its therapeutic potential.

title: Behavioural and resistance genomics in an invasive urban malaria vector in Africa.
description: Malaria in Africa is a predominantly rural disease, but the recent invasion and rapid spread of an urban vector of malaria, Anopheles stephensi, has created widespread concerns of malaria epidemics in Africa’s large urban centres. This health emergency requires an urgent response of improved surveillance and vector control informed by a fundamental understanding of the evolution and demographics of this spreading, invasive population in the face of vector control. A major obstacle to this is our limited understanding of An. stephensi genomics. This proposal will use genomic analysis to address three major challenges to informed An. stephensi control. 1. I will use genomics, transcriptomics and CRISPR gene editing to identify and validate genetic markers of insecticide resistance, so that the spread of resistance can be monitored and appropriate insecticides can be deployed. 2. I will use genomic tools to the evolution and demographics of An. stephensi after insecticide deployment, so that the effect of control interventions can be measured. 3. I will elucidate the genetic basis of key behaviours that could lead to behavioural resistance to control, to understand the risks that this poses, monitor its spread, and improve our understanding of these behaviours in malaria vectors as a whole.

title: Defining the local and systemic metabolic networks underpinning male gametogenesis
description: Somatic cells support gamete development and ensure adaptation to nutrient conditions through an intricate network of intercellular metabolite transfer. Yet we understand little about this network or the somatic metabolism that underpins germline development. Using the Drosophila testis, we showed in vivo for the first time that germline survival depends on somatic lactate production and transfer, a hypothesis first proposed from in vitro studies in mammals, highlighting a remarkable degree of evolutionary conservation and the tractability of our model. Here, we will explore the metabolic pathways that sustain gametogenesis in both germline and soma. In Aim 1, we will define germ cell metabolism, by first addressing how lactate is used in germ cells, a question that remains unsolved in mammals and flies. Aim 2 will establish the metabolic needs of gonadal somatic cells focusing on fatty acid oxidation which we have shown is important for differentiation. Aim 3 will address the mechanisms by which a distant somatic tissue, the fat body, controls the adaptation of the testis to nutrient levels. Overall, by studying germline metabolism not in isolation but in the context of intercellular metabolic networks, this project will provide a comprehensive understanding of the metabolic requirements of male reproduction.

title: A Multidisciplinary Bioimaging Platform for Quantitative Force Mapping in the Beating Heart
description: Physical forces are fundamental drivers of tissue-level biological processes, yet we still lack tools to quantify how subcellular forces drive the collective behaviour of the cell populations forming developing organs, and how this shapes overall architecture and function. The heart is an extraordinary example of this complexity, where the cellular behaviours underpinning heart morphogenesis can only be understood if we can measure the tissue-level forces in the presence of cardiac contractile forces. Progress is frustrated by the absence of any bioimaging technology with the performance and temporal resolution for direct quantitative imaging of intercellular forces in highly dynamic 3D environments such as the beating heart. We are addressing this gap with a purpose-built bioimaging platform to achieve the ambitious goal of mapping the force landscape throughout the beating heart, in a live intact organism. To achieve this we are developing novel optical and computational imaging approaches for single-photon motion-corrected fluorescence lifetime imaging, alongside new optical molecular tension sensors – delivering for the first time subcellular-resolution, whole-organ force imaging in vivo in highly dynamic environments. This will reveal how the intercellular force landscape is modulated by contractile activity, tissue architecture and cell crowding – and the implications for cardiac development and disease.

title: Cell competition in X chromosome usage and disease
description: The unique biology of the mammalian X-chromosome means that the impact of X-linked genetic variation is sex-specific; while males have a single X-chromosome, females have two. As X-linked sequence variants cause ~600 diseases, having an extra copy can be advantageous. Nevertheless, the manifestation of X-linked traits is highly variable between females. Such variability arises from the random inactivation of one X-chromosome in each female cell, which creates a mosaic of cells that selectively express genetic variants located on either X chromosome. We have recently demonstrated that variants in the X-linked genes Stag2 and Hdac8 can drive cell competition in heterozygous females. Competition profoundly skews the proportion of cells that use one or the other X-chromosome in specific tissues and cell-types. This discovery raises many important questions; how does X-linked competition work, how many other X-chromosome variants drive competition, and how does competition affect the phenotypic manifestation of X-linked traits? Here we propose to address this knowledge gap to uncover how competition impacts female disease susceptibility/resilience. Leveraging human population data, preclinical models and in vitro systems we will systematically evaluate the extent, mechanisms and impacts of X-linked cellular competition in female development and X-linked disease manifestation.

title: Investigating the response of human microglia to amyloid beta in an in vitro tri-culture model of neuroinflammation
description: Dementia is a leading cause of death, responsible for more than one in 10 UK deaths in 2023. Alzheimer’s disease is the leading cause of dementias, and presents a significant social and medical challenge, especially in the context of nations with aging populations and inadequate memory care resources. Alzheimer's disease is extremely complex in its aetiology and difficult to research. Additionally, there is an as-yet-unexplained sex difference in incidence, with 2/3 of patients being female. A characteristic element of its pathophysiology- and therefore a target for study- is the presence of amyloid plaques, aggregations of amyloid beta protein that form first in the neocortex and are gradually found in deeper areas of the brain as the disease progresses. Normally, amyloid is phagocytosed by microglia, brain-resident immune cells. In Alzheimer's, microglia lose this function, polarising towards a more proinflammatory phenotype. My project aims to investigate the cellular- level changes behind this change in function, using human IPSC-derived microglia, neurons and astrocytes cocultured in brain-like ratios. This will then be a base platform for amyloidosis experiments. We will also interrogate cellular-level sex differences in response to amyloid, using sex-matched IPSC lines from a donor with Klinefelter’s syndrome and the original chromosomes XXY.

title: openScopes AIDDiA: Advancing Infectious Disease Discovery Research in Africa with open-source imaging technology
description: openScopes AIDDiA (Advancing Infectious Disease Discovery Research in Africa; “idea”) will develop and deploy technologies towards overcoming barriers to bioimaging in Africa, and to enable discovery research focused on endemic infectious diseases. We propose a technology development and distribution programme driven by a diverse, multinational team comprising specialist, multidisciplinary expertise located across five collaborating sites in South Africa, Kenya, Uganda, Côte d'Ivoire, and the UK. By combining (i) the deployment of mobile instruments (travellerScopes) that will serve as nodes for training and preliminary investigations with (ii) the development and implementation of advanced microbeScope-based imaging modalities for discovery research focused on live, infectious clinical material, our intention is to seed a sustainable network of active researchers spanning anglophone and francophone sub-Saharan Africa, supported by hubs of technological and research excellence. In linking these hubs to centres focused on hardware design that is responsive to African research needs and the realities of diverse environments, limited resources, and variable infrastructure, we aim to establish a template that illustrates the benefit of partnering technology developers with researchers in discovery research teams – especially in low- resource settings where access to instrumentation alone is inadequate to support sustained uptake of bioimaging for investigations of endemic infectious diseases.

title: Leveraging the clinical, genetic, and molecular heterogeneity of type 2 diabetes to improve screening and treatment strategies
description: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) affects over half a billion people globally, but its causes, symptoms, and outcomes vary widely between individuals and populations. South Asian populations in particular develop T2D at a younger age and lower body weight, and have higher risks of complications – yet they remain underrepresented in research. I aim to better understand variations in T2D diagnoses in South and Southeast Asian (SSEA) populations by applying ‘soft’ clustering methods. These methods describe how individuals can belong to a mixture of disease subtypes, rather than assigning them to single disease categories – better reflecting the real-world complexity of T2D. I will use clinical, genetic, and molecular data from SSEA cohorts to explore how these subtypes relate to disease progression, complications, and response to treatments like metformin. I will also investigate how genetic risk scores and molecular markers can help improve our understanding of disease causes and progression. Ultimately, I aim to develop evidence that will help doctors choose the most appropriate treatments for SSEA patients with T2D. By reflecting the real-world complexity of T2D more accurately, my research aims to make diabetes care more personalised, effective, and equitable – in a disadvantaged community that is not well represented in medical research.

title: RESPECT-TB: RESistance Prevalance, Emergence and Clinical impact in TB
description: Since the 1960s, rifampicin has been at the centre of anti-TB regimens that have achieved treatment success rates of >90%. The emergence of rifampicin- resistant TB (RR-TB) reduced survival back to around 50-60% for patients with these strains, not much better than in the pre-antibiotic era. Major advances in the past decade have led to regimens such as BPaL(M) (Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, +/- Moxifloxacin) that demonstrate cure rates of around 90% for RR-TB in clinical trials. It is therefore of great concern to now see drug resistance mutations to bedaquiline – the backbone of almost all RR-TB treatment today – being observed with increasing frequency in parts of southern Africa. What is not well understood is how widespread these drug- resistance mutations are globally, nor what drives their emergence, nor their impact on treatment outcomes. We will conduct prevalence surveys of resistance to drugs used in new RR-TB regimens (including bedaquiline) in five countries across Africa and Asia, generating both genomic and Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) data. We will also investigate why people fail treatment for RR-TB and acquire drug resistance, and how individual mutations in M. tuberculosis contribute to patient outcomes. The results will inform how RR-TB is managed globally.

title: Understanding oral-gut immunological crosstalk in response to Periodontitis
description: We aim to investigate the mechanisms through which the oral inflammatory disease periodontitis, potentiates inflammation at extra-oral sites. Previous studies conducted by Kitamoto et al and Nagao et al have demonstrated that periodontitis augments gut inflammation by supplying the gut with colitogenic pathobionts and Th17 cells, and that the oral pathobiont-responsive Th17 cells in the gut migrate to the mouth and exacerbate periodontitis, confirming that immunological communication occurs along the oral-gut axis. Our study will utilise an established periodontitis mouse model to ascertain the immunological changes occurring throughout the digestive tract following induction of periodontitis. We will undertake holistic approaches to explore the entire length of the GI tract using; (a) A tissue-rolling technique encompassing the whole GI tract, to carry out spatial transcriptomic profiling of the tract. (b) Flow cytometric analysis of immune populations. (c) Fluorescence microscopy and RNA-scope to explore alterations in candidate cytokine pathways, the extracellular matrix (eg collagen networks) and the mucous barrier. We will generate a comprehensive gene and protein expression profile of the whole GI tract detailing the impact of periodontitis on GI homeostasis. Our project will delineate whether periodontitis is a disease modifier for inflammatory disorders affecting the GI tract.

title: Cleave-to-modify: exploring proteolytic processing in Ubl-fusion proteins
description: The life cycle of proteins, from synthesis to modification and degradation, is controlled by a wide range of cellular processes. Classically, the ubiquitin- proteasome system tags the small ubiquitin protein onto targets to signal for their degradation. Ubiquitin shares its folding structure with ubiquitin-like (Ubl) proteins, a diverse family of proteins. Ubl-fusion proteins are larger proteins containing within them a ubiquitin-like domain, the implications of which are poorly understood and under-studied. Maniaci lab has recently uncovered the mechanisms for SDE2, a Ubl-fusion protein which undergoes enzymatic cleavage of the Ubl-domain from the wider protein. With this project I aim to uncover other Ubl-fusion proteins which undergo similar cleavage events by using a range of chemical and cell biology techniques. Candidate proteins will be assessed for cleavage by cloning of an over-expression system in mammalian cells. Where processing is observed, these reactions will be explored using lysate fractionation screening and proteomics to identify the interactors and enzymes responsible. Tools will be developed to study the fate of cleaved Ubl-domains, exploring the possibility of substrate conjugation similar to other Ubls. This study will provide great insight into the Ubl- fusion class of proteins, with the potential to discover vital new pathways in cellular regulation.

title: The Night Shift 1850-Present: Re-imagining Sleep, Work and Wellbeing for Healthcare Professionals in English and Scottish Hospitals
description: Night Shift aims to radically re-imagine sleep work and wellbeing for healthcare professionals working at night on the general hospital ward in England and Scotland. Complimenting a burgeoning field of clinical and epidemiological research on healthcare fatigue, the project will reveal the ways in which long-standing working cultures and professional identities have normalized unsafe and unsustainable working conditions. Working across medical, environmental and labour histories, the project will provide the first systematic history of the British hospital at night. By drawing on cutting edge research in the studies of the night, sleep and everyday temporalities, Night Shift will also deliver a new framework to understand the lived experience of night shift work in the hospital. The project team will bring historical insights into conversation with contemporary challenges through semi-structured interviews and Participatory Action Research (PAR) with night shift workers. This interdisciplinary work will feed into better policy and practice supported by partnerships with three NHS Foundation Trusts in the North East of England, as well as the charity sector. Over five and a half years, the project team will deliver an ambitious programme of academic, public engagement and policy outputs, including an exhibition at the Royal College of Nursing (RCN).

title: Investigating epidermal cell fate plasticity in response to intrinsic and environmental perturbations
description: Skin is essential to homeostasis, as well as protection from injury and infection. Unsurprisingly, cellular plasticity to maintain barrier function is well established within the literature: hair follicle and sebaceous gland cells can dedifferentiate and contribute to wound healing in the interfollicular epidermis (IFE). Despite large genetic and physiological changes in aged and environmentally-exposed skin, very little research has been dedicated to the role of plasticity in these processes. Previous work by Dr. Maria Alcolea and colleagues identified KLF4 as a marker of a “differentiation-committed” population in skin and oesophagus. They demonstrated a novel role for KLF4 IFE cells, which can lose their commitment and recontribute to homeostasis in the IFE, through a process of plasticity that increased in prevalence in aged tissues. We hypothesise that this increased plasticity may also occur in aged and contaminated skin, causing tissue fragility and delayed healing. This project therefore aims to investigate how age and environmental (pollutant) perturbations influence epidermal cell fate plasticity. We hypothesise that such changes in plasticity may compromise skin integrity and contribute to an aging phenotype. To address this, we will examine how these perturbations affect cellular behaviour and identify the underlying molecular regulators.

title: Investigating the structural basis for HIV-1 hijacking cytoskeletal motor adaptors and in situ studies of microtubule trafficking
description: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) caused over 600,000 deaths in 2024 and over 40 million people are currently infected worldwide. During the HIV replication cycle, its RNA genome is reverse transcribed into DNA and integrated into the host’s genome. The viral genome must be transported from an infected cell’s plasma membrane to the nucleus. The HIV-1 capsid (CA) hijacks the host’s microtubule motors to achieve this. Dynein-1 and Kinesin-1 are recruited and it is unknown how the capsid modulates their activity for productive trafficking. This project will build on the Zhang lab’s research on capsid binding host factors and in situ structural studies. I will focus on five specific adaptors that bind HIV-CA: BICD2, BICDR1, CLIP-170, FEZ1, MARK2. I specifically aim to: 1\. Determine the first structures of HIV-CA bound to a motor protein adaptor using recombinant expression and cryo-electron microscopy. 2\. Perform in situ structural studies of human cell lines infected with HIV-1, using correlative cryo-FIB and cryo-ET These aims will provide i): unprecedented structural detail of a virus’ interactions with host motor adaptors and HIV-1 association with microtubules, and ii) potential new targets for antiretroviral therapy and applications in biotechnology for designing proteins that hijack the cytoskeleton.

title: Coordinating decision-making and the cell cycle: the role of signal dynamics
description: A limited set of signalling molecules drive embryonic cells to self-organise, pattern tissues and construct the entire body plan. Mutations that corrupt accurate signal interpretation are common drivers of human disease, however, embryonic development remains highly robust to these perturbations. Using a combination of quantitative imaging approaches and optogenetics, my aim is to uncover the basic design principles of dynamic signal interpretation and understand how the embryo coordinates tissue growth and cell decision-making, using Ras-Erk signalling in craniofacial patterning as a paradigm. Tissues that contribute to craniofacial development display differential sensitivity to the same perturbed signal in a family of developmental disorders, known as RASopathies. I will combine imaging approaches with whole embryo single-cell RNA-seq to determine what aspects of craniofacial development (signalling, gene expression, cell numbers) are sensitive to perturbation in the context of disease. Our ability to investigate the role of signal dynamics in embryonic development and disease has been limited by technology. However, I and others have pioneered new biosensors that enable the tracking of single-cell signalling and decision-making in vivo. Using zebrafish and Drosophila embryos as optically accessible models, I will reveal how tissues interpret normal and corrupted signals and identify buffering mechanisms that safeguard development.

title: Sex Specific Differences in Psychedelic Therapies
description: Research examining the therapeutic potential of psychedelic substances has expanded rapidly in recent years. However, there is a distinct lack of research examining effects specific to women. This is especially pertinent given the gender imbalance in some mental health disorders such as depression, as well as the presence of female-specific disorders like premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Previous research has shown that ovarian hormones such as estrogen and progesterone upregulate 5HT-2A, the primary target of classic psychedelics. However, whether monthly cyclical changes to these hormones impact the acute psychedelic experience and subsequent therapeutic outcomes is currently unknown. The current research aims to address this gap through three strands of work. First, a scoping review of sex-based differences in current psychedelic research. Second, a two-arm experimental study in which health participants will receive a single, fixed dose of psilocybin to compare differences in acute psychedelic experiences and outcomes at two different stages of the menstrual cycle (follicular and luteal). Qualitative (interviews), quantitative (standardized psychometric subscales), and physiological data (EEG, heart rate, blood pressure) will be collected. Third, within this experimental cohort, we will conduct exploratory analysis of whether a single psilocybin session reduces self-reported premenstrual distress.

title: Improving care pathways for migrant women with gestational diabetes in Scotland
description: This project aims to improve the management and outcomes of gestational diabetes (GDM) for migrant mothers and children. GDM is a form of diabetes that pregnant women develop with onset around 2nd or 3rd trimester. It is often associated with several complications for maternal and fetal outcomes, including increased odds of pre-eclampsia and caesarean sections, as well as long-term outcomes such as increased odds of cardiometabolic disorders, i.e. diabetes, obesity. Prior studies have flagged ethnicity as a risk factor for GDM complications and migrant women in the UK are known to face important barriers that limit their access to maternity care services. However, there is a lack of high-quality data that explores how these challenges impact antenatal care access and perinatal adverse outcomes. In turn, without more insights, little can be done to advise policymakers and improve care pathways for migrant mothers and their children. I aim to use quantitative and qualitative methods to characterize how care and perinatal outcomes between migrant and UK-born pregnant women differ, and to explore the perspectives and personal experiences of migrant women to develop recommendations towards more equitable and inclusive GDM management in Scotland and the UK at large.

title: Investigating the PTSNtr in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
description: During infection, bacteria are often in a dormant state, where they are less active and are resilient to stresses, including antibiotic treatment. The nitrogen-related phosphotransferase system (PTSNtr) helps control the cell during dormancy. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, it consists of three proteins that transfer a modifying phosphate from one to the next: PtsP, PtsO, and PtsN. Phosphorylation of PtsN changes its interactions with binding partners. A prior pulldown identified some interactors of PtsN. I will confirm the key interactors and use a proximal labelling method to identify transient interactions. PtsO/PtsP are theorised to be influenced by metabolic signals, recognising the cell status and altering PtsN activity. I will construct bacterial strains lacking PTSNtr components and measure changes in the level of phosphorylated PtsN and the interactions between PtsN and its partners identified in the first part of the project. I will investigate how conditions relevant to P.aeruginosa infections alter PTSNtr signalling, including nutrient-limiting media and macrophage presence. I will attempt to disrupt PTSNtr signalling to sensitise P.aeruginosa to antibiotics, identifying combinations of antibiotics using compound libraries. The PTSNtr has wide- ranging effects but remains poorly understood and studying it may enhance our understanding of how slow growing bacteria regulate different activities.

title: Identifying a novel polymorphic toxin system in Gram-positive bacteria and determining the activity and mechanism(s) of action
description: Bacteria exist in polymicrobial communities where they must compete for space and nutrients. Correspondingly, microbes have evolved survival mechanisms that allow them to out-compete other microorganisms. One such mechanism is “interference competition”, whereby one bacterial cell actively kills or disables another, often using proteins that are toxic. There is a newly discovered toxin system that is used for inter-bacterial killing, called the S8-polymorphic toxin system (S8-PTS). The S8-PTS was only recently identified and there are many unanswered questions. We aim to determine if there is species specificity for different toxin families and determine the range of species the toxin is active against and within. This aim will initially require a computational analysis of all the S8-PTS clusters in bacteria. Using the information obtained, we will be able to explore the activity of S8-PTS clusters in different species and establish the range of organisms susceptible to the toxins. To elucidate the mechanism(s) of toxin entry to susceptible cells, we will isolate S8-toxin resistant clones and sequence their whole genome. We will identify the location of mutations and use these to understand mechanism of toxin entry into the cell. This work will aid our understanding of how bacteria interact in the environment.

title: Dynamic 3D super-resolution ultrasound imaging of micro-circulation and genetically encoded acoustic reporters in vivo
description: Non-invasive, high-resolution whole-body imaging capable of visualising cellular identity and function in vivo has the potential to revolutionise our understanding of many physiological systems and diseases, but remains a major challenge in biological research. This project develops and integrates cutting-edge ultrasound technologies with acoustic-reporter genetics to address this challenge, delivering an accessible and high resolution 3D imaging platform capable of longitudinal imaging of biological systems across cellular, organ and whole-body scales. The team will develop a large field-of- view volumetric in vivo imaging platform enabling whole-body dynamic imaging of microcirculation and genetically encoded acoustic reporters, the “GFP for ultrasound”, at sub-diffraction resolution in rodents. Novel acoustic reporter genes will be engineered to sense and image multiple biomarkers of cellular function in defined cell populations. These tools will be validated across cellular and temporal scales in metabolic research contexts, addressing critical questions about pancreatic beta cell mass dynamics and gut enteroendocrine cell signaling that current imaging methods cannot resolve. The final aim focuses on developing resources, including mouse lines, protocols, and training programs, to enable wide adoption of this transformative technology across the life sciences community.

title: Junk Foods: A Transnational History of Childhood, Diet, and Health in Post-War Europe
description: This project provides the first integrated history of junk food and childhood health in post-war Europe. It asks how branded snacks, drinks, and fast food became embedded in children’s lives, how they were represented and contested, and how they were remembered by those who grew up with them. By combining archival research with a large-scale digital ethnography initiative, it captures both institutional discourses and lived experiences. The project challenges the assumption that “junk food” is a stable or objective category. From the 1950s onwards, products dismissed by health professionals were often cherished by families as affordable, exciting, or aspirational. What counted as “junk” in one decade or country might be a treat, a convenience, or even a necessity in another. By analysing how such labels were applied, resisted, or ignored, the project reframes present anxieties about childhood diet and health as part of deeper cultural histories. Four national case studies - Britain, Ireland, Poland, and Italy - provide the foundation for a transnational synthesis of products, ideas, and anxieties. Outputs include a monograph, peer-reviewed articles, an open-access archive, and public exhibitions. The project leaves a legacy in scholarship, public engagement, and policy, showing how histories of food illuminate contemporary health debates.

title: International Brain Laboratory Core: global dissemination and outreach
description: The International Brain Laboratory (IBL) has collected unique, open datasets of brain-wide recordings during a standardized mouse behavior. In the next phase, core IBL staff will support the collection, analysis, and dissemination of new experimental datasets from neuroscientists around the world.These datasets are an unprecedented resource, for example enabling scientists globally to perform cutting-edge neuroscience research through data analysis, even if they do not have resources for large-scale experiments. Nevertheless, further work is required to maximize their use and impact in a global and equitable manner. We will do so using four main strategies: 1. Community- building through data analysis workshops, hackathons and competitions, prioritizing under-resourced regions; 2. Development of data pipelines, web interfaces, and analysis tools that simplify use of our data and tools; 3. Lowering barriers to access via a custom AI interface that enables natural- language queries and automated analyses of IBL data; 4. Creating Large Neural Models trained on IBL-scale data to enable state-of-the-art analyses to be performed by labs without large-scale computing resources. Together, these efforts will expand and democratize global access to cutting-edge neuroscience research.

title: Structural and Functional Characterisation of the MIWI2 Silencing Complex
description: The piRNA pathway is composed of PIWI proteins and small RNA guides termed piRNAs. The murine nuclear piRNA pathway, orchestrated by the PIWI protein MIWI2, safeguards the developing germline against the deleterious activity of transposons. MIWI2, guided by piRNA, target-engages nascent transposon transcripts and initiates transcriptional inhibition via the recruitment of transcriptional repressor proteins to form the MIWI2-piRNA-induced silencing complex (MIWI2-piRISC). Our lab has recently identified a host of MIWI2 interactors; however, we have not established how these proteins contribute to the MIWI2-piRISC, nor how these proteins achieve transcriptional inhibition at a mechanistic level. To address this knowledge gap, I will first determine the structure of target engaged MIWI2 and assess how this structure supports its role as a structural scaffold. I will then characterise the MIWI2-piRISC in vivo and examine its structure using a biochemical approach. Concurrently, I will explore the how TEX15, one of the putative MIWI2-piRISC components, induces transcriptional inhibition and whether this possible function of TEX15 is essential for piRNA pathway function in vivo. By taking both a structural and functional approach, this work will provide novel insights into how the piRNA pathway defends the mammalian germline from the threat of transposons during germline development.

title: Understanding how trajectories of maternal health both pre and during pregnancy relate to postnatal outcomes and future health outcomes
description: This study will investigate how maternal cardiometabolic health before, during, and after pregnancy shapes long-term cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Pregnancy acts as a natural “stress test” of metabolic and vascular resilience, with complications such as gestational diabetes and preeclampsia revealing underlying susceptibility to later CVD. However, gaps remain in understanding the timing of when cardiometabolic risk peaks, adherence to guideline-recommended postnatal checks, and whether incorporating pregnancy history improves risk prediction. Using linked UK electronic health records (CPRD), birth cohorts (ALSPAC, Born in Bradford), Ugandan data, and genetic data, we will address four aims: (1) describe adherence to NICE postnatal care guidelines and identify underserved groups; (2) model trajectories of BMI, blood pressure, glucose, and lipids from pre-pregnancy up to two years postpartum, to identify optimal screening timepoints; (3) explore whether adding pregnancy information improves CVD risk prediction beyond standard models such as QRISK3; and (4) apply Mendelian Randomization (MR) to test causal relationships between adverse pregnancy outcomes and long-term cardiometabolic health. By integrating diverse datasets and advanced analytic approaches, this research will help inform policy on postnatal care, improve CVD risk prediction, and support more equitable prevention strategies for high-risk women. Keywords: cardiometabolic health, adverse pregnancy outcomes, electronic health records

title: Understanding Risks and Discourses Surrounding Weight Loss Injectables Purchased Through Private Online Pharmacies
description: 1.4 million people across the UK are taking Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP1-RA) weight loss injections, becoming ‘big business’ due to online social media trends. There are strict guides that clinicians must follow to safely prescribe GLP1-RAs and check-up on patients’ weight loss, exercise, and dieting progress. This means that some people turn to private online pharmacies (POP) to get their hands on this medication. However, taking GLP1-RAs without professional guidance comes with additional health risks, and some POPs advertise claims outside of guidelines to appeal to those who may not meet the criterion. Research is needed to understand the impact that content from private online pharmacies have on patients’ perception of risks associated with GLP1-RAs and understanding of obesity and weight loss. By exploring how people talk about GLP1-RAs, how POPs use online content to communicate to people, and how people use POP websites to access these injections; we can better regulate the risks and rewards attached to GLP1-RAs use for weight loss. Using qualitative methods, the research is divided into 4 stages: analysing online discussion fora, in-person focus group discussions of POP content, think-aloud protocols exploring POP websites, and participants' ‘digital diary’ collection of POPs and GLP1-RA content.

title: Understanding the relationship between mental health and NEET status in young adults
description: 13% of UK 16-24-year-olds were classified as NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) in December 2024, representing a growing economic and public health challenge. Young people experiencing NEET face elevated risks of mental health disorders, substance abuse, and suicide. While cross-sectional studies demonstrate associations between NEET and mental health problems, longitudinal evidence is needed to establish directionality. Understanding mediating mechanisms will inform interventions aimed at supporting young adults experiencing NEET or mental health problems. Additionally, we aim to explore whether certain longitudinal patterns of mental health (i.e. timing and duration of symptoms) confer greater NEET risk. Key Goals: Explore bidirectionality: Longitudinal modelling to assess whether mental health problems lead to NEET status, vice versa, or both. Identify mediating mechanisms: Examine potential mediators between mental health and NEET such as academic attainment, school attendance, self-esteem, and substance abuse. Map mental health trajectories: Growth mixture modelling will identify distinct longitudinal patterns of mental health symptoms and their associations with NEET, informing targeted interventions. Data: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) - birth cohort study with repeated measures of mental health and education/employment activity. Next Steps - longitudinal cohort study with repeated measures of mental health and focus on post- education transitions.

title: Structure and mechanism of translation initiation in picornavirus infection
description: Picornaviruses cause approximately one billion infections annually, leading to diseases ranging from the common cold to meningitis and myelitis. Their extensive genetic diversity has hampered antiviral drug development, but all picornaviruses share a critical dependence on the host translation machinery. Exploiting this vulnerability requires a detailed understanding of viral translation initiation, therefore this proposal investigates how picornaviruses hijack ribosomes via internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs). By comparing initiation mechanisms across Type 1, 2 and 5 IRESs, we aim to define conserved structural and mechanistic features for targeting by new broad- spectrum antivirals. Aim 1 will determine high-resolution cryo-EM structures of initiating ribosomes, both in vitro and in virus-infected cells, revealing the atomic details of interactions between IRES elements, initiation factors, ribosomal subunits and RNA-binding proteins. Aim 2 will apply TIRF microscopy to track initiation on single IRES molecules, monitoring the real-time recruitment of initiation factors and ribosomal subunits to establish the sequence and interdependence of assembly events. Aim 3 will evaluate different inhibition strategies, by designing peptides that block IRES contact sites on the ribosome, and screening for RNA-binding compounds targeting structured IRES domains. Together, these studies will provide fundamental insights into translational control, and lay foundations for developing novel antivirals.

title: Investigating how cell size alters the RNA-associated proteome and its role in RNA concentration homeostasis
description: Size is an important property for cellular physiology and sets the scale for biosynthesis of RNA and protein. In oversized cells, mRNA, rRNA and protein concentrations decrease, relative protein synthesis and cell growth is reduced. We aim to elucidate the causal links between these size-related effects. These effects are alleviated by increasing cell ploidy, which indicates that a DNA-templated process is limiting for growth. We hypothesise that transcription limits protein synthesis in oversized cells.
