By integrating cutting-edge science with structured career development, this award will better position me to establish an inclusive, translational cancer research program focused on improving outcomes for underrepresented communities and addressing the disparities affecting Black populations in cancer research, despite the disproportionately high cancer burden they face. Keywords: Triple-negative breast cancer, hypoxia, ATR kinase, Black women, Autophagy

title: Investigating the spinal biomechanics of zebrafish: Insights into vertebral structure and function with implications for human skeletal bone health
description: Back pain is the leading cause of disability in the UK, with lower back pain accounting for over 11% of the total national burden. Yet, the biomechanical basis of spinal ageing and degeneration remains poorly understood. This project investigates the mechanical performance of the ageing vertebral column using zebrafish, a genetically tractable and imaging-accessible vertebrate model that mimics many key features of human skeletal biology, including axial loading and vertebral deterioration with age. We will apply finite element analysis, microCT, synchrotron imaging, and morphometrics to quantify how vertebral mechanics change across the life course and between sexes. These analyses will test how stress, strain, and vertebral deformation vary with age, and identify regions of potential mechanical failure relevant to human conditions such as osteoporosis and spinal stenosis. Crucially, we will incorporate a zebrafish mutant that undergoes premature vertebral skeletal ageing (lmx1b) to model early-onset spinal decline, a feature with strong translational relevance. In parallel, we will use confocal imaging and histological staining to examine cellular and matrix-level changes in vertebral tissues, linking structural mechanics to underlying biological processes. This multi-scale approach will examine vertebral ageing, sex differences in spinal robustness, and the biomechanical foundations of back pain and spinal disease.

title: LIGMAP
description: This proposal describes LIGMAP, a research project developing advanced AI methods for characterising and predicting protein pockets and their natural ligand interactions across the human proteome. The work integrates modern pocket detection algorithms, evolutionary analysis, and machine learning to systematically assign endogenous metabolites or cofactors to protein binding sites. By doing so, the proposal seeks to illuminate the roles of uncharacterised proteins, trace metabolic and signalling pathways, explain disease-associated mutations, and support drug discovery and enzyme engineering. A central innovation is EvoPockets, a new approach that combines geometric, physicochemical, and evolutionary data to identify and analyse binding sites that are conserved and biologically significant. The project further leverages evolutionary conservation and protein family clustering to improve ligand prediction and functional annotation. LIGMAP is organised into five interconnected work packages, focusing on pocket identification, structural modelling, pocket characterisation, AI-based protein ligand prediction, and open data access. LIGMAP will provide a comprehensive, openly accessible framework linking protein structure to biological function and disease, providing valuable tools for researchers in academia, healthcare, and industry. We will report endogenous ligands for human, viral and Neglected Tropical Disease pathogen proteomes. Thus, LIGMAP will advance understanding of protein function and facilitate discoveries in biology and medicine.

title: Uncovering the mechanistic basis for trophectoderm lineage commitment during mammalian pre-implantation development
description: The life of mammals starts with fertilization of an egg, which subsequently undergoes multiple rounds of cell division and develops into a complex multicellular organism. The first lineage segregation involves cells segregating to the inner cell mass (ICM) and trophectoderm (TE). Lineage- defining transcription factors (TFs), including CDX2 and GATA3, play a key role in establishing the gene regulatory networks that define these cell types. How they achieve this is poorly understood, in part due to the scarcity of cells during these early stages of development. In this proposal, I will apply my unique combination of expertise in low cell number functional genomics and biochemistry to reveal the molecular mechanisms by which TFs drive TE lineage commitment in mouse embryos. I will (1) define the mechanisms of transcriptional and epigenetic regulation during the sequential process of TE cell differentiation, (2) identify co-factors that modulate the action of TFs in specifying TE both as activators and repressors, and (3) determine how TFs engage with chromatin during gene activation and repression. The principles uncovered in this study will inform future studies of human development and further understanding of why inefficiency in the early stages of development is often a cause of infertility.

title: FUTURE-D = Forecasting Depression Trajectories: Early Network-Guided Prediction of Severe and Persistent Disease Courses
description: FUTURE-D redefines early detection and intervention strategies for individuals at risk of severe and persistent depression by adopting a systems-level framework grounded in network science, dynamical systems, and control theory. The MACS and NESDA cohorts provide a unique foundation for modeling the dynamic evolution of neural, symptom, and psychosocial networks underlying severe and persistent depression. To validate and generalize our findings, we will leverage large, harmonized longitudinal datasets—UK Biobank, NAKO, and diverse treatment datasets. Using neuroimaging, digital phenotyping, and novel measures of lived experience, we aim to identify early warning signals of network destabilization predictive of an adverse disease course. A central innovation is to guide TMS interventions tailored to individual network trajectories and informed by robust Patient and Public Involvement. This paradigm shift moves from symptom-based reaction to mechanism-informed prevention, offering a precision mental health approach tailored to individual network trajectories. Early warning signals and individualized control targets will be developed and validated through a co-design process, with strong emphasis on real-world scalability and suitability in LMICs. These efforts will lay the groundwork for future clinical decision-support tools, enabling clinicians to tailor treatments and prevent adverse outcomes.
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: Climate, Children, and Consequences: The Impact of Climate Change on Child Health in Southern Mozambique
description: As climate change intensifies, extreme heat is becoming a growing threat to health—particularly for young children in low and middle income countries. This project explores how rising temperatures affect child health in Mozambique, a country already facing high burdens of infectious disease, malnutrition, and health system strain. The research will investigate whether heatwaves and high temperatures are linked to increased hospital admissions for illnesses such as diarrhoea, respiratory infections, and fever in children under five. Using 15 years of hospital and climate data from Manhiça District, the project aims to identify patterns and risks, and to generate evidence that can inform health services and climate adaptation planning. The research also supports local collaboration, ensuring Mozambican voices and institutions are central in the design, analysis, and use of findings. The project is part of a broader effort to strengthen climate resilience in child health and contribute to global efforts to reduce climate-related health inequalities. Ultimately, this work will provide much-needed data for policymakers, clinicians, and communities seeking to protect children from the growing health risks of a warming world.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Real-world evidence on Hormone Replacement Therapy for menopause: long-term benefits and outcomes
description: Menopause and perimenopause affect nearly all women, with up to 80% experiencing symptoms such as hot flushes, sleep disturbance, mood changes and urogenital problems. For many, these symptoms are severe and persistent, with substantial impacts on quality of life, relationships, and work. Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) is the most effective treatment and is now used by over two million women annually in the UK. Yet key evidence gaps remain. Benefits are rarely quantified beyond symptom relief, long-term outcomes are uncertain for modern regimens, and younger women and women from ethnic minority backgrounds are often underrepresented in existing studies. This fellowship will generate robust, contemporary evidence on HRT benefits and outcomes using population-scale UK electronic health records (EHRs) linked to hospital and cancer registry data. I will combine traditional epidemiology with advanced causal inference and machine learning approaches (e.g. target trial emulation, counterfactual modelling) to: (i) characterise clinical profiles of women approaching menopause, (ii) quantify potential benefits of HRT such as reduced healthcare use and co-medication, (iii) evaluate long-term outcomes including cancer, cardiovascular disease and dementia, and (iv) examine effects in under-researched groups. This will address critical questions about who should receive HRT, when to start and when to stop treatment.

title: Comparative Investigation of Macrophage Lipid Pathways in Liver Infection and Metabolic Disease
description: My career aspiration is to establish an internationally recognized research programme that fundamentally advances liver disease therapeutics through spatial immunometabolism while creating inclusive research environments that overcome intercultural communication barriers. This award will establish me as an independent leader in liver immunometabolism through four transformational activities: First, I will conduct a systematic comparison of how LPCAT2-expressing macrophages— immune cells I have identified as key metabolic controllers—rewire their metabolism when fighting parasitic infection versus metabolic liver disease, revealing therapeutic pathways for diseases affecting 1 in 25 deaths worldwide. Second, an 8-week visit at the University of Queensland will position me at the forefront of metabolic liver disease methodology using unique model systems while embedding me within international networks. Third, I will create the world's first annotated web-based cartography resource for liver immunology—the "Google Maps" for liver disease research—enabling researchers globally to generate hypotheses about immune interactions. Fourth, building on my Research England-funded work on intercultural communication, I will scale this programme to national impact through evidence-based guidelines and workshops. This integrated approach will establish me as a unique leader advancing both cutting-edge spatial biology and research culture, fundamentally transforming our understanding of liver pathologies while creating frameworks for international scientific collaboration.

title: Indigenous Peoples and Vital-Toxic Relations in Brazil (In-VITAL)
description: This research project aims to examine how vital and toxic substances intertwine in shaping Indigenous conceptions of reproduction and kinship relations within an emic understanding of the 'living.' Among Indigenous collectives of lowland South America, bodily substances ground kinship relations, especially blood, semen and breast milk. However, mercury and pesticides have become materialised in the bodies and territories of Indigenous peoples. They are currently made visible through the impairment of reproductive health and children's cognitive-neurological development. Although chemical exposure is an issue that affects both human and other-than- human beings in the era of the Anthropocene, already vulnerable and marginalised collectives are disproportionately impacted. This project asks what happens when substances deemed toxic become entangled with those conceived as vital. Or, in other words, what happens when what is considered vital becomes a weakening agent? What kind of colonialities become material - and how – in this context? Alongside the Guarani-Mbyá, the Kaiowá, the Yanomami, and the Munduruku Indigenous peoples in Brazil, the In-VITAL will generate a robust ethnography of reproduction, kinship, and their socio- material relations with vital-toxic substances, and develop collaborative methodological techniques to investigate the feedback loops between environmental devastation and the embodiment of health inequalities across diverse spatial-temporal scales.

title: Internal states in the space of neuromodulation
description: An animal's survival hinges on its capacity for flexible cognition, relying on a continuous dialogue between external information and internal state. Neuromodulators like acetylcholine (ACh), noradrenaline (NA), and serotonin (5-HT) are key candidates to orchestrate internal state. However, past studies investigated these neuromodulators in isolation, creating a fragmented picture with seemingly redundant roles and often conflicting findings, likely due to unappreciated synergistic effects between neuromodulators. Moreover, neuromodulators’ role in shaping internal state is complicated by its elusive nature, which encompasses spontaneous behaviour, brain activity and cognition. Thus, the fundamental question of how different neuromodulators jointly shape internal state remains unanswered. To bridge this critical knowledge gap, I propose an unprecedented set of experiments, combining simultaneous measurements of three neuromodulators with cutting-edge brainwide functional ultrasound imaging in mice engaged in spontaneous behaviours and a cognitive task, complemented by causal manipulations. I will test the hypothesis that ACh, NA and 5-HT jointly define a space of neuromodulation that determines the different facets of internal state: behavioural states (Aim 1), brain states (Aim 2) and cognitive states (Aim 3). The results will uncover the unique and synergistic roles of three major neuromodulators in shaping internal state, revealing the essential mechanisms for cognitive flexibility.

title: Decoding how pathogenic mtDNA mutations influence innate immunity and susceptibility to infection
description: Pathogenic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations, including those affecting mitochondrial transfer RNAs (tRNAs) and protein-coding genes, are a leading cause of inherited mitochondrial disease. Clinical observations suggest that patients with mtDNA disease are predisposed to recurrent infections and sepsis, but the mechanisms underlying this vulnerability are unknown. While these mutations disrupt oxidative phosphorylation, their impact on innate immunity remains poorly defined. This proposal aims to elucidate how different classes of heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations influence innate immune responses, focusing on macrophage activation, anti-microbial defence and systemic inflammation. Building on my teams recent discovery that the m.5019A>G mutation in the mt-tRNA for alanine (mt-Ta) drives aberrant type I interferon signalling in macrophages and in vivo, we will compare this to the m.5024C>T mutation in mt-Ta and the m.8069G>A mutation in mt-Atp6 to determine whether immune perturbations are mutation-specific or generalisable across mtDNA disease. We will use metabolic and immunological profiling of primary macrophages and mice in vivo to define how mitochondrial mutations shape innate immunity. Additionally, we will assess whether boosting mtDNA levels with a mtDNA polymerase activator can restore respiratory chain function and re-balance immune responses. This work will uncover fundamental mechanisms linking inherited mtDNA mutations to immune dysregulation and infection susceptibility.

title: Dynamics and plasticity of neuropeptidergic circuits
description: Neurons communicate with each other using two main modes of signaling: signal transmission via synaptic contacts (chemical and electrical synapses) and transmission via diffusible molecules, including neuropeptides, that can mediate signaling between neurons that are not directly connected by physical synapses. Understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics of these distinct routes of communication is essential to our understanding of brain function. While the dynamics of synaptic circuits are relatively well-studied, much less is known about the dynamics of "wireless" networks of peptidergic signaling. The proposed work will address fundamental questions about neuropeptide signaling in neural circuits: how fast and how far do peptidergic signals travel in nervous tissue?, how do they alter the patterns of activity in neural circuits?, how are converging neuropeptide pathways integrated in individual neurons?, and how is the dynamics of neuropeptides altered by changes in their expression? We will address these questions in the feeding circuit of the nematode C. elegans, where the dynamics of peptidergic signaling can be probed with cutting-edge optogenetic tools in live animals. We will also use human cell models to identify conserved principles of neuropeptide signaling that can be translated to understand human disease.

title: Integration of a prediction tool for early detection and management of depression and anxiety among youth with HIV in Kenya
description: Over a quarter of youth living with HIV (YLH) have a common mental disorder (depression, anxiety or trauma symptoms), which significantly impact clinical outcomes by directly contributing to poor treatment adherence and subsequently poor viral suppression and mortality. Early detection of poor mental health has the potential to improve individual YLH treatment outcomes and reduce onward HIV transmission. Low-intensity mental health interventions are effective and scalable; however, these interventions are often used to manage YLH who are already symptomatic. Our proposal aims to: 1) leverage unique cohort datasets of ~2800 Kenyan YLH (15-24 years) to develop and validate a risk prediction model for early detection and detection of prevalent depression and anxiety symptoms among YLH, 2) co-design and pilot the delivery of a mental wellness intervention for YLH at high risk for depression and anxiety adapted using information from the prediction model, with the goal of early detection and management of depression and anxiety, and 3) extend follow-up to 3 years for ~500 YLH that received a brief psychological intervention to address depression, anxiety and trauma symptoms to identify predictors of long term treatment response and relapse.
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: What should we target to treat depression? From receptors and circuits to remission.
description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating condition with most existing treatments being slow-acting or ineffective for many patients or depressive symptoms. Ketamine has shown promise as a fast-acting antidepressant that alleviates symptoms within hours; however, its effects are short-lived and it poses risks of abuse, highlighting the need for safer, more precise and longer-lasting treatments. Using an established chronic stress model, which elicits depression-related phenotypes in rodents, my recent research shows that ketamine’s antidepressant action begins with the inhibition of somatostatin-expressing (Sst+) interneurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)—identifying this heterogenous neuronal population as key initiators of antidepressant effects. Here, I will delineate the Sst+ subtypes initiating antidepressant effects, to determine the precise circuit mechanisms induced by antidepressants. Next, I will uncover how different Sst+ subtypes influence distinct depression-related behaviours to identify precise ways to alleviate specific symptoms by targeting these subtypes. I will also investigate how ketamine restores cell-type-specific, stress-induced changes, with the goal of modulating these pathways to prolong antidepressant outcomes. Ultimately, I aim to deepen our understanding of mPFC-mediated antidepressant mechanisms and the pathophysiology underlying depressive symptoms to support the development of novel, multi-target treatments with lasting effects for MDD patients.

title: Human Air pollution exposure and Variation in neurochemical Activity (HAVA) Study
description: This project investigates how long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) - a traffic-related air pollutant - affects brain chemistry in healthy adults. Using advanced magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H-MRS) and quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), the study will examine whether individuals living in areas with higher NO₂ exposure show measurable differences in glutamate levels and brain iron accumulation. Modelled air pollution data from Imperial College London will be used to classify residential exposure across South London, and participants with at least 10 years of stable residence will be recruited. This pilot study will generate preliminary effect sizes and assess the feasibility of integrating environmental modelling with neuroimaging. The findings will inform future research into the environmental determinants of psychiatric vulnerability, supporting the development of early detection strategies and policy-relevant evidence on air quality and brain health.

title: Magnetic Nanoparticle Mediated Alignment of the Internal Architecture of Brain Organoids for Parkinson's disease modelling.
description: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 150,000 people in the UK in 2023, with prevalence projected to rise to 173,000 by 2030. Beyond classical motor symptoms, PD patients suffer from falls, swallowing and speech impairments, depression, and anxiety. Current pharmacological treatments have limited ability to modify disease progression. Whilst cell therapy techniques have been developed as an alternative to pharmaceutical interventions, these techniques have shown limited efficacy to date. This project aims to use iron oxide magnetic nanoparticles (MNP) to directionally influence axon growth on induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived neurons and brain organoids to help understand and address challenges in cell therapy for PD. Functional changes in neurons and organoids subjected to MNP mediated forces will be characterised using high throughput micro electrode array (MEA) analysis, spatially resolved single cell transcriptomics, RNA sequencing and proteomics. Engineering structurally textured organoids relevant for PD research will enhance their physiological relevance for producing structured cell therapy grafts with improved integration potential.

title: The Origins of Melanocyte Heterogeneity in Health and Disease
description: How embryonic cells make cell fate decisions to give rise to adult tissues is a fundamental question in developmental biology with significant implications for understanding genetic disease. Our collaborative team, including a network of discovery and clinical scientists, will address this question in the context of the melanocyte lineage that gives rise to the pigmented cells found in our skin and throughout the body. We hypothesise that cells of multiple distinct known and unknown origins give rise to melanocytes, and that the origins contribute to variation in melanocytic disease in humans, including distinct subtypes of melanoma. Harnessing advanced zebrafish and human cell models, we will apply genomic technologies and experimental perturbation experiments to build the first cellular map of the origins of all melanocytes in a vertebrate, from embryo to the adult. We will reveal the gene regulatory circuitries that function as cellular “guides” through this living map, and that underpin melanocyte health and disease states. Our Team’s discoveries have the potential to alter our understanding of how melanocytes pigment our body, and how the embryological origin of cells influences disease.

title: A mouse to human approach to trace stem cell dynamics in development and cancer of salivary glands
description: Salivary glands (SG) exhibit a remarkable ability to regenerate following mechanical injury by enhancing the lineage potential of epithelial stem cells (EpSC) to adapt fates of adjacent compartments. Radiotherapy or autoimmune disorders can impair this process leading to xerostomia that severely compromises oral health and digestion. Although pharmacological stimulation of developmental pathways can enhance regeneration, their constitutive activation can lead to preneoplastic transformation. Therefore, to design better therapeutic strategies it is important to understand the signals that regulate EpSC plasticity in development, homeostasis and preneoplastic transformation. While mouse models are instrumental in uncovering key developmental and regenerative mechanisms, interspecies variation in size, developmental timing, and cellular composition requires a comparative analysis. This research will explore the human-specific adaptation that regulate EpSC dynamics in development and how conserved mechanisms drive preneoplastic transformation. By combining human organotypic cultures with in vivo 3D deep tissue imaging, lineage tracing and biophysical modelling I will identify the extrinsic and intrinsic signals that regulate human SG development. In parallel by combining mouse models of tumour initiation with human organotypic tumour cultures, I will resolve the conserved transformation mechanisms. Collectively, this research will facilitate strategies to regenerate diseased SGs by harnessing the mechanisms of normal tissue development.

title: Early Detection and Dynamic Relapse Monitoring in Bipolar Disorder: A Longitudinal Cohort Approach
description: This application represents a groundbreaking advance in the early detection and management of bipolar disorder (BD) by establishing the for the first time dynamic, time-varying predictive models tailored to BD and identified trajectories. Unlike traditional static approaches, BEACON will uniquely integrate longitudinal cohort data with routine clinical care data and with genomics, other -omics and experimental validation, enabling improved risk stratification. BEACON is built on four large, real-world population cohorts, with ongoing longitudinal follow-up that reflect diverse populations and healthcare settings, considerably enhancing both model development and validation. Throughout the development of the proposal, co-production with individuals with lived experience has shaped the research questions and initial design and this will continue throughout the delivery, evaluation, and implementation of the programme. The framework’s use of experimental approaches and multi-omics for putative causal pathway discovery marks a significant step toward interpretable, biologically informed modelling. Our team bridges data science, cellular modelling, precsion psychiatry, epidemiology, computational biology. This will enable future translational validation pioneering the first truly holistic and proactive model for BD care—offering unprecedented potential for early detection to reduce duration of untreated illness, delineate different trajectories of illness, feasibly prevent episodes, and transform relapse management.
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: Enigmatic bacterial sphingolipids; elucidating their biosynthesis, transport and function within the host.
description: Sphingolipids (SLs) play essential roles in membrane structure, cell signalling, and disease pathogenesis in eukaryotic cells. Our understanding of the biosynthesis and function of these enigmatic lipids in higher organisms has been built on decades of research. It was assumed that SL producing bacteria are rare and found in unusual biological niches. However, we discovered that many diverse microbial species have the potential to make SLs. Despite their apparent ubiquity, our existing knowledge of the biosynthesis and function of bacterial SLs is in its infancy. Mounting evidence indicates that SLs are key players in bacterial adaptation and homeostasis within the microbiome. The precise details of the bacterial enzymes that regulate, make and transport SLs are unknown, since they share little homology with their eukaryotic counterparts. Knowledge of how SLs contribute to bacterial fitness and survival within their host is also lacking. Our team will use complementary expertise in structural biology, enzymology, genetics, lipidomics, and bacterial pathogenesis to address two overarching aims: (1) Understand the molecular details of how bacteria make and transport SLs. (2) Characterise what roles bacterial SLs play in host-microbe interactions. Our research will transform the fundamental understanding of bacterial SL biosynthesis and their functional roles in nature.

title: Discovering the essential mechanisms behind Cryptosporidium invasion of epithelial cells
description: Cryptosporidium is an intestinal pathogen that has a substantial disease burden throughout the world. As an intracellular parasite, Cryptosporidium must invade intestinal epithelial cells to survive and replicate. Understanding this process of invasion is crucial to developing new interventions, both for treatment and protection. Here, we will leverage the combined expertise of three laboratories to investigate the molecular mechanisms that Cryptosporidium employs during the invasion process: how the parasite recognises and engages intestinal epithelial cells, how these epithelial cells are manipulated by injected parasite virulence factors, and how these host-parasite interactions influence the host range of Cryptosporidium. This work will address large gaps in our understanding of Cryptosporidium pathogenesis with broad implications for the development of new interventions across the one-health spectrum.

title: Using an integrated One Health approach to eliminate rabies
description: Rabies provides a powerful model for understanding ecological and evolutionary mechanisms that sustain multi-host pathogens and drive cross-species transmission. While mass dog vaccination can eliminate rabies locally, uncertainties about viral persistence across interconnected populations and spillover to wildlife are features of reservoir dynamics that pose challenges beyond rabies to emerging zoonoses globally. In southeast Tanzania, my research has revealed transmission chains involving domestic dogs and wildlife. Following dog vaccination campaigns, rabies declined but resurged when campaigns ended, raising questions about whether wildlife maintain rabies independently or if outbreaks spread from connected dog populations. I will test whether (1) rabies is maintained solely by domestic dogs despite frequent spillover into wildlife, and (2) resurgence arises through reintroductions from neighbouring unvaccinated dog populations rather than cryptic local persistence. Through a One Health framework integrating large-scale vaccination, high-resolution viral genomics, and enhanced surveillance, I will investigate: (1) the ecological mechanisms underlying rabies circulation following dog vaccination; the contributions of (2) wildlife and dog population connectivity to rabies persistence; and (3) how community behaviours impact effectiveness of control measures. Findings will contribute to understanding multi-host pathogen persistence, assessing risks of long-term host shifts and development of transferable frameworks for managing complex zoonotic systems.

title: Harmony – An AI tool for contextual data harmonization, translation and cooperation in research
description: For decades governments, and funding bodies have invested considerable amounts of money and resources to collect valuable data, which have been instrumental in driving scientific progress, addressing important social and health problems. However, much of the world’s data are under-utilised and the opportunities that these data resources can offer are widely untapped. There is great potential in retrospectively harmonising, pooling and re-using datasets from existing sources to answer new research questions, however current workflows to achieve this are slow, error-prone and subject to human biases. With Harmony we have shown that AI can facilitate fast, efficient, accurate and reproducible harmonization. Harmony (https://harmonydata.ac.uk/app/) uses large language models (LLMs) to screen meta-data and identify semantically similar survey questions from different sources. This proposal aims to build on our success in Wellcome’s Mental Health Data Prize and increase our impact on the global research community by transforming Harmony into a commercially viable, end-to-end data harmonization product. Our pathway to success will focus on a) product enhancements, b) expanding our evidence base (e.g. validating Harmony across languages and cultures) and c) developing our operational business model and bringing the tool to market to create consistent revenue streams that will support Harmony’s future growth.

title: Revealing Endothelial Extracellular Vesicle Biology Using CRISPR-Engineered Human Systems
description: Understanding how endothelial cells communicate is key to unravelling mechanisms underlying cardiometabolic disease. This project will generate CRISPR/Cas9-edited human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived endothelial cells to fluorescently tag key extracellular vesicle (EV) markers, enabling for the first time live-cell imaging of EV biogenesis and release at physiological expression levels in response to cardiovascular stimuli. These tools will drive focused, high-impact studies on EV function in vascular health through new international collaborations in RNA profiling, proteomics, EV bioengineering, and fundamental EV biology, areas not covered by my current British Heart Foundation Intermediate Fellowship. The project will apply these technologies to define how EV production and cargo are modulated under defined vascular stress conditions, ultimately linking mechanistic insights with translational relevance. This award will support the retention of a skilled postdoctoral researcher, ensuring continuity and accelerating delivery of key publications and preliminary data needed to underpin future funding. It will also provide protected time and tailored leadership training, positioning me strongly to apply for a Wellcome Career Development Award. By combining genome editing, live imaging, and systems biology, this work will comprehensively map EV pathways and identify future targets for therapeutic intervention and bioengineering strategies to modulate cellular responses.

title: Pathways to the diagnosis of symptomatic breast cancer among Black women in the UK: a qualitative interview study
description: Women of black African and Black Caribbean descent in the UK are diagnosed with breast cancer at late stage and have the worst survival of any ethnic group. Delayed diagnosis of breast cancer in Black women in the UK has been attributed to delayed presentation to healthcare professional, therefore, interventions to address this have focused on tailored messaging to promote awareness. Recent evidence reports that Black women experience a longer primary care interval than any other ethnic group, that is, the time from the first GP encounter with a symptom to the point where they are referred to secondary care for investigation. This suggests a more comprehensive approach may be required to achieve earlier diagnosis in black women. The study aims to explore black women’s pathways to diagnosis of symptomatic breast cancer using qualitative interviews. The goal is to gain an understanding of their journey from the first notice of a symptom to the point where they receive a histological diagnosis. A workshop will be held with relevant stakeholders to interpret the study findings and set priority actions for earlier diagnosis in Black women with symptomatic breast cancer in the UK.

title: Identifying Depression Early in Adolescence for Maximising Prevention and Clinical Translation (IDEA-IMPACT)
description: Identifying Depression Early in Adolescence for Maximising Prevention and Clinical Translation (IDEA-IMPACT) aims to transform early identification and prevention of adolescent depression globally. Despite growing interest in early intervention, current approaches often lack precision in identifying and supporting youth before symptoms fully emerge. IDEA-IMPACT addresses this gap by advancing the Identifying Depression Early in Adolescence Risk Score (IDEA- RS), an empirically developed tool that aggregates 11 sociodemographic variables to estimate adolescents’ probability of developing depression within three years, independently of current symptoms. This tool has demonstrated beyond-chance discriminative ability across diverse settings on five continents. Recognising that effective prevention requires more than accurate prediction, IDEA-IMPACT emphasizes translating risk identification into actionable preventive interventions, guided by lived experience insights. Using advanced, context-sensitive methods, the project will begin by enhancing the generalisability of IDEA-RS across diverse settings. It will then broaden the scope of risk and outcome domains, as well as identify modifiable protective factors that buffer against depression among at-risk adolescents; analyse differential responses to existing interventions based on risk profiles; and co-design a new, low-intensity preventive intervention specifically tailored for high-risk adolescents. This comprehensive approach promotes youth engagement, equity, resilience-building, and sustainability in adolescent mental health globally.
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: Digital signatures of asthma: mechanisms and trajectories from multimodal wearable data
description: Failing to detect and respond to deteriorating asthma costs lives. Each year, patients experience avoidable attacks and unnecessary admissions because warning signs are missed. The days after hospital discharge are especially high-risk. Current monitoring of asthma is inadequate, relying heavily on self-report and lacking objective, timely signals. Wearable sensors allow continuous capture of physiology in real-world settings. Beyond single measures such as heart rate, respiratory rate and cough frequency, wearables can reveal complex physiological patterns, known as digital signatures. Continuous multimodal physiology from wearables has not yet been applied in adult asthma care, leaving a critical gap. This Fellowship will define digital signatures of asthma through multimodal wearable data integrated with clinical outcomes. I will generate a unique dataset linking high-dimensional physiology with clinical trajectories, enabling discovery through machine learning across rest, activity and sleep transitions, and providing mechanistic insight into altered physiological coordination. I will examine how digital signatures vary across asthma phenotypes and recovery trajectories and evaluate their potential to serve as continuous markers of lung physiology, supporting personalised monitoring. The discoveries made in this Fellowship will lay the foundations to minimise the high-risk period following discharge, reduce readmissions, and pave the way for proactive monitoring.

title: Accelerating the detection and treatment of perinatal depression and anxiety in low- and middle-income countries through advanced analytics
description: Perinatal mood disorders (depression and anxiety) are common worldwide and have major negative consequences for parent and child. Expanded screening, personalized medicine and risk-guided care have the potential to transform early identification and treatment of perinatal mood disorders, but research is needed in three areas. First, among women without antenatal depression, can risk-guided care that tailors the intensity of follow-up improve early identification of incident postnatal mood disorders? Second, among women with antenatal depression, can risk-guided care that tailors the intensity of treatment improve outcomes? Third, can risk-guided care achieve better overall mental health outcomes and improve resource efficiency for the health system overall? Such work is particularly critical in low-resource settings with limited mental health resources. Shaped by our collaborators with lived experience and guided by theory, we will apply advanced data science to four perinatal cohorts in low-resource countries to quantify the risk of perinatal mood disorder onset, early progression, and treatment non-response. We will then complete a randomized trial to test, compared to one-size-fits-all care, whether risk-guided perinatal care and follow-up improve outcomes and health system efficiency. This multi-country work will set the stage for a step- change in perinatal care to maximally impact mental health.
recipient: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: Decoding the Molecular Mechanisms of GPCR Biased Signalling
description: G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) are central regulators of human physiology and the most successful class of drug targets. However, many GPCR-targeting drugs activate multiple signalling pathways, leading to undesirable side effects. Biased signalling, where ligands preferentially activate specific GPCR pathways, offers a promising route to more selective therapies. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying this bias remain unknown, limiting the development of next-generation drugs. This project will clarify how biased signalling is shaped by the interplay between ligand binding, receptor conformation, phosphorylation, and effector recruitment. Building on my work developing advanced backbone NMR methods for GPCRs, I will investigate how ligand-induced conformational changes in the receptor core propagate to disordered intracellular regions targeted by GPCR kinases. These phosphorylated segments form key regulatory sites that are often inaccessible to other structural techniques. By combining structural insights with biochemical and cellular assays, I will examine the β1-adrenergic receptor as a clinically relevant and well characterised model. This framework will be extended to GPR3, an understudied receptor whose dysregulation is implicated in metabolic and neurodegenerative disorders. This research will shift the field from static views of receptor activation to a dynamic model of signalling specificity, guiding the design of functionally selective ligands.

title: FarajaMH: Culturally Adapted Generative AI Model for Mental Health Screening in Kenya and Tanzania; Leveraging Longitudinal Data, Clinical Notes and Conversational Chats
description: This project aims to build, validate, and ethically evaluate a bilingual (English and Swahili) generative AI (FarajaMH) model for screening of depression, anxiety, and psychosis (DAP) through natural language interactions. The project combines research and lived experiences to address the lack of culturally attuned tools for early screening and referral in Kenya and Tanzania. The word Faraja means “comfort” in Swahili, symbolising the project’s goal of creating a compassionate GenAI model that will recognize DAP, expressed in everyday metaphors. FarajaMH is a model trained with mental health conversational chats, clinical notes, audio and textual screening data from Health Demographic and Surveillance Systems (HDSS), for screening DAP from sampled populations in Kenya and Tanzania. It will be evaluated and validated entirely within a controlled research environment, testing its screening accuracy, usability, and safety. The expected outcomes include (1) a harmonised multimodal data repository of mental health information mapped to the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM); (2) a bilingual generative AI model for screening for DAP; (3) a mental-health data catalogue and visual analytics dashboard; and (4) publications and conference presentations on GenAI in mental health in East-African context.
recipient: African Population and Health Research Centre
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Brain Circuits for Hormonal Control: Sex differences and ageing in growth hormone regulation
description: Pulsatile growth hormone (GH) secretion is essential for growth, metabolism, and tissue maintenance. These pulse patterns are influenced by sex, age, and hormonal feedback, yet the neural circuits remain poorly defined. This research aims to establish a mechanistic framework for how hypothalamic GH- releasing hormone (GHRH) and somatostatin (SST) neurons generate and regulate sex- and age-specific GH pulses. Using in-vivo tools including fibre photometry, optogenetics, chemogenetics, and miniscopes, we will record and manipulate GHRH and SST neuron activity, examining how they encode GH pulses and how their activity is shaped by hormonal feedback and sex steroids across the lifespan. Preliminary data reveal sex-specific GHRH neuron dynamics and demonstrate feasibility of these approaches. In later stages, we will investigate non-canonical roles of GHRH neurons beyond pituitary regulation. GHRH neurons also appear in the zona incerta (ZI), a region implicated in arousal and cognitive flexibility, where they may serve distinct functions from their hypothalamic counterparts. Using viral tracing, gene expression, and neural manipulation, we will map their connectivity and test roles in memory and cognition. This work will broaden the conceptual scope of neural control of growth hormone and behaviour and lay a foundation for future sex- and age-informed strategies targeting hormonal dysregulation.

title: Interlinked burdens: Understanding the diabetes-depression syndemic in continental Africa
description: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and depression are major global health challenges that often co-occur, leading to worse outcomes and increasing health system burdens. In Africa, both conditions are rising rapidly, yet their interplay remains poorly understood - particularly among African-ancestry populations, who are underrepresented in biomedical research and often present with distinct disease phenotypes. This fellowship aims to uncover shared biological and psychosocial mechanisms linking T2D and depression in African settings, generating foundational insights to inform future interventions. Building on my leadership in studies such as the Generation Malawi Birth Cohort and DepGen Africa, I will use rich, harmonised data from Malawi and other African countries to explore interactions between biological systems, social environments, and lived experiences. The programme comprises three work packages: (1) identify shared metabolic and inflammatory signatures using large-scale metabolomics; (2) investigate causal pathways through genetic analyses, including Mendelian randomisation; and (3) apply qualitative methods to understand how individuals experience comorbidity and navigate care. This interdisciplinary, discovery-focused research will advance our understanding of a critical but understudied public health challenge. Through a tailored training and mentorship programme, it will also support my development as a leading African scientist at the intersection of physical and mental health.

title: Human-in-the-loop Evaluation of Assisted Depression Screening (HEADS)
description: We develop and evaluate HEADS (Human-in-the-loop Evaluation of Assisted Depression Screening), a multilingual, modular, interpretable, HIL, LLM-based automated pipeline for clinical depression diagnosis (DSM-5) and severity (PHQ-9) in diverse clinical populations. Psychiatrists will collect data via QuickSCID-5 and PHQ-9, with adaptive sampling across languages, genders, comorbidity. HEADS has individually trainable modules: (i) Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) supporting five languages (Kannada, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, English); (ii) Domain-sensitive translation (Indic to English); (iii) Inference module providing contextual summaries, DSM-5 diagnoses, PHQ-9 score-bands, reasoning and confidence scores. Key deliverables: (a) HEADS solution; (b) de-identified datasets: 4500 Indic language clinical interviews; native-language transcripts and English translations; DSM-5 diagnosis, PHQ-9 scores, clinical reasoning by psychiatrists; 6000 synthetic English transcripts simulating edge cases; (c) well-documented pipelines for eliciting clinical reasoning from psychiatrists in Chain-of-Thought format and synthetic data generation for training diagnostic models. The key goal is to create safe (HIL), scalable, non-intrusive automated system to help non-specialists measure depression in culturally diverse populations, potentially addressing mental health gaps due to shortage of psychiatrists, underdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, with lived experience experts embedded at all stages of study, who will also co-design bias and safety analysis protocols. Keywords: Depression, Culturally-sensitive care, Human-in-the-loop, Generative-AI, Automatic Speech Recognition
recipient: National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: AI4You(th): Advancing Generative AI for Personalised and Collaborative Youth Mental Health Care
description: The global youth mental health (YMH) crisis demands scalable, effective solutions, yet current care models remain insufficiently engaging and effective. Critical barriers include limited personalisation, reduced youth agency in collaborative decision-making, and poor care continuity. Generative AI has the potential to address these challenges. However, key limitations prevent clinical translation: LLMs cannot reason longitudinally over evolving clinical contexts; lack frameworks for ensuring safety, youth agency, and evidence-informed decision-making; and operate as standalone tools disconnected from face-to-face care. This project will address these limitations through SensAI, a multi-stakeholder AI collaborator that supports young people with depression and anxiety and their clinicians to enhance personalisation, agency, and continuity in YMH. We will: (1) develop novel methods for longitudinal LLM reasoning using personalised knowledge graphs; (2) produce the first YMH-specific constitutional principles that enable LLMs to deliver safe, agency-supportive, and evidence-aligned guidance; (3) integrate these methods into SensAI, an AI collaborator that supports young people and clinicians across the care journey; and (4) evaluate SensAI’s feasibility, safety, and preliminary effectiveness of through a pilot randomised controlled trial. Co-designed with young people and clinicians, this research will establish the foundational methods and evidence required for future generative AI applications to transform YMH care.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Co-designing culturally sensitive youth-centred mental health services in Malawi with young people and stakeholders
description: Substance abuse which includes harmful drinking and drug use among young people in Malawi is on the rise. Like many African countries, Malawi faces treatment gaps and severe workforce shortages, leading to substance abuse being managed under the broad category of mental, neurological and substance use (MNS) disorders within under-resourced mental health services. Only 2% of Malawi’s health budget is allocated to mental health, and there are virtually no specialist services for children and adolescents. As a result, young people with MNS disorders are disproportionately affected and underserved. This reflects a broader global trend in which African populations are systematically underserved by mental health services. My project will explore how to establish much-needed youth-friendly mental health services in Malawi by: 1) conducting a situation analysis of existing infrastructure; 2) using participatory action research (PAR) with adolescents and caregivers to explore community-level understanding of substance abuse; and 3) co-designing a culturally relevant intervention framework with young people to appropriately address mental, neurological and substance use (MNS) disorders. The Wellcome Accelerator Award will support my mid-career researcher progression, consolidating findings from my previous research with this proposed project to inform culturally grounded mental health interventions for young Africans locally and globally.

title: AURORA: Adaptive Understanding through Real-time Observation, Reporting, and Assistance
description: Depression acuity can rapidly shift, yet weekly assessments detect change slowly and often unreliably, delaying treatment personalization and compounding disability. AURORA (Adaptive Understanding through Real-time Observation, Reporting, and Assistance) pairs passive sensing with voice- native, conversational GenAI check-ins to capture rich context plus objective multimodal signals. This enables sensitive, safe, and equitable measurement—the foundation for just-in-time adaptive interventions that address stakeholder concerns about privacy, context, and the risk of dehumanizing, metric-driven care. AURORA’s passive triggers launch brief, adaptive audio-visual assessments of depressive symptoms and provide psychoeducation and CBT-inspired engagement prompts/cues, while collecting high-quality audio–visual signals and lived context. The result is an actionable, valid depressive symptom measurement that can individualize treatment. Following development and refinement, we will evaluate AURORA in a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial of 1,000 patients through 100 clinician dyads across 4 continents. With an international team of researchers and lived experience experts, we leverage our strengths in GenAI, digital phenotyping, global clinical studies, ethics, and advanced analytical methods. We aim to: (1) Develop AURORA; (2) Validate AURORA as a psychometrically robust, responsive, and fair measurement system for depression; (3) Demonstrate engagement, acceptability, and clinical utility; and (4) Explore AURORA’s impact on clinical outcomes relative to treatment-as-usual.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Molecular basis of Fidgetin family functional diversity
description: The dynamic microtubule cytoskeleton is essential for cellular function, and its disruption leads to severe human diseases. Microtubule-severing enzymes are key in ensuring the dynamism of the microtubule network. These enzymes function by removing tubulin, the building blocks of microtubules, from the microtubule lattice. The Fidgetin family of microtubule-severing enzymes (FIGN, FIGNL1, FIGNL2) are key regulators of microtubules, but the molecular mechanisms behind their diverse functions are unknown. I propose a multi- disciplinary approach to bridge this knowledge gap. First, I will use in vitro reconstitution and microscopy to quantify the unique enzymatic activities of each Fidgetin protein and their response to the tubulin code. Second, I will use gene editing to map their subcellular locations and determine the function of their constituent domains in live cells. Finally, I will use cryo-EM, and advanced machine-learning processing tools, to reveal the molecular mechanism linking ATP hydrolysis to microtubule severing at the atomic level. This integrated study using complementary approaches will provide important insights into the regulation of the microtubule cytoskeleton by the Fidgetin enzymes, clarifying their roles in health and disease.

title: STELLAR – Steering-Vector Enhanced LLM Agents for Realistic Digital Twins in Mental Health
description: The scarcity of mental health training resources worldwide creates critical shortages in qualified health workers. Complex psychiatric presentations make it difficult for trainees to gain sufficient clinical exposure. To address these gaps, we propose STELLAR (Steering-Vector Enhanced LLM Agents for Realistic Digital Twins in Mental Health), AI-powered patient simulations using Large Language Models enhanced with Conceptors – advanced steering vectors enabling precise control over model outputs – to create realistic digital patient twins with controllable psychiatric symptoms for scalable clinician training. We leverage Conceptors to encode specific symptom constructs (Anxious/misery, Psychosis, Behavioral/externalizing, Fear) with scalable intensity and combinability, surpassing traditional prompting. We will develop Conceptors using the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort, a community sample of 9,500+ individuals with comprehensive psychiatric assessments and diagnostic criteria. A key innovation is Conceptor shareability. Once validated, symptom-specific Conceptors can be distributed to other institutions, accelerating training and collaborative research. Primary applications include: (1) interdisciplinary clinical training through safe interactions with diverse patient presentations; (2) validation of language-based diagnostic tools against reproducible digital twin presentations before clinical deployment. This collaboration unites clinical expertise for symptom annotation with AI capabilities for Conceptor development. STELLAR will be tested by an experienced clinical team with global reach and diverse stakeholder input.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: GENSCORE Project: Leveraging Generative AI to adapt and enhance the scoring of widely used mental health assessment tools in low-resource context
description: In Nigeria where about 250 psychiatrists serve over 220 million people, contextually accurate mental health screening tools are not just beneficial, they are essential. Our GENSCORE Project aims to develop and validate a culturally grounded, multimodal AI platform/software to improve depression and anxiety screening for Pidgin English, Hausa, and Yoruba speakers in Nigeria. The project will build on our successful pilot to co-develop GENSCORE-DATA v2.0, one of Africa’s largest multilingual mental health dataset, and fine- tune GENSCORE-LLM v2.0 for culturally aligned interpretation. Our culturally relevant model, GENSCORE-LLM, will enable the development of contextually relevant mental health screening (GenPHQ and GenGAD) tools co-designed with people with lived experience and mental health experts. These tools will be integrated into an open-access, multimodal GENSCORE platform combining voice (audio) and self-reported text, facilitating real-time screening and decision support. The GENSCORE tools will undergo rigorous community and clinical validation and benchmarked against SCID-5-CV assessments among 990 participants in language-specific sites: Lagos State (Pidgin English), Abuja, FCT (Hausa) and Oyo State (Yoruba). Robust ethical, governance, and safety frameworks will ensure fairness, data sovereignty, and responsible AI use, with broad national and international dissemination.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: SYLFAEN-PSY: SYmptom Learning through Foundation models to Augment and ENhance measurement in PSYchosis
description: Dimensional symptom scales are sensitive measurements of the course of psychosis. While they are recommended for routinely monitoring psychotic symptoms, their use is inconsistent at best: Fewer than 30% of psychiatrists report even occasionally using them, while research studies often differ substantially in which and how many scales they assess, even when measuring the same symptoms. Thus, most people with psychotic disorders, either in the clinic or as research participants, only get their experiences partially translated (if at all) into quantitative dimensions. One main argument against dimensional scales is that they are lengthy to complete, and our project offers a pragmatic alternative. We will create a system, informed by lived experience and based on Large Language Models, to generate proxy measurements of psychotic symptoms by integrating multimodal data. These proxies will be validated against gold-standard scales in deeply characterised cohorts of individuals with psychotic disorders, and in research data from mental health NHS services. Through extensive assessments of uncertainty and bias, we will develop a new standard for AI-based information extraction and inference in mental health research, delivering a solution for assessing the experiences of people with psychosis at scale, and removing a long-standing barrier for symptom-based research.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: “B-ZERO” - Accelerating progress towards HBV elimination in Africa by using treatment to deliver aviraemia
description: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) causes over 250 million chronic infections worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in Africa. Oral nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) treatment is prescribed to suppress viraemia and curb transmission, but is not curative. New WHO guidelines increase treatment eligibility from 50% of people living with HBV. However, new real-world data suggest one-quarter of those treated may not achieve durable viraemic suppression (VS), for reasons not yet explored. Therefore, the impact of treatment expansion is unknown. B-ZERO will address this evidence gap through three integrated approaches: ● Registry analysis: interrogation of the HEPSANET HBV ‘living registry’, representing 12 African countries, to quantify VS prevalence and identify predictors of treatment outcome. ● Deep phenotyping: longitudinal study of HBV cohorts in South Africa and Ethiopia for laboratory profiling to assess the role of viral genotype, antiviral resistance, drug levels, and liver reservoir in treatment outcome. ● Policy-focused modelling: use of transmission modelling to project population-impact of scaling up HBV treatment in Africa, while incorporating non-VS and drug resistance, to inform intervention strategies. The programme will identify risk factors for treatment failure, reveal mechanisms for persistent viraemia on treatment with actionable interventions, and deliver policy guidance for HBV elimination in Africa.

title: Prediction and Early Intervention in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
description: While obsessions (intrusive, unwelcome thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive, cumbersome behaviors) are experienced by many children and young people, we currently cannot predict when these features might become highly impairing for an individual, sometimes leading to a diagnosis of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). To meet this gap, we aim to develop a tool to pinpoint who is likely to develop OCD and when. We will combine easily obtainable information, often found in medical records, with more complex information on genetic make- up and brain features, to find out which type of information helps most in prediction. Along with those living with OCD and clinical teams, we will explore how, when and where such tools are best used. We also aim to develop an online intervention for parents of children likely to develop OCD that is accessible, usable and effective. We are working in three nations, Brazil, the UK and Sweden, so this intervention can incorporate the experiences of those with OCD across several cultures, ensuring the intervention can be used widely. At each step of this research, those with lived experience of OCD will shape our goals, help with the research, and make sure findings are meaningful and shared widely.
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: Discovering new therapeutic strategies for tuberculous meningitis
description: There are opportunities to improve tuberculous meningitis (TBM) treatment, reducing its 30% case-fatality. A resurgent pipeline of new anti-tuberculosis drugs may kill bacteria faster than current drugs, and targeted anti- inflammatory drugs may control life-threatening brain inflammation better than standard-of-care corticosteroids. However, the opportunities are impaired by poor understanding of disease and therapeutic mechanisms; a lack of animal models that predict likely efficacy of new drugs/regimens in humans; and no biomarkers of successful treatment outcomes. We will therefore create a platform for the pre-clinical/clinical discovery and development of new therapeutic strategies for TBM, linking human experimental medicine in Vietnam and South Africa with animal models. We will study two potent bedaquiline- containing anti-TB regimens and two TNF-targeted anti-inflammatory drugs in humans and mice with TBM. We aim to quantify the relationship between anti- tuberculosis drug concentrations, bacterial killing, inflammation, and outcome; define the mouse model’s ability to recapitulate human therapeutic relationships; and discover novel inflammatory and physiological biomarkers of outcome. We will also study the therapeutic potential of three new drugs for TBM (ganfeborole; telecebec; TBAJ-876) in the rabbit and mouse TBM models, establishing their role in the discovery and development of new therapeutic strategies for TBM. Key words: tuberculous meningitis; therapeutic strategies

title: CRITICAL SEEING: using film, ethnographic, and deliberative methods to form multimodal representations of ICU decision-making dispute, and to model practices of conflict reduction
description: Deciding whether to continue intensive care is increasingly complex. Mismatched expectations and cultural differences often lead to conflict between clinicians and families—sometimes ending in court, where rulings are inconsistent and rarely establish clear precedent. Many families experience moral injury and clinical staff face burnout from protracted disputes. Better policy and processes are needed, but these require deeper understanding from all parties of the intricacies, benefits, and potential harms of modern ICU treatments. Traditional survey methods are limited in their ability to represent dispute complexity. Our vision is to unite intensive care experts, patient groups, nurses, and legal professionals through the multimodal practices of film, ethnography, and citizen science, to foster more meaningful engagement. Using observational, deliberative, participatory, and reenactment techniques, we will record the emotional and procedural dynamics of ICU decisions, encourage critical dialogue among stakeholders and with the wider public, and model alternative conflict‑resolution methods. Our outputs include a shareable toolkit and online materials, a feature film, and a multiscreen installation. The aim is to discover better ways of communicating the social, legal, ethical, and cultural dimensions underpinning ICU conflict, in order to facilitate new approaches to reducing its incidence and the harms that arise.

title: Impact of laboratory rearing and colonisation of mosquitoes on the mating behaviour, reproductive fitness and genetic diversity of malaria vectors for informed future release efforts
description: In the context of insecticide resistance in mosquitoes, biological control through the releases of sterile, genetically-modified or Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes represents promising complementary strategies for effective malaria control. The success of these strategies critically depends on the mating success of laboratory-reared males with wild females in the field. To optimise these strategies, several knowledge gaps crucial for effective field implementation need to be addressed. In this proposal, I aim, through a set of laboratory, semi-field and field experiments, to assess the impact of laboratory-rearing and colony maintenance of malaria mosquitoes on mating behaviour, fitness and genetic diversity of males. I will use these data to build a reliable mathematical model to predict the mating success of laboratory-reared male malaria mosquitoes in the field. This study will therefore provide tools and a framework for monitoring the fitness of male mosquitoes and help optimising the implementation of mosquito release strategies for effective malaria control in sub-Saharan Africa. Keywords: Malaria mosquitoes, Laboratory-rearing, Mosquito colonisation, Mating success, Male release strategies, Predictive model.
recipient: Institut de Recherche en Sciences de la Santé Direction Régionale de l'Ouest

title: Generative AI for Identifying Mechanisms and Intervention Points in the Intergenerational Transmission of Anxiety
description: Understanding how anxiety is transmitted from parent to child remains one of the most important yet elusive challenges in clinical science. Parental anxiety profoundly shapes children’s emotional development, yet we lack tools to capture these processes as they unfold in real-world interactions. This is a critical knowledge gap and persistent barrier to developing effective interventions. RAISE-AI (Resilience Across Intergenerational Stresses and Emotional Health through AI-Enabled Discovery) applies generative AI to detect and explain how stress, worry, and fear pass between parents and children. We will develop models that identify when and how anxiety signals are transmitted through multimodal cues (e.g., language, prosody, facial affect, posture) during naturalistic interactions and evaluate these models for accuracy, interpretability, and fairness across racially, ethnically, and socioeconomically diverse families. Finally, we will generate outputs (e.g., summaries, real-time feedback) to inform pediatric anxiety prevention and treatment plans. If funded, RAISE-AI will reveal the mechanisms through which parental anxiety shapes children’s emotional responses and establish one of the first pediatric benchmarks for generative-AI performance in mental health. By translating subtle emotional signals into interpretable feedback, it will help providers support families and advance ethical, culturally responsive pediatric mental health interventions. Key Words: Anxiety; Parent-Child Interaction; Developmental Psychopathology
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Culturally Aligned Generative AI to Support Para-Counselors in Low-Resource Community Mental Health Settings
description: This project aims to develop culturally grounded generative AI tools to support para-counselors in Bangladesh who provide front-line mental health support for anxiety, depression, and psychosis. Para-counselors are often embedded in community-based services but work with limited training and diagnostic tools, leading to oversimplified or incorrect attributions (e.g., financial hardship as the cause of all distress). Our goal is to integrate a causal reasoning framework with large language models (LLMs) to help para- counselors understand their clients using explanatory models that are culturally and contextually appropriate and align better with client experiences and scientific understanding, thereby informing the development of culturally resonant care plans and intervention strategies. We adopt a rigorous, participatory approach: lived experience experts are embedded throughout the project lifecycle-as co-researchers, evaluators, advisory board members, and compensated co-designers-to shape tool functionality, language, and deployment strategy. During the research, we will build on data centered on people with lived experiences, develop a causal graph library reflecting local idioms of distress, and evaluate language and reasoning performance with stakeholders. The solution will be open source, interoperable with existing systems, and designed for future scaling across LMIC contexts. Long-term capacity-building with partner organizations will ensure sustainability and continuous improvement.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Serotonergic orchestration of frontal cortical neural dynamics underlying economic decision-making
description: Animals make economic decisions, weighing potential costs and payoffs of each option. Past studies have linked both frontal cortical activity and neuromodulatory release to economic decision-making, yet how these work together to influence choice remains unclear. A key technical limitation has been the lack of tools to perform simultaneous, high-resolution imaging of neuromodulatory and cortical signals. To study the relationship between these signals, this proposal focuses on serotonin release in dorsal frontal cortex as a testbed for two reasons: first, dorsal frontal cortex is readily accessible to cutting-edge dual-color two-photon (2p) imaging techniques, and second, serotonin encodes economic variables such as state value and reward, and projects strongly to frontal cortex. I first plan to conduct dual-color 2p imaging from mice performing visual decision-making tasks, allowing the construction of cell-type-specific spatial maps of serotonin release. Next, using optogenetic tools, I will clarify the relationship between serotonin release and cortical encoding of economic variables. Finally, using advanced optical tools, I will determine whether the precise spatial structure of serotonin release in frontal cortex is necessary to guide complex economic decisions. This work will provide fundamental insights into how neuromodulatory release and cortical dynamics work together to control economic decision-making.

title: Advancing methods for pharmacological fMRI to improve discovery and development of treatments for mental health
description: This project aims to advance pharmacological functional magnetic resonance imaging (pharmaco-fMRI) as a robust and reliable tool for accelerating the clinical development of novel mental health treatments and to develop pharmaco-fMRI-based precision approaches for predicting individual responses to drugs. Treatment effectiveness in psychiatry is often unpredictable due to varied responses and subjective diagnoses, contributing to high drug trial failure rates. Funders and regulators now promote objective measures, such as functional neuroimaging, to improve precision drug development. Pharmaco-fMRI is a validated method for quantifying brain function changes in response to drugs, but small sample sizes have limited its impact. This fellowship will aggregate existing datasets, already pledged by over 15 leading PIs, harmonise the largest pharmaco-fMRI dataset to date, and establish a consortium to facilitate sharing with researchers. Using this dataset, this fellowship will develop novel methods to characterise subject-specific drug effects free from confounds like scanner and acquisition sequence, enabling drug response prediction from resting-state brain function. This will be done using a new foundation model of brain function, BrainLM. The project will also validate advanced methods like Receptor Enriched Analysis of Connectivity by Targets (REACT), which provides molecular insights from fMRI scans without the need for costly PET scans.

title: Reimagining Prevention Science: LGBTQ+ Collective Action to Prevent Depression and Anxiety in Urban Vietnam
description: This project investigates how LGBTQ+ communities in the Global South are forging new forms of care and activism amid high rates of depression, anxiety, and exclusion from both public health systems and heteronormative society. Existing interventions—individualised, clinical, and Global North-derived—are often inadequate in the face of structural discrimination. I ask: can community-led collective action prevent depression and anxiety among LGBTQ+ people? Focusing on LGBTQ+ networks in urban Vietnam—one of the most dynamic sites of queer solidarity in the Global South—I reimagine collective action as a pathway to mental health. I define it as 'voluntary group efforts to support mutual well-being and respond to structural discrimination.' I will (1) theorise how LGBTQ+ collective action emerges, unfolds, and shapes mental health through a grounded theory study, (2) model reciprocal dynamics between collective action and depression/anxiety using an observational cohort, and (3) co-adapt and evaluate a promising collective action-based intervention through participatory and realist methods. Bridging the social and health sciences, this project integrates qualitative and quantitative approaches into a unified, three-stage pipeline. It sheds light on a neglected field—LGBTQ+ mental health in the Global South—and offers a new blueprint for prevention science, centring empowerment and structural transformation where traditional systems have failed.

title: Cilia: a new therapeutic target for type 1 diabetes?
description: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system destroys insulin-producing β-cells in pancreatic islets, leading to lifelong insulin dependence and increased risk of multi-organ complications. Despite advances in care, the triggers of β-cell destruction remain poorly understood, limiting efforts to develop preventative therapies. This proposal investigates a virtually unexplored aspect of islet biology: the role of cilia, specialised signalling structures found on islet cells, in regulating cell communication and controlling vulnerability to immune attack. Using advanced imaging and genetic tools, I will: (i) map cilia-associated genes and proteins across islet cell types to identify disrupted signalling pathways; (ii) determine how cilia dysfunction alters intercellular communication, potentially exposing β-cells to immune destruction; (iii) compare cilia structure and gene expression in healthy, at-risk, and diabetic human and mouse islets; and (iv) assess how cilia loss affects islet composition, hormone secretion, and immune infiltration in cilia-deficient mouse models. This work proposes a shift in understanding T1D, suggesting that cilia-mediated signalling is essential for maintaining islet homeostasis and that its disruption contributes to disease. By uncovering how cilia coordinate islet cell interactions, I aim to reveal new immune triggers and identify therapeutic targets to prevent or halt T1D progression.

title: Back to the Beginning: Understanding mechanisms regulating human intervertebral disc development and their dysregulation in degenerative disease using an integrated multi-omic approach
description: Intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration is a leading cause of chronic low back pain and disability, impacting millions of people worldwide. The IVD is made up of a central nucleus pulposus (NP) surrounded by an annulus fibrosus and is essential for flexibility and movement. During development, the NP is populated by notochordal cells, and these are replaced by chondrocyte cells by adolescence. Loss of notochordal cells coincides with the onset of degeneration, suggesting that early signals are essential for disc homeostasis. While most research focuses on end-stage degeneration, early events driving the onset of disease in humans remain poorly understood.
