As a result, current therapies lack long-term efficacy, and we need better treatments for disc degeneration. Preliminary transcriptomic data revealed that specific genes are upregulated during development, repressed in maturation and reactivated during degeneration, suggesting a dysregulation of developmental mechanisms. SPP1 (secreted phosphoprotein-1) is one such gene and has been selected as a candidate for analysis. This proposal aims to elucidate the function and mechanisms regulating SPP1 in human IVD development and how dysregulation contributes to degeneration. I will apply an integrated workflow combining long-read sequencing, ATAC-sequencing, proteomics, bioinformatics, gene-editing and biofabrication to define these mechanisms, revealing potential targets for regeneration.

title: Bridging the Treatment Gap with AI-Enhanced Supervision (BRIDGE-AI)
description: BRIDGE-AI aims to strengthen the quality and scalability of evidence-based psychological treatments in low-resource settings by designing and evaluating an AI-enabled supervision feedback tool for non-specialist counselors in India. Leveraging the CARE platform (an existing, validated AI-powered feedback tool) and over 4,000 Behavioral Activation therapy sessions delivered in Hindi by non-specialists, the study will: (1) Develop the BRIDGE-AI tool to identify key therapeutic techniques and generate timely, culturally-grounded feedback that helps counselors strengthen their practice and supervisors prioritize cases needing additional support; (2) Evaluate the tool’s acceptability, feasibility, and impact on counselor performance and patient outcomes through a pilot trial; and (3) Co-develop an ethical, participatory framework to ensure safe, transparent, and equitable integration into supervision systems. BRIDGE-AI integrates expertise in AI, ethics, lived experience, psychological science, quality-assured supervision, and global mental health to strengthen task-shared care in primary care settings in the Global South. The project combines participatory design with technical innovation to ensure the tool reflects local realities, strengthens therapy- quality measurement, and generates evidence on how AI can safely and effectively collaborate with non-specialist counselors and supervisors. Together, these efforts will lay the groundwork for scalable, trustworthy, and ethically governed quality-assurance systems in global mental health care.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Uncovering the interplay of synaptic activity and TDP-43 pathology in neurodegeneration
description: TDP-43 pathology and altered states of synaptic activity are defining hallmarks of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD), and Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), yet it remains unclear how these features interconnect to drive neurodegeneration. This project proposes that TDP-43 dysfunction and abnormal states of synaptic activity are tightly interlinked, forming a feedforward loop that exacerbates their respective pathological states. The project will first characterise how progressive TDP-43 pathology drives evolving states of synaptic activity, arising from both loss- and gain- of-function mechanisms. Advanced electrophysiological approaches in human neurons will be leveraged to examine individual synapses through to emergent network dysfunction and combined with detailed synaptic profiling to uncover molecular mechanisms driving altered activity states. Subsequently, the project will characterise how synaptic activity in turn modulates TDP-43, first focussing on how acute synaptic activity regulates phase separation and condensation of physiological TDP-43, leading to altered protein interactions and downstream RNA processing. Subsequently the project will focus on how these processes deteriorate into pathological states, exploring how chronically dysregulated synaptic activity exacerbates existing pathological conditions of mis-localised TDP-43. Together, this work aims to define a feedforward loop between TDP-43 and synaptic activity that underpins neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Conformational Switches in Action: A New Framework for Understanding Macromolecular Machines in Genome Maintenance
description: Macromolecular complexes perform essential cellular activities by harnessing chemical energy to drive biological processes. My recent discovery of the "entropy switch" mechanism in replicative helicases (Nature, 2025) established a new paradigm in understanding how such machines work, revealing that ATP hydrolysis achieves mechanical work not through power strokes – but by releasing constraints to permit molecular motions that drive function. Building on this breakthrough, I aim to establish an independent research program investigating how annealing helicases – SMARCAL1 and ZRANB3 – harness ATP to drive DNA rewinding during replication stress. Using my pioneering integration of time-resolved cryo-EM with AI-driven conformational analysis, I will: (1) dissect SMARCAL1's mechanism for displacing RPA from single-stranded DNA, (2) reveal how ZRANB3 employs substrate-dependent conformational switching between annealing and nuclease activities, and (3) define how mechanochemical coupling drives reverse reactions in these specialised enzymes. This work will address fundamental questions about energy transduction while providing mechanistic insights into diseases caused by annealing helicase mutations. The Accelerator Award will accelerate my transition to independence and establish the foundation for investigating diverse genome maintenance complexes. It will enable me to develop leadership skills, build preliminary data for major funding applications, and establish my distinctive scientific identity.

title: Mental illness in perimenopause: Longitudinal predictors and preventive treatment opportunities
description: Perimenopause is increasingly recognised as a high-risk period for mental illness. Yet, despite its relevance to a global population of ~725 million middle-aged women, it remains strikingly under-investigated. This project aims to transform early prediction and intervention by identifying women at heightened risk of first-onset or recurrent anxiety, depressive, bipolar, and psychotic disorders during perimenopause. We will leverage four large-scale longitudinal cohorts—the Danish Nurse Cohort, Danish Twin Registry, Swedish Women’s Lifestyle and Health cohort, and Swedish Twin Registry—linked to national registers in Denmark and Sweden. Our three aims are to: (1) quantify risk of psychiatric disorders and functional impairment during perimenopause compared to pre- and post-menopause and the general population; (2) develop and externally validate dynamic prediction models for perimenopausal psychiatric episodes; and (3) emulate a target trial estimating the effect of hormone therapy (HT) on mental health outcomes. Key deliverables include population-level psychiatric risk estimates across menopause stages, two web- based risk calculators to support clinical decision-making, and evidence-based guidance on HT for psychiatric risk reduction. Drawing on multidisciplinary expertise and lived experience, this project addresses long-standing sex- and age-related disparities in mental health and delivers actionable tools to support early detection and personalised prevention, advancing healthy ageing in women.
recipient: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
programme: Leveraging longitudinal data to transform early intervention in mental health

title: Decoding Mechanisms of Early Antipsychotic Response in First-Episode Psychosis: A Multimodal Approach
description: Psychotic disorders affect more than 3% of the global population and rank among the most disabling health conditions worldwide. Over 40% of individuals with first-episode psychosis (FEP) do not respond to first-line antipsychotic therapy; however, the neurobiological basis for early-treatment non-response remains poorly understood. Converging evidence points to differences between responders and non-responders across multiple brain systems—including dopaminergic, glutamatergic, and large-scale neural networks—however, integrative studies at illness onset are lacking. This project will use a multimodal approach to understand the disease mechanisms underlying early- treatment non-response in FEP. Participants will undergo neuromelanin- sensitive MRI (to probe dopamine system integrity), magnetic resonance spectroscopy (to quantify glutamate levels in the anterior cingulate cortex), resting-state fMRI (to examine large-scale network dynamics), alongside neurocognitive assessment. Structured clinical assessments will determine treatment response at six weeks, with plasma antipsychotic levels to confirm adherence. Healthy controls will provide normative reference data. The study will generate preliminary effect sizes, evaluate feasibility, and identify candidate markers for future mechanistic models. An international placement at a centre of excellence will support training in multimodal data integration and explainable machine learning. This work will lay the foundation for a more personalised and mechanistically informed approach to psychiatric care.

title: Diversity in Chronobiology: Discovering dynamics and interactions in chronobiology using multimodal, multiscale, and multinational data
description: This project will elucidate dynamics and interactions of human biological rhythms – vital for mental and physical health – through multimodal, multiscale, and multinational data. We will specifically address a critical knowledge gap about how real-life biological rhythms vary in non-Western populations. The three major aims of this proposal are to: 1) collect and curate a geographically and ethnically diverse dataset of healthy human biological rhythms from communities in Brazil, Botswana, Indonesia, Singapore, and the UK over 12 weeks using wearable-sensor technology; 2) combine cutting- edge signal processing with modern dynamical systems and machine learning to identify “low-dimensional latent rhythms” from multimodal wearable data streams (e.g., actigraphy, photoplethysmography, skin temperature, etc.); and 3) build normative models that capture how biological rhythms change with age, sex, and environment. The developed methods and models will form the basis of an open-source software toolbox to help future research quantify and interpret biological rhythms in real-world contexts. Importantly, this proposal will lay the foundation for future global studies on chronobiological health and pave the way for rhythm-based precision medicine, including chronotherapy. Moreover, it will provide an unprecedented dataset for exploring how geographical, ethnical, cultural, and biological factors shape our biological clocks in naturalistic settings.

title: A Life in Sound: Transforming Understandings of Health and Wellbeing through Music, Sonic Arts, and Modes of Listening
description: This practice-based project explores how music, sound, and modes of listening can transform understandings of the human body. It establishes a new theoretical framework of corporeal acoustemology: a mode of embodied, auditory knowledge of the body as sonic field. Using the compositional methodology of artistic sonation, biomedical and experiential information is creatively transducted and expressed through music and sonic arts. At the intersection of health humanities, sound studies, and composition, this project asks how non- lexical sonic artworks might express physiological processes; how corporeal listening can foster affiliation and address health misinformation; and how these approaches can be ethically and creatively evaluated. Outputs include a monograph, composition portfolio, listening events, a radio documentary series, and an interdisciplinary conference. The project also engages with medical sound archives, illness narratives, and develops engaged research events involving participants from boroughs with significant health inequalities. While sound and music are often associated with therapeutic practices and creative health activities, the objective of this project is to extend beyond these applications, positioning sonic artworks and musical compositions as significant psychosocial resources and interventions in their own right which, in turn, help people better understand their bodies and foster beneficial, relational, corporeal listening practices.

title: The Role Of Antibody Feedback In Anti-Viral Humoral Immunity
description: Everyone experiences multiple infections and vaccine exposures throughout life, despite this, viral disease remains a huge global health problem. Here we will take our understanding of how prior exposure controls humoral responses to a completely new level. We hypothesise antibodies “feedback” by competing with pre-existing memory B cells for antigen and so limit immune imprinting. This feedback leads to increased epitope coverage and clonal diversity because only B cells targeting new epitopes can steal the antigen back and participate in germinal centres. This project will discover the rules of this system to hijack and programme superior vaccine responses. We plan three transformative immunological and computational aims: (1) Determine how antibody feedback modulates viral imprinting in humans (2) Define how antibody feedback works mechanistically in the germinal centre (3) Test whether antibody feedback can be manipulated to tailor the breadth and specificity of antibody responses after immunisation. We have a unique combination of computational and 3D organoid models, human pre- and post-vaccination samples and an established experimental immunisation model to facilitate these aims. This programme promises to redefine our understanding of how antibody responses are regulated and to provide the most complete understanding of how to tailor vaccine outcomes to date.

title: Strengthening Adolescent Resilience to Improve Sexual and reproductive hEalth (ARISE) Uganda
description: This study will generate new evidence on how resilience—defined as positive adaptation despite adversity—shapes sexual and reproductive health (SRH) outcomes among Ugandan adolescents aged 10–19. In Uganda, where adolescents comprise a quarter of the population, rates of HIV, STIs, and unintended pregnancy remain among the highest globally, posing a critical and urgent public health challenge. Drawing on my experience leading research on gender, violence, and adolescent SRH across sub-Saharan Africa, this study applies the Candidacy Framework in a novel way to examine how resilience is shaped, enacted, and constrained across social and structural contexts. Shifting from risk-focused paradigms, it foregrounds adolescents’ strengths—across individual, relational, community, and structural levels—and how these interact with gender and context to influence SRH trajectories. A rigorous mixed-methods design—including longitudinal and cross-sectional surveys, biological testing, participatory approaches, and qualitative methods—will generate generalisable data and deep insight into lived experience. This integrative approach supports nuanced, dynamic analysis of resilience over time. A context-specific tool to measure resilience will be developed and validated, contributing conceptual and empirical innovation. Strong ethical safeguards, youth-led engagement, and collaborative partnerships will ensure cultural relevance and impact. Findings will inform scalable, equity-focused policy and programming aligned to Ugandan and global adolescent health priorities.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: shamiriAI – Scalable, Culturally-Informed AI for Fidelity Feedback and Adaptive Training in Youth Mental Health
description: Training and supervising non-specialists to deliver evidence-based mental health interventions (“task-shifting”) is a promising strategy for closing the youth mental health treatment gap. However, scaling this approach is constrained by supervision bottlenecks, as traditional methods are labor- intensive and rely on scarce professionals. To address this, we’ve developed shamiriAI, an AI-augmented supervision tool for non-specialist lay-providers. shamiriAI processes session audio, using multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and prosodic analysis to generate structured feedback for supervisors. Operating within an "AI-in-the-loop" design, shamiriAI supplements—rather than replaces—supervisors, who remain the primary agents of supervision. Our proposal seeks to further develop, deploy, and rigorously evaluate shamiriAI through three aims: (1) Further develop shamiriAI through co-design to ensure a safe, contextually-grounded system with advanced multilingual ASR and prosodic modeling; (2) Conduct a comprehensive implementation science evaluation by deploying shamiriAI within training and supervision workflows of a task-shifted youth mental health program; and (3) Conduct a well-powered randomized non-inferiority trial (N=1,000 youth; N=20 lay providers) to test if AI-augmented supervision maintains clinical effectiveness while improving fidelity and cost-effectiveness. Outputs include open-source models and datasets, implementation guides, and peer-reviewed manuscripts. Ultimately, we hope to create a template for safe, contextually- grounded AI-augmented supervision in mental health programs globally.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Investigating non-professional efferocytosis through two new, in vivo models
description: Apoptotic cell death is fundamental to life – sculpting tissues during development; underpinning homeostatic tissue turnover; and driving repair and regeneration. However, apoptotic corpses must be rapidly engulfed and cleared, a process called efferocytosis, to avoid triggering inflammatory responses which cause disease. Professional phagocytes, such as macrophages, are well known in apoptotic corpse clearance, yet in many tissues non-professional phagocytes also make important contributions to efferocytosis. These non- professionals are largely overlooked and remain poorly understood due to a lack of quality models and tools for their study. To address this, I will develop and define two new, complementary in vivo models of non-professional efferocytosis in the developing fruit fly. Capitalising on Drosophila’s powerful genetic toolkit, which allows live visualisation of apoptosis and efferocytosis, I will characterise cell-level mechanisms employed by these non-professional phagocytes to engulf and process apoptotic corpses. I will then identify conserved features in vertebrate systems. Finally, I will take a tissue-level perspective and investigate the functional contributions and consequences of apoptotic corpse clearance by different phagocyte populations. This will deliver major advances in understanding of non-professional efferocytosis, relevant to development, homeostasis and disease, with the models I establish providing a powerful platform for my future independent research programme.

title: Feeling the credit crunch: The intergenerational impact of problem debt, 1980 to the present
description: Feeling the Credit Crunch will comprehensively connect lived experiences of problem debt and mental health to changing welfare logics and cultural discourses of credit use in Britain since 1980. Through intergenerational participatory workshops, oral histories and archival research, the project will generate a new evidence base to drive more integrated policy responses to problem debt and mental health in the present. From 1980, the liberalisation of consumer credit facilitated a credit boom. In less than a decade, levels of problem debt – characterised by the inability to meet credit commitments – soared across Britain. As access to consumer credit expanded, state welfare support contracted, and personal debt became an essential means by which some families maintained a basic standard of living. Contemporary research demonstrates a growing awareness of the effects of indebtedness on mental health amidst ongoing cost of living crises, but in what ways is this relationship reciprocal, and how has it been experienced across generations against the backdrop of shifting political, welfare and cultural climates since 1980? Only by understanding the lived interconnections between problem debt and mental health in the longer term can we begin to address issues that continue to affect families, healthcare and the economy today.

title: Shedding new light on tissue mechanobiology with multimodal multiphoton nano- rheology microscopy
description: Mucosal tissues are essential components of our body. For example, in the lung, mucus provides a barrier that entraps foreign pathogens/nanoparticles and is moved into the oesophagus by coordinated ciliary beating of epithelial cells. Mucus viscoelasticity is crucial to this movement, and poor mucociliary clearance correlates with lung diseases. In the living tissue, mucus is changing in space and time, dynamically regulated by neighbouring cells which are heterogeneously organised. However, existing methods cannot measure mucus mechanics at the spatio-temporal scale relevant to nanoparticle transport, correlatively with the behaviour of the cell/tissue environment changing in real time. We propose to develop a transformative multiphoton-microscopy technology that measures mucus viscoelasticity by tracking the trajectories of individual nano-probes with unprecedented nanoscale precision, and correlatively maps the 3D structure and composition of living airway tissues with sub-cellular resolution and molecular chemical specificity. We will apply the technology to healthy and diseased tissues, in response to inflammatory triggers, infections and drugs. This research will unlock new discoveries on how mucus mechanics interconnects to cellular/molecular regulatory pathways, including airways remodelling/fibrosis which is a massive unmet medical need. Beyond the lung, our microscopy technology is applicable to any biofluid- tissue system, enabling wide-ranging discoveries to improve human health.

title: EMPHASIS – Electron Microscopy Platform for High-throughput Analysis and Spectroscopic Imaging Systems
description: This project develops EMPHASIS—a novel hybrid imaging platform that combines quantum technology control techniques with electron microscopy to transform how biological samples are visualised at the nanoscale. Using a novel quantum platform rather than mechanical stages, EMPHASIS enables six-dimensional control over proteins, viruses, and nanomaterials, reducing imaging times from hours to minutes while enhancing spatial resolution and long-term stability. By integrating the new platform directly into the microscope environment, EMPHASIS unlocks real-time, in situ control and spectroscopic readout, paving the way for richer structural and functional characterisation of individual biomolecules. This fusion of quantum technologies with biomedical imaging opens a new frontier for studying complex biological systems with unprecedented clarity and speed. The research builds on foundational work in quantum control and aims to deliver a step-change in the tools available to molecular biology, structural medicine, and pharmaceutical science. EMPHASIS will ultimately empower researchers with a faster, more precise method for probing disease mechanisms, tracking therapeutic interactions, and accelerating drug discovery at the single-particle level. Keywords: Electron Microscopy, Biophysics, Imaging, Structural Biology, Nanotechnology, Tomography, Quantum Technology

title: PHOENix: Planetary Health Optimisation for Enhancing Nutrition and Food Security through School Feeding Programmes in Egypt
description: School feeding programmes reach 418 million children globally. Egypt, the most populous Arab country and third largest in Africa, is projected to reach 120 million people by 2030, with 42 million children under 18 and the largest school feeding programme in Africa. In 2021, while 4.9 million children were anaemic, over 9 million received nutritionally inadequate, ultra-processed dry meals heavily reliant on imported wheat. This undermines local producers and raises serious concerns around nutrition, food security, and environmental sustainability. PHOENix aims to optimise school feeding programmes in Egypt to deliver essential nutrition during critical stages of development, enhance environmental sustainability, and empower small agroecological producers and local communities. Following a planetary health perspective, I will use mixed and creative methods to map challenges and co-produce transformative, decolonial solutions for school food systems that build resilience to climate change and can be scaled across Egypt and other Global South contexts. Building on my doctoral and postdoctoral research in England, where I pioneered a planetary health framework for school meals, this fellowship will enable me to adapt this approach to the Global South, where food insecurity and climate change impacts are most acute, and the link to school feeding programmes remains under-explored.

title: Decoding Competition in the Brain
description: Competition is a key evolutionary force that drives organisms to exceptional performance in pursuit of critical goals, such as sex or food. Yet it can also induce excessive risk-taking and maladaptive behaviours. Despite its ubiquitous role in nature and human society, we still lack a mechanistic account of how the presence of rivals (‘competitive pressure’) is translated into changes in decision-making. This programme pioneers a multiscale dissection of how competitive pressure recalibrates motivational choice, using Drosophila for its unique genetic and neural-circuit tractability. We discovered that flies exposed to rivals persist in mating and feeding despite visual threats. This behaviour requires prior social experience, implicating long-lasting changes in neural circuits. We will investigate circuit signalling from molecules to networks to understand the underpinnings of competition-driven decision-making. We seek to (1) establish how competitive pressure affects the neural dynamics underlying high-risk decisions; (2) uncover the molecular and cellular-plasticity mechanisms by which competitive context induces long-term effects on decision-making; and (3) test whether common neuromodulatory networks (dopamine/serotonin/neuropeptides) and core neural principles bias decision-making across competitive contexts. This research will address whether competitive pressure functions as a ‘master motivation’, a high-level organiser of behavioural priorities that governs how animals arbitrate between conflicting drives.

title: Institutional practices, community action, and individual resistance: Understanding the mechanisms generating LGBTQ+ health inequities
description: This Discovery project establishes a bold vision for investigating and addressing LGBTQ+ health inequities. There are very few, if any, health outcomes where LGBTQ+ inequities are not substantial and entrenched across the lifecourse. Existing theories suggest why health inequities occur, but research documenting mechanistic processes is lacking. This gap results from a heightened focus on individual-level processes that overlook the multi-level mechanisms leading to poor LGBTQ+ health. To address this gap there is an urgent need for approaches that bring together data and insights within and across different levels (institutional, community, individual) to generate robust evidence that identifies how to address LGBTQ+ health inequities. This project meets this need by galvanising interdisciplinary, multi-methods, and inter-sectoral expertise to: 1) investigate how UK institutions structure LGBTQ+ health inequities; 2) explore how community initiatives mitigate or further exacerbate institutional practices; and 3) establish how institutional, community, and individual-level processes result in LGBTQ+ health inequalities across the lifecourse. Bringing together an innovative combination of substantive, experiential and methodological expertise across sectors and academic disciplines, the project will develop new theoretical and methodological frameworks to forge a transformative, systematic multi-level approach to investigate and address LGBTQ+ health inequalities.

title: Neural representations of compositional elements in flexible behaviour.
description: Flexible behaviour depends on the brain’s ability to extract structure from experience and apply it to novel situations. This is thought to rely on latent states – internal representations that capture hidden structure in the world and serve as behavioural frameworks for planning and decision-making. To support flexibility, these models must also be compositional – generalise to new scenarios by combining and rearranging their individual components. While growing evidence suggests that the hippocampus encodes abstract latent states and organises simple representations into sequences, the neural mechanisms underlying the development and compositional use of abstract latent states remain poorly understood. This project will investigate how latent states are constructed and used compositionally and uncover the learning algorithms and neural mechanisms that support their development. Using a complex spatial navigation task in mice, I will combine high-density electrophysiology, two- photon calcium imaging, and causal manipulations to track the emergence, organisation, and compositional use of latent state representations in the ventral hippocampus. I will test how hippocampal replay and dopamine signalling shape and update these representations. This work will establish a mechanistic account of how the brain abstracts experience into compositional elements to support flexible behaviour – core process of complex cognition often disrupted in mental illness.

title: The Developing Children’s Connectome Project (DCCP)
description: The Developing Children’s Connectome Project (DCCP) will establish a fundamental understanding of brain, cognitive and socio-emotional development by acquiring, in unprecedented detail, neuroimaging, cognitive, behavioural and socio-environmental data from a large cohort of children aged 6 to 12 years, that were already deeply phenotyped during fetal, neonatal and toddler stages as part of the Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP). We will elucidate, at the individual level, how socio-environmental and clinical factors influence children’s longitudinal brain maturation, shaping resilience to known risks (i.e., perinatal events, psychiatric family history, socio- economic circumstances) and/or susceptibility to mental health problems, as they enter and progress through school. This new information will provide clinically meaningful evidence to guide well-being strategies supporting the development of all children. Overarching goals: to create the most comprehensive ultra-high field neuroimaging dataset to date spanning age 6 to 12 (n=548 children) (Aim 1) and explore dynamic associations between changes in brain structure/function and phenotypic heterogeneity (Aim 2); to study how perinatal brain features inform later brain trajectories into middle childhood (Aim 3); to precisely model, at the individual level, the factors defining differences in mental health vulnerability in childhood (Aim 4).

title: Uncovering the biological basis of probiotic non-response in preterm gut health
description: This project aims to revolutionise probiotic therapy in preterm infants by uncovering why some individuals fail to respond to current treatments. Our unpublished data shows ‘non-response’ to treatment increases the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), an inflammatory bowel disease that represents a leading cause of death in preterm infants. The absence of specific maternal milk bioactive components and/or infant-related factors likely contribute. This will be investigated through three key aims: 1) Identify dietary and host factors associated with probiotic response, focusing on bioactive components in mother’s milk and infant immune/metabolic profiles. 2) Determine how diet and gut microbiome influence probiotic growth and function, using high- throughput microbial assays and metabolomics to test milk components and microbial interactions. 3) Mechanistically study host-microbe interactions using preterm intestinal organoids and a novel anaerobic co-culture system to assess how probiotics and milk components affect inflammation and gut health. The latter stages of the project will validate the results using other probiotics/cohorts and uncover the mechanisms using genetic manipulation approaches. This project leverages extensive biobank resources, advanced multi-omics, microbiology, and cutting-edge organoid models to generate fundamental discoveries. The outcomes will guide the development of personalised probiotic, prebiotic, and/or postbiotic therapies to improve preterm infant gut health.

title: Target Validation of Interleukin-4 Receptor Alpha for Major Depressive Disorder
description: We propose to validate interleukin-4 receptor alpha (IL-4Rα) as a novel immune target for major depressive disorder (MDD). IL-4Rα is the shared subunit of the IL-4 and IL-13 receptors and modulates the T-helper 2 (Th2) immune pathway. To our knowledge, IL-4Rα has not been investigated in psychiatric drug development, representing a novel mechanism for therapeutic intervention in MDD. Our rationale stems from converging evidence across immunology, psychiatry, and translational biology. Our proteomic analyses show that MDD shares immune signatures involving Th2/Th17 pathways with inflammatory skin disorders, and that the immune signature specific to MDD is reversed by dupilumab, an anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody approved for atopic dermatitis and asthma. We will use dupilumab as a repurposed tool compound in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate whether IL-4Rα inhibition modulates the MDD immune signature and reduces depressive symptoms. Study outcomes will include peripheral immune changes, depressive symptom improvement, safety, and exploratory behavioral measures. This proposal focuses on a patient group with high unmet need. Given the favorable safety profile and tolerability of dupilumab in real-world populations, this study offers a low-risk, high-impact opportunity to de-risk a novel immune pathway in MDD and enable biomarker-driven development of IL-4Rα-targeted therapeutics in psychiatry.
recipient: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: Decoding gene repression: how transcription factors and corepressors pioneer chromatin silencing to shape cell identity
description: Cellular differentiation enables a single genome to give rise to the diverse range of specialised cells required for multicellular life. Transcription factors (TFs) direct the gene expression patterns governing cellular differentiation. TFs bind specific regulatory sequences and recruit chromatin- modifying complexes to regulate expression, with activators and repressors working in concert to canalise cell fate. While the mechanisms by which TFs open chromatin, activate enhancers, and induce expression have been extensively studied, how TFs remodel the chromatin landscape to induce repression remains poorly understood. Using the hematopoietic TF Ikaros as a model, I will elucidate how TFs and corepressors initiate repression during differentiation, and how this process safeguards against malignancy. Ikaros is essential for B-cell differentiation and a tumour suppressor in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. I discovered that Ikaros acts as a potent repressor that rapidly silences gene expression by dismantling active enhancers. Ikaros interacts with chromatin remodellers and DNA/H3K9 methylation machinery, but how TFs like Ikaros bind and precisely deploy corepressors to disrupt active regulatory networks to drive differentiation remains unclear. This research will identify new TF–corepressor interactions and uncover the molecular mechanisms by which TF-induced repression shapes cell identity and restrains tumourigenesis.

title: Mapping host responses in the nasal mucosa during respiratory viral infections to identify cellular determinants of severe disease
description: Respiratory viruses impose a significant burden on healthcare systems worldwide, with the greatest impact on children in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). While previous studies, primarily in high-income settings, have characterized virally-induced mucosal cell states, their relevance in LMIC populations, where genetic diversity, environmental exposures, and nutritional factors differ, remains unknown. We aim to uncover the full spectrum of respiratory virus-induced epithelial and immune cell states in the nasal mucosa of children in Bangladesh. Our primary focus will be studying the response to Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in children under the age of two years at two sites (one community, one clinical) in Bangladesh, representing diverse demographic and environmental contexts. Using single-cell transcriptomics, cell culture models including air-liquid interface, and flow cytometry assays, we will define pathogenic cell states linked to severe disease by RSV, gradually expanding to other viruses, and investigate viral and host factors driving these states. We will also assess demographic and socioeconomic risk factors underlying severe respiratory disease in children in LMICs. This work will be a collaboration between research groups in Bangladesh and the USA and will generate critical insights into respiratory viral pathogenesis and foster capacity for cutting-edge cellular and molecular research in Bangladesh.

title: Neuroinflammation in Schizophrenia: Targeting IL-1ß Signaling with NLRP3 Inhibitors
description: This proposal aims to validate the NLRP3 inflammasome as a novel therapeutic target in a biologically defined subgroup of schizophrenia patients with neuroinflammation, marked by elevated IL-1β. Schizophrenia affects 1 in 100 people worldwide, yet current treatments are only partially effective, highlighting the urgent need for new therapeutic strategies. Emerging evidence implicates NLRP3–IL-1β signalling in immune dysregulation within a subset of patients. This study will use patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models to recreate brain-like environments and validate the NLRP3 inflammasome as a potential therapeutic target in schizophrenia. Specifically, we will (1) investigate aberrant NLRP3 activation in patient-derived iPSC models and (2) assess whether brain-penetrant NLRP3 inhibitors can reverse the deleterious effects of neuroinflammation. Shaped by input from people with lived experience, the project prioritises biologically informed, early-stage interventions. Overall, this work will generate a key dataset that could accelerate the translational pipeline for immune-targeted treatments in a subset of patients who are not well served by current therapies.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: TargetMDD: Validating microRNA-186-5p as a molecular target for early intervention in Major Depressive Disorder
description: This project aims to validate a novel therapeutic strategy for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) by targeting miR-186-5p, a microRNA elevated by chronic stress and linked to synaptic dysfunction in the prefrontal cortex. Targeting this upstream, stress-responsive microRNA offers a distinct approach compared to conventional treatments focusing on downstream neurotransmitters. Our approach combines chronic stress animal models and human iPSC-derived neurons with data from post-mortem brain, serum, and cerebrospinal fluid of MDD and other stress-related psychiatric patients. We will assess if miR-186-5p inhibition reverses neuronal and behavioural changes caused by stress, establishing its therapeutic potential. In vivo validation will utilize i) light-activatable nanoparticles to deliver inhibitors with precise temporal control and ii) small extracellular vesicles loaded with the miR-186-5p inhibitor, with translational value. By correlating peripheral miR-186-5p levels with patient clinical data, we further aim to establish its potential as a patient stratification biomarker. This strategy holds promise for early intervention by potentially halting disease progression before symptoms become severe, but also for refractory MDD cases, where synaptic disruption is critical. The inclusion of animal models and patient samples from both male and female subjects addresses the significant sex bias in MDD prevalence, enhancing potential impact on all patients.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: CRF1 Receptor Agonists as an Adjunct Treatment for Major Depression and Treatment-Resistant Depression
description: Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects ~16% of the global population, yet existing treatments like SSRIs/SNRIs are slow to act and leave ~30% of patients treatment-resistant. Although ketamine offers rapid antidepressant effects, its efficacy varies widely. Our preclinical work demonstrates that acute activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, particularly through corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), is essential for ketamine’s behavioral and synaptic efficacy. We show that CRF facilitates ketamine’s behavioral and cellular effects, while CRF1 receptor (CRF1R) antagonism blocks them, highlighting the therapeutic potential of transient CRF1R activation, a largely unexplored strategy. We propose a novel approach using CRF1R agonists as adjuncts to enhance antidepressant response. Aim 1 will validate the efficacy of CRF1R agonists in combination with ketamine, examining behavior, pharmacokinetics, and circuit-level engagement. Aim 2 will test whether CRF1R agonists can accelerate or enhance SSRI response in a chronic stress model. Aim 3 will generate a detailed safety profile of CRF1R agonists, including CNS and gastrointestinal effects, and use bioinformatic tools to assess translational relevance through human data. Our multidisciplinary team integrates expertise in neuropsychopharmacology, bioinformatics, and drug discovery. This work will advance CRF1R agonists as promising fast-acting, adjunctive treatments for early intervention in treatment-resistant depression.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: Generative AI for Simulated Conversations: Preparing Frontline Workers and Volunteers to Support Youth with Anxiety and Depression
description: This 24-month project brings together Kids Help Phone (KHP)—Canada’s only 24/7 eMental Health service offering free, multilingual, confidential support to youth— and Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU), a leading institution known for community-engaged, equity-promoting innovation and education. Our project addresses the urgent need for scalable training solutions for frontline mental health providers through the co-development and evaluation of a generative AI system built on a multi-agent infrastructure. Key components include a conversation simulator and a performance assessor. The simulator, co-designed with youth and frontline providers will create realistic single-session counselling and crisis response text conversations of youth experiencing anxiety and depression. The performance assessor delivers real-time feedback to trainees that is grounded in KHP’s established supervision and quality assurance measures. Using a developmental evaluation approach, we will iteratively refine the prototype and assess its validity, usability, and acceptance. We will complete a pragmatic evaluation to assess the tool’s effectiveness on provider confidence, knowledge, skills, and retention, as well as its impact on youth anxiety and depression. We will also leverage an established partnership with Childline Trinidad and Tobago to explore tailoring the developed simulator and assessor to their context.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Spatial Dysregulation of mRNA at the Peripheral Neuro-Glial Interface in ALS
description: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease driven by dysfunction of the RNA-binding protein TDP-43, whose early pathology emerges in axons and neuromuscular junction (NMJ) synapses at the neuronal periphery, preceding hallmark TDP-43 aggregation. Although its splicing function is well-characterised, TDP-43 also mediates mRNA trafficking and local translation essential for motoneuron and glial function at the NMJ. However, how TDP-43 dysfunction perturbs peripheral RNA-metabolism and initiates early NMJ degeneration remains poorly understood. I recently discovered that peripherally-localised glial/neuronal NMJ mRNAs are highly- enriched for ALS-risk genes, notably glutamate homeostasis and cell-contact regulators. Importantly, their glial-specific expression directly influences adjacent motoneuron plasticity. Therefore, I hypothesise that TDP-43 mutations disrupt peripheral mRNA localisation at the NMJ, triggering synaptic instability and neuro-glial miscommunication. I propose to use versatile Drosophila ALS models to: (1) Map transcriptome-wide mRNA mislocalisation and local translation changes at the motoneuron/glial periphery; (2) Dissect the molecular basis of TDP-43’s mRNA target choice and transport granule assembly at the NMJ; (3) Determine how ALS-induced mRNA mislocalisation disrupts synaptic function, neuro-glial communication and organismal behaviours. This research will establish a mechanistic framework for TDP-43-mediated peripheral RNA dysregulation in ALS, and support its extension to mammalian models in my future independent research.

title: HAI-Team: Human–AI Teaming Therapeutic Companion for Torture Survivors with PTSD
description: Torture survivors with PTSD experience severe distress between weekly therapy sessions, yet no digital intervention supports this vulnerable, culturally diverse population. This programme develops a generative AI therapeutic companion providing continuous stabilisation and grounding support, co- designed with survivors. Working with Freedom from Torture (FfT), the UK's largest specialist treatment centre, we create a multilingual system bridging care gaps whilst maintaining primacy of human therapeutic relationships. The AI operates within a three-way loop: providing grounding support to clients, generating clinical reports, and adapting strategies based on therapist guidance. We deliver five outputs: a validated therapeutic companion with multi-agent architecture; ethical, privacy and security frameworks addressing survivor-specific threats; human-AI teaming methods for mental health; clinically validated datasets combining recordings, roleplay and synthetic dialogues; and multimodal affect recognition with edge deployment for on- device use. Our consortium—FfT, UCL, University of Hamburg, and CISPA—places survivor co-design at its core. Developing frameworks for the most vulnerable population first, we create methods transferable to other trauma contexts including interpersonal violence, forced displacement, and childhood maltreatment. Datasets, models, and toolkits will be openly released to advance trauma-informed AI research globally. Keywords: generative AI, PTSD, torture survivors, therapeutic companion, human-AI teaming, affect recognition, stabilisation, ethics, privacy.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Transforming the experience of dementia in Kenya through community-led action and support
description: This study aims to build local research capacity and deliver insights that inform national strategies and contribute to efforts to reduce global inequalities in dementia care in Kenya. Conducted by a Kenyan researcher with deep community ties and global research experience, this project will foster cultural sensitivity, social justice, and equity in dementia care. Dementia is a rising yet overlooked public health challenge in many African countries, where there is no national policy, limited public awareness, training and limited research. As ageing populations grow, and with formal services still developing, traditional caregiving structures are strained, and family members bear the pressure of dementia care without adequate support. This research aims to address critical gaps in knowledge, policy, and practice by generating an in-depth, intersectional understanding of the lived experiences of people with dementia in rural, urban, and Maasai pastoralist communities in Kenya. A qualitative approach grounded in Participatory Action Research and Narrative inquiry will be implemented. Action learning sets, participatory film, and multiple interviewing methods will enable understanding of socio-cultural beliefs, systemic challenges, and community perspectives of dementia aligned with local culture. Co-produced outputs will help raise awareness, reduce dementia stigma, while promoting sustainable, community development and co- produced policy briefs.

title: Validation of the complement C4-C1s interaction as a novel therapeutic target to modulate synaptic plasticity in schizophrenia
description: Imbalanced complement activity, particularly excessive complement C4A-driven synaptic pruning, has been associated with disrupted neurodevelopment and schizophrenia onset. Genetic studies have identified increased expression of the complement C4A variant, relative to C4B, as a risk factor for schizophrenia. We aim to validate complement C4A as a novel drug target for schizophrenia, focusing on modulating excessive synaptic pruning, a process that eliminates extra synapses during brain development. Our hypothesis is that rebalancing C4A:C4B activity will mitigate excessive synaptic elimination and its associated neuropathology (Figure 1). We have developed a panel of small molecules that modulate complement activity, with selective effects on C4. This project will validate the C4A variant as a suitable target to rebalance synaptic pruning and normalise synaptic plasticity in patients with schizophrenia. We use established molecular and cellular assays and validate plasma C4A:C4B as a biomarker to determine the relevance and druggability of C4A for drug discovery. By specifically modulating C4A activity, this approach has the potential to reduce or prevent brain changes in individuals with C4A:C4B imbalance, alleviating symptoms, halting disease progression or even preventing schizophrenia onset. This work aims to enable early intervention strategies and contribute to a broader understanding of complement-mediated mechanisms in psychiatric disorders.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: Validating novel, selective CaV2.3 inhibitors as oral, small molecule therapies for posttraumatic stress disorder
description: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a prevalent mental health condition with significant unmet medical need. Over 5% of trauma-exposed adults worldwide develop PTSD during their lifetimes, with those exposed to certain types of trauma such as combat and assault carrying a particularly high burden. The few approved drug treatments (e.g. paroxetine and sertraline) have limited efficacy and significant side effects. A recently published multi-ancestry meta-analysis of genetic data from >1 million individuals exposed to trauma reported significant risk of PTSD associated with the CACNA1E gene which encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel (CaV2.3) with high expression in brain areas (hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex) involved in memory, emotional regulation, and stress response. Genome-wide analyses of transcription indicated that the highest risk alleles are linked to significantly higher expression of CACNA1E, suggesting that inhibition of CaV2.3 function has potential therapeutic benefit. Lario Therapeutics has developed first-in-class, small molecule inhibitors of CaV2.3 which are potent, selective, and brain-penetrant. This collaborative proposal aims to validate CaV2.3 as a target for PTSD and to test potential CaV2.3-targeted therapeutics in mouse models of PTSD including stress-induced alterations in anxiety, fear conditioning and in paradigms showing learned flexibility of instinctual fear behaviours.
recipient: TCG Centres for Research and Education in Science and Technology
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: Dynamics at the Fork: Molecular Dissection of Human DNA Replication and Fork Reversal Mechanisms
description: Faithful DNA replication is essential for genome integrity, yet the replication machinery, the replisome, is frequently challenged by replication stress. When unresolved, replication stress leads to genome instability, a hallmark of cancer and genetic disorders. Fork reversal is a critical stress response mechanism that stabilises stalled forks and enables fork restart, but how reversal factors coordinate with the replisome and engage stressed forks to promote fork reversal remains poorly defined. My project addresses these gaps by developing novel, integrated single-molecule and biochemical approaches to visualise human DNA replication and fork reversal dynamics at single-molecule resolution. These methods will allow me to track replisome composition, motion, and reversal factor recruitment in real time. I will systematically dissect replisome dynamics during normal replication, under stress, and how reversal factors access stressed forks to facilitate reversal in coordination with the replisome. Complementary AFM imaging will provide structural validation of reversed forks and replication intermediates, defining key architectural features across distinct stages of reversal. My work will uncover key mechanisms underlying human DNA replication, the replisome’s response to stress and fork reversal. It will also establish a robust platform for investigating diverse replication-associated processes.

title: Brain bioenergetics and the menopause in bipolar disorder (MENO-BD)
description: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a common and severe mental illness affecting at least 1 in 100 people. The perimenopause is a time of risk for new onset or relapse of BD, but mechanisms are unclear. Key to this proposal is the novel idea that disrupted brain bioenergetics represent a point of pathophysiological convergence of BD and menopause, specifically, reduced brain energy (adenosine triphosphate (ATP)) reserve, driven by mitochondrial dysfunction. My overarching hypothesis is that brain bioenergetic changes during the menopause drive mental health symptoms in women with BD. This is a co-designed observational study incorporating menopause as a “natural experiment”: prospective clinical cohort study in healthy people and people with BD who are pre, peri, post menopause (n= 75 per group, total n = 150), assessed at baseline and 12 months. Aims a) Quantify brain bioenergetics (phosphocreatine/ATP ratio, lactate) across menopausal stages using Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy. b) Test associations of brain bioenergetics with perimenopausal mental health symptoms (cognition, mood), and c) Explore putative compensatory mechanisms by quantifying metabolomic changes across menopausal stages. This innovative approach to understanding metabolic mechanisms of relapse in women with BD represents a novel potential avenue for intervention in a highly morbid but currently under-served patient group.

title: ARIADNE: ARtificial Intelligence-based Assessment to Detect iNdividuals with Emerging psychosis risk
description: The Clinical High Risk for Psychosis (CHR-P) state offers a vital chance to step in early and prevent the onset of psychosis. But right now, almost 9 out of 10 people in this phase are not identified in time. The best way to detect CHR-P individuals is with a specialist clinical interview. However, these interviews are long, require highly trained clinicians, and are only done in specialist services. Many people who are referred for these assessments do not actually meet CHR-P criteria, meaning a lot of time is spent on unnecessary interviews. Reports are also often difficult for patients to understand and are not always useful for research. To address these problems, we are developing ARIADNE - a new voice-based interview system powered by generative artificial intelligence. ARIADNE will be able to hold a natural conversation, ask the right questions, and produce clear, tailored reports for patients, clinicians, and researchers. This would make assessments faster, more accessible and more empowering for patients while supporting research and clinical care. In this project, we will demonstrate that it is secure, accurate, safe, ethical, acceptable and cost-effective. This will support medical device registration to facilitate ARIADNE helping young people access preventive care.
programme: Generative AI for Anxiety, Depression and Psychosis

title: Hijacking Hinges: Cracking the coiled-coil code to control intracellular transport
description: Kinesin and dynein motors transport cargo bidirectionally along microtubules. Proper regulation is essential for cellular health, and its disruption is linked to neurodegeneration, cardiac disease, and cancer. Motor proteins and adaptors are autoinhibited and activated by specific motor-cargo–adaptor interactions. Coiled-coil domains are highly conserved in motors and adaptors and are emerging as dynamic regulatory elements. This project tests the hypothesis that “coiled-coil hinges” are fundamental regulatory elements in transport systems and can be manipulated to target motor dysfunction in disease. Our proof of concept work on kinesin 1 uncovered a novel autoinhibitory mechanism involving a coiled-coil hinge. I designed a conformational switch, triggered by a cell-penetrating peptide, to activate kinesin-1 allosterically. I will extend this approach to BicD2, the most intensively studied dynein adaptor. Mutations in BicD2 cause neuromuscular and developmental disorders and viruses and bacteria hijack BicD2 to subvert dynein; however, its regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. I will elucidate the mechanisms of coiled-coil regulation in BicD2, engineer switchable variants to control dynein activation, and explore how coiled-coil adaptors regulate bidirectional transport more broadly. This work will deepen mechanistic understanding of motor protein regulation and pave the way for novel therapeutic strategies for diseases associated with motor dysfunction.

title: Zinc transporter-3 as a novel target for fast and long-lasting antidepressant actions
description: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability worldwide, with up to 30% of patients developing treatment-resistant depression (TRD). There is an urgent need for novel therapeutic targets that drive rapid and sustained antidepressant effects. Zinc transporter-3 (ZnT3) is a novel and unexplored target. We recently showed that psilocybin enhances proliferation and survival of human hippocampal progenitor cells and promotes neurogenesis and neurite outgrowth. Single-cell RNAseq indicates stage-specific ZnT3 expression, suggesting a role in neurogenesis. In mice, we showed that ZnT3 expression and the activation of adult-born neurons are required for psilocybin’s rapid and lasting antidepressant effects. This project will validate ZnT3 as a novel therapeutic target to elicit rapid and long-lasting effects without hallucinogenic effects, by examining its role in neuroplasticity using preclinical models and patient-derived samples. First, we will assess ZnT3 expression in adult-born neurons following chronic stress and antidepressant treatment, in mice and brain-derived exosomes from MDD and TRD patients. Second, we will determine whether modulating ZnT3 or increasing intracellular Zinc elicits antidepressant-like effects. Targeting ZnT3 will offer a new therapeutic approach for MDD, with the potential to provide rapid and long-lasting benefit to patients resistant to existing treatments.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: From principle to practice: Reimagining ethics for public health futures
description: The COVID-19 pandemic intensified interest in public health ethics, yet a critical gap remains: public health is rarely examined as an integrated ethical practice, and professionals often lack structured support for complex ethical decisions. This methodologically innovative project aims to reconceptualise ethics support within health protection, a key public health subspecialty, so that it is fit for the significant challenges it is likely to face in the future. The projects aims are to: 1\. Analyse health protection ethics challenges in practice 2\. Develop and justify what good public health ethics support in practice should entail 3\. Design a context-responsive ethics support intervention for health protection 4\. Build an evidence basis for the ethics support intervention 5\. Develop a model for integrated ethics research at the intersection of health protection practice and academic research. As one of the few clinical academics bridging public health and ethics, I am uniquely positioned to lead this research. Drawing on methods in empirical ethics and public health, this project will reimagine public health ethics to better serve professionals in the field, transform approaches to ethical decision-making in health protection, and develop new methodologies for designing and evaluating bioethics support.

title: Defining neutrophil functional heterogeneity & dysfunction in COPD using single cell proteomics
description: Neutrophils are vital innate immune cells. Recent work has detailed their transcriptional heterogeneity related maturity and tissue residency. However, neutrophils display a pronounced discordance between mRNA and protein abundance, making proteomics a highly valuable technique to study them. Neutrophils play essential roles in Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a disease which is the third leading cause of death in adults >50 years old. I propose that pathogenic neutrophil subsets drive disease onset and progression. In this proposal I will leverage mini-bulk and single cell proteomic approaches combined with analytics pipelines to study neutrophil populations and functional states across the bone marrow, blood and airways in healthy controls, healthy smokers and COPD patients. This will enable me to define the differences of neutrophil phenotypes across tissues, delineating changes specific to the airways compared to those centrally programmed in the bone marrow. It will also enable a comparison of COPD to healthy volunteers and healthy smokers, determining phenotypes exclusive to patients with established airway disease and those shared with healthy smokers. This proposal will significantly expand our understanding of neutrophil diversity and function in COPD, empowering the discovery of phenotypes and populations that can be targeted to improve patient outcomes.

title: The Translocator Protein (TSPO) as a Multimodal Target for Generalised Anxiety Disorder
description: Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a prevalent and debilitating mental health condition. Current pharmacotherapies suffer from delayed onset, side effects, or poor long-term efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for novel, mechanism-based interventions. The Translocator Protein (TSPO) is a promising, yet under-investigated, target for GAD due to its dual role in neurosteroid synthesis and neuroinflammation regulation, two key pathways implicated in GAD pathophysiology. Despite compelling pre-clinical evidence, TSPO’s therapeutic potential remains unproven due to critical knowledge gaps, particularly regarding the impact of the single nucleotide polymorphism (A147T, rs6971), which impairs TSPO function and druggability, affecting up to 50% of the Caucasian population. Our project will deliver the first comprehensive target validation of TSPO for GAD using a novel pharmacological approach. Using ground-breaking ligands developed in our laboratories that bind both wild-type (WT) and A147T TSPO with nanomolar affinity, we will assess steroidogenic and anti-inflammatory functions in clinically-relevant isogenic iPSC-derived glial cells. In parallel, we will evaluate behavioural and molecular outcomes in WT and A147T TSPO mouse models. This integrative strategy will rigorously define the functional relevance of TSPO in anxiety regulation and its tractability as a therapeutic target, paving the way for the development of genetically robust, fast-acting treatments for GAD.
programme: Advancing target validation for novel mental health drug discovery

title: Harnessing complex sparse data for the phylodynamics of RNA virus emergence and elimination
description: The emergence and elimination of viruses are critical junctures for disease control to prevent spread or resurgence. Rapid response is essential, but policymakers are invariably held up by a lack of data. Phylodynamics can provide rapid insights where traditional epidemiology may fail, but has yet to be applied effectively to more epidemiologically or ecologically complex and data-limited contexts. I will extend the use of phylodynamic methods by developing frameworks to estimate viral transmission where data are spatiotemporally limited. I will 1) develop a framework for using spatially heterogenous data, using phylodynamic methods to infer transmission in locations with no epidemiological or genomic data, aiding intervention design and providing an evidence base for further data collection. I will 2) use novel phylodynamic applications to contextualise ongoing transmission and spillover risk when historical data are sparse, including developing the use of phage-display immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-Seq) for estimating historical viral genetic diversity from contemporary serum samples to fill in temporal gaps in our genomic datasets. Overall, I will develop strategies to fully harness contemporary genomic data to provide information critical for the early prevention of further spread of (re-)emerging viruses, and closure of transmission chains of viruses under elimination.

title: Understanding chikungunya virus adaptation and transmission dynamics in Cameroon
description: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is a significant public health challenge in sub- Saharan Africa, where its transmission dynamics and adaptation mechanisms are poorly understood. This is concerning, given that CHIKV has caused outbreaks across Africa, with the potential for rapid spread and severe health consequences. The virus's capacity for adaptation to different mosquito vectors, notably Aedes albopictus, could substantially alter transmission patterns and expand the geographical range of CHIKV. Climate change also impacts mosquito vector distribution and CHIKV transmission dynamics, thereby necessitating proactive research to understand and mitigate these effects. Limited diagnostic capabilities in resource-constrained settings like Cameroon is another challenge, emphasizing the need for improved detection methods to facilitate timely surveillance and outbreak control. We aim to address this knowledge gap by i-analyzing CHIKV genetic diversity and its prevalence in patients with acute febrile illness, and Aedes mosquitoes in Cameroon, ii- assessing Aedes mosquitoes vector competence and transmission factors (viral, mosquito), and iii-evaluating the diagnostic performance of Reverse Transcriptase Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (RT-LAMP) to detect CHIKV. This study will provide critical knowledge to guide targeted interventions, improve diagnostic tools, and strengthen overall preparedness against future CHIKV outbreaks.
recipient: Centre for Research in Infectious Diseases (CRID), Cameroon

title: Hypatia Health
description: Many psychiatric and psychological treatments don’t work for everyone, and when they do, it’s often unclear why. In routine care, there’s a gap between symptom-level and brain-level understanding. As a result, patients are left navigating trial-and-error approaches with a clinician to find what works. Computational models can help close this gap. These models support mechanistic phenotyping, offering better ways to shape treatment plans, structure therapy sessions, and develop new treatments. But current methods are inconsistent across teams and lack a simple, user-friendly interface for clinicians, researchers, and service-users. Hypatia Health aims to change that. We’re building a scalable platform that gives scientific and clinical teams easy access to gold-standard computational models and matching gamified tasks. Researchers worldwide can simulate and predict human behaviour, while clinicians can use interactive games to generate computational phenotypes for service users. By making these tools accessible, we reduce wasted time and resources—and bring care closer to the causes of mental ill health.

title: Europe PMC 2026-2031
description: Europe PMC is a critical open scholarly infrastructure that preserves and enriches biomedical research literature, including abstracts and full text for publications, including preprints. It is a vital and trusted resource accessed by ~25 million website users in 2024. It offers powerful discovery tools and open APIs for literature analysis, and creates an interconnected knowledge network by integrating publications with associated research outputs. It enables users to find and access scientific evidence, conduct meta research, and build new services and tools for the wider community. During this grant, our vision is to deliver a sustainable, resilient, and independent resource that integrates open science outputs and supports open publication workflows to meet the needs of people, computational systems, and AI. We will transform Europe PMC’s search capabilities through AI integration to develop state-of- the-art literature research tools. We will enable efficient analysis of Europe PMC’s rich metadata, allowing programmatic users to easily traverse the APIs, integrating new information sources and improve transparency through metadata provenance. We will support open science practices with new preprint indexing capabilities and improved citations metrics to showcase the full impact of research. This will be underpinned by collaborations to drive adoption of open science and new technologies.

title: Mechanisms of Emergence and Spread of Artemisinin and MultiDrug Resistance (AMRED) Malaria Parasites in West Africa
description: The recent emergence and spread of artemisinin resistant Plasmodium falciparum parasites in Africa pose grave threats to control/elimination programs utilising artemisinin combination therapies (ACTs), the last stronghold for malaria treatments. Over 10 mutations in the parasite’s Kelch 13 gene, K13, have been associated with artemisinin resistance in Africa; particularly, West African parasites harbouring K13 resistant markers also show reduced ex vivo susceptibility to artemisinin. The typical high parasite transmission/recombination rates in West African parasites could rapidly expand these resistant markers on diverse genetic backgrounds, associated with multidrug resistance to partner drugs, and the former first-line treatments, chloroquine and sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine. We are not well equipped, and lack critical knowledge in the evolutionary mechanisms underlying the emergence/spread of these resistant markers, to forestall containment measures in West Africa; how do artemisinin- and multidrug resistant (AMRED) marker combinations influence heterogenous susceptibilities to ACTs in contemporary infections? This study aims to investigate these questions in Ghana, a low- high transmission setting, with ideal parasite populations that harbour resistance markers to most antimalarials. It will innovate genetic tools and approaches to unravel the complexity in resistance evolution and build local capacity in functional genetics studies to detect, track and stop artemisinin resistance.

title: The learning disability art of care – centring actors with learning disabilities to develop novel understandings of care
description: The health inequalities experienced by people with learning disabilities are perpetuated by stigmatisation and clinicians’ inconsistent disability literacy, both of which are exacerbated by learning-disabled people’s marginalisation in healthcare research where they rarely figure as knowledge producers. This project addresses these interlinked issues by engaging learning-disabled actors in a Participatory Action Research project to generate new understandings of care through the development—and subsequently application in research with medical students—of a novel methodology for investigating care. The expertise of actors with learning disabilities is central to this: as a co-constructed and embodied practice that relies on sensorial presence, spontaneity, improvisation, and indeed playfulness, care—a concept at once elusive and ubiquitous—has many parallels with performing arts. Moreover, as members of inclusive theatre companies, the actors are at the forefront of daily enacting sophisticated care practices to promote the empowerment of people with learning disabilities. Thus, centring the needs, values and expertise of people with learning disabilities to develop a novel embodied methodology to research care, this project builds on transdisciplinary scholarship associated with care aesthetics and emancipatory disability research to—by generating new understandings of care—interrogate dominant models of care and benefit health-related research.

title: Salinity and Reproductive Health: Exploring the impacts on reproductive health and psychosocial health of women and adolescent girls in coastal Bangladesh
description: Climate change-driven salinity intrusion is silently but profoundly damaging the reproductive and psychosocial health of women and adolescent girls in coastal Bangladesh. Exposure to saline environments increases risks of infections, preeclampsia, emotional distress, and stigma, threatening health and dignity in some of the most climate-vulnerable communities. This project offers an urgent, community-powered response. Through interdisciplinary research, we will assess reproductive and mental health impacts, identify service gaps, and pilot sustainable, locally-led solutions — such as solar- powered water kiosks and peer-supported psychosocial interventions. Our integrated approach will generate new evidence linking climate stress to women's health, a critical and underexplored area in global health research. The outcomes will directly influence the revision of Bangladesh’s National Population Policy and guide scalable health adaptation strategies. Our findings will strengthen primary care services, build emotional resilience, and deliver low-cost, gender-sensitive innovations for safe water services. Community voices are at the heart of this project. Using participatory research frameworks, women and adolescents will co-design tools, lead peer education, and drive local change. Together, we will not only document climate impacts — but also create pathways of hope, dignity, and resilience for generations to come.

title: Building a coordinated and sustainable SBE research and development ecosystem

title: BLOOMS (Babies' Longitudinal 'Omics, Outcomes, and Milestones Study)
description: We address the challenge of improving life-course trajectory through early detection of antecedents of poor health and educational outcomes. Infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICU) are at high risk of adverse health and educational outcomes, including ~30% chance of not meeting expected national educational targets aged 5. We will link multi-omic data, clinical and developmental deep-phenotyping, and routinely collected national health and educational records in a 1000-trio prospective cohort of NICU graduates. The resulting platform, managed within the UK NIHR Bioresource, will be continually updated to maximise phenotyping, maintain cohort engagement, and make data accessible. We will enhance diversity and validate key results through a Singapore-based mirror-cohort. Inclusivity of our approach is assured through co-design with our PPIE team and basing recruitment in ethnically-diverse and socio-economically deprived East of England cities. Families will receive clinical results reports to ensure bidirectional benefits of participation. Findings from the study are intended to (i) enhance diagnosis and maximise predictive value of neonatal whole genome sequencing (WGS) combined with multiomic-derived biomarkers and detailed phenotypic information, (ii) identify risk-markers allowing targeted early interventions to promote children’s health and developmental potential, and (iii) elucidate fundamental mechanisms leading to adverse physical-mental health and developmental outcomes.

title: Measuring the Impact of Heat and Heat Adaptation Strategies on the Health and Livelihoods of Women Working in the Informal Economy in India
description: Extreme heat poses an escalating threat to health, particularly among the world’s working poor. Critical data on both exposure and impact in the most at-risk populations are limited. Existing evidence is largely derived from laboratory or workplace settings, athletes and armed forces, and mostly men. Without a comprehensive understanding of the impact of the sustained heat exposures experienced by the working poor in their homes and workplaces, it is hard to evaluate the range of behavioral, technical, and financial adaptation strategies being presented to these communities globally. Our project proposes a longitudinal study to assess the impact of heat on the health and livelihoods of women in India’s informal economy, all members of the Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA). By integrating environmental sensors, wearables, biomarker assessments, and surveys, we will measure thermal exposure and quantify impacts on physiological responses, reproductive, renal, and cardiovascular health, and work productivity, across all seasons. Building on a 2024-25 feasibility pilot, the proposed study will generate context- specific evidence on the impact of sustained heat stress on the working poor. Outcomes will inform workplace regulations, early warning systems, adaptation interventions, and result in a generalizable research platform for community- led organizations to lead future climate-health adaptation efforts.
