title: What Works Climate Solutions: Building an open, equitable, inclusive, and sustainable initiative to support evidence-based climate policy
description: The What Works Climate Solutions (WWCS) initiative aims to transform climate policy-making by identifying and advancing evidence-based climate solutions. By applying proven evidence synthesis methods from fields like medicine and education, WWCS builds a rigorous, inclusive evidence culture across researchers, policymakers, funders, and civil society. Its vision is to accelerate climate action by identifying what works, for whom, and under what conditions. WWCS focuses on three main aims: (1) professionalize and sustain an inclusive, equitable, and diverse initiative; (2) generate rigorous, policy-relevant evidence on climate solutions; and (3) enhance capacity and engagement across global stakeholders. Key activities include organizing the 2026 WWCS Summit, seeding a Living Evidence Bank, developing a citizen-science crowd platform, conducting blueprint living systematic reviews on climate and health, and expanding the WWCS Network. The initiative will also scale its Evidence Accelerator training program, professionalize coordination through a Secretariat, and grow a diverse funding base to ensure long-term sustainability. WWCS is committed to equity, diversity, and global inclusion, ensuring broad participation, and democratizing access to evidence that drives action across sectors and regions. Through collaboration, transparency, and shared learning, WWCS seeks to democratize access to evidence and build a global community driving effective and context-specific climate solutions.

title: Clean Land, Equitable Air, and Resilience (CLEAR): Advancing Health Equity by Addressing Waste-Driven Climate Risks
description: India has 3084 garbage dumpsites that emit Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCP) and other pollutants, leading to significant health problems. Unmanaged waste in India contributes to 4% of total GHG emissions and emissions of volatile organic gases. Chronic exposure to pollutants from dumpsites contributes to respiratory issues, increased cancer risk, oxygen deprivation to vital organs, mental health issues, and reproductive impairments. Vulnerable communities like residents near dumpsites and informal waste pickers bear the brunt of such environmental degradation. India’s national regulations, complex environmental governance, and programmes like Swachh Bharat Mission 2.0 promote circularity in solid waste management to address climate and health risks from dumpsites. However, the progress is slow and India’s health sector response such environmental health issues is weak. India needs comprehensive public health data on the implications of open dumpsites and its mitigation efforts. In this context, the M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation (MSSRF) proposes to undertake transdisciplinary action research aimed at 1) generating comprehensive data on environmental health, 2) strengthening the health system to improve preparedness and responsiveness to environmental issues, 3) provide support to selected States in improving solid waste management and 4) empower the vulnerable communities associated with dumpsite.

title: Decoding the triad: the interplay between Environment, Pathogen, and Host in melioidosis (DeEPH)
description: Melioidosis, caused by the environmental bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, is a neglected tropical disease with an estimated global fatality rate of 54%. In the Lower Mekong Basin, 22% of patients die before receiving a culture- confirmed diagnosis, 26% of diagnosed patients die within a month, and 24% of one-month survivors are readmitted within a year. Disease progression – from acquisition to acute infection and recovery – is influenced by a range of bacterial, host, and environmental factors. My research in northeast Thailand has identified genetic variation in B. pseudomallei and host genes associated with clinical outcomes at distinct stages of disease progression. However, the mechanisms linking these genetic variants to the outcomes remain poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, I will combine population genetics and multi-omic approaches to investigate how genetic variants influence molecular pathways and contribute to disease outcomes. I will also examine how environmental factors, such as exposure to contaminated soil and water, treatment timing, and patient adherence, modify risk throughout the disease trajectory. This work will enable the identification of biomarkers to stratify patient risk and inform targeted interventions to improve melioidosis outcomes, while expanding omic databases for underrepresented populations, and strengthening genetic research capacity in Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia.

title: A multi-scalar, stakeholder-focused investigation of the health co-benefits of climate change mitigation strategies, backed by empirical research interventions in India
description: Having declared a 2070 net-zero target at COP26, India will benefit greatly from aligning its climate action strategies with public health goals. This project seeks to fill crucial evidence gaps and inform equitable, health- centered climate mitigation policies and practice. We propose to analyze and implement climate mitigation solutions at national, city, community, and individual levels, explicitly engaging diverse government and community stakeholders to reduce uncertainties, build capacity, and multiply impact. We will collaborate with NITI Aayog to forecast the health impacts of climate mitigation strategies through 2070. Thereafter, we will advocate for mitigation policies that best protect health in regular convenings with NITI. Second, we will analyze Climate Action Plans in Delhi and Chennai that reduce the emissions from electricity supply at the city level and provide policy briefings to city mayors recommending specific policy action. Third, we will co-design community level e-cooking interventions that support a transition away from coal for domestic use in Rajhara Coal-mine, Jharkhand and evaluate its health and socioeconomic impacts. Finally, we will develop a fellowship for a diverse, transdisciplinary cohort of health professionals to learn about climate change’s impacts on health and develop climate action projects to improve the health of their communities.

title: INNOVETH: Innovative Health Intervention for Ethiopian Migrant Domestic Workers in the Middle East
description: Every year, more than 350,000 Ethiopian women migrate to the Middle East legally, and many others illegally, seeking domestic work. Economic crisis, rising unemployment, and internal conflict contribute to this massive migration. The bilateral agreement between the Ethiopian government and each destination country requires recruitment agencies to undertake rigorous pre- migration medical check-up for migrant domestic workers (MDWs). Nevertheless, MDWs in the Middle East are subject to overwork; mental, sexual and reproductive health challenges; and limited healthcare access. Studies on MDWs are mostly exploratory or cross-sectional; longitudinal and intervention studies are lacking. We propose to provide healthcare support to these vulnerable women by leveraging social networks, social media, and innovative technology. In Phase I, we explored key health challenges of MDWs through a scoping review, stakeholder consultation, and analysis of pre-migration data. We hypothesized that, by utilizing epidemiological and data science intelligence methods, we could stratify MDWs based on their level of risk and provide tailored intervention. We developed an intervention package, including training, peer-support and self-help groups, and mobile applications. In Phase II, we propose to i) develop, refine and validate a risk stratification tool, ii) refine and pilot the intervention and iii) implement and evaluate its impact and cost-effectiveness.

title: Fostering LMIC Engagement at the AMR Summit 2026
description: CSIRO and The Fleming Initiative are jointly organising the "AMR 2026: From Global Vision to Local Action" summit in Sydney, Australia, February 18-20, 2026. This summit aims to drive tangible progress in tackling antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by fostering collaboration, knowledge sharing, and innovative solutions. A key objective is to ensure the active participation of researchers and stakeholders from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), who are disproportionately affected by AMR. LMICs face unique challenges in combating AMR due to factors such as limited resources, inadequate infrastructure, and high burdens of infectious diseases. Insights and experiences from individuals in these countries are crucial for developing effective and equitable solutions. The AMR 2026 summit seeks to: • Provide a platform for LMIC researchers to share their experiences, challenges, and successes in addressing AMR. • Facilitate knowledge exchange and collaboration between LMIC and high-income country (HIC) researchers. • Ensure that AMR strategies and interventions are relevant and adaptable to LMIC contexts.

title: In-person gathering of negotiators towards successful outcomes at COP30 on the Global Goal on Adaptation
description: With support from Wellcome Trust, SLYCAN Trust will organize an in-person gathering of key negotiators back-to-back with the final mandated workshop under the UAE-Belém work programme, in partnership with the COP30 Presidency. This two-day gathering will facilitate an in-depth discussion towards finding convergence on the GGA and aims to lay the groundwork for a strong decision at COP30/CMA7. The event will be held in person in Bonn with the participation of approximately 30 key negotiators from all relevant negotiating groups from developing and developed countries, comprising 20 participants from the mandated workshop as well as 10 additional negotiators, including leads on finance, technology and capacity-building. Additionally, a hybrid setup with virtual participation will allow for contributions from other relevant negotiators and widen participation through engagement for selected sessions. This event will follow-up on the first such gathering, which was facilitated by SLYCAN Trust with support from Wellcome Trust in May 2025, after the mandated GGA workshop and ahead of SB62.

title: Advancing Health and Climate Justice Nexus Issues in Africa Climate Summit -2 in Addis Ababa
description: The “One Health Approach’ has been a guiding rod in driving holistic action on health issues in Africa, capturing the multifaceted nature of the climate and health nexus. The Global Goal on Adaptation, is aligned to the Common African Position on Climate and Health. The convening in Addis Ababa, taking place ahead of COP30 in Belem where the GGA indicators will be adopted is a vantage space to position the health deliverables across all the GGA themes. It’s equally a vantage space for the continent to demonstrate its leadership on climate, leveraging on health to support robust resilience building. This action will catalyze a transformative shift that places health at the center of Africa’s climate resilience, anchoring it in national and continental climate policies and in Africa’s agenda for COP30. Specifically, it seeks to: 1\. Position health as a central pillar of Africa’s climate agenda, securing its prominence in ACS-2 proceedings and outcomes 2\. Advocate for mainstreaming of health across African climate policy frameworks 3\. Strengthen accountability and transparency mechanisms for tracking progress on climate and health commitments. 4\. Promote use of evidence to identify key nexus points for climate change and health
recipient: Pan African Climate Justice Alliance PACJA

title: A Latin American pangenome for mapping structural variation of medical relevance in underrepresented indigenous ancestries
description: Large-scale genomic studies of non-European cohorts are urgently needed to propel the discovery of medically relevant variants in diverse ancestries that remain underrepresented. Otherwise, population-specific variation will continue to be missed, perpetuating health disparities. To tackle this challenge, the LatinGenomes consortium brings together more than 30 researchers representing ten countries across Latin America to build a pangenome representative of indigenous ancestries across LATAM. This will allow us to discover structural variants relevant for the region and investigate their role in gene expression changes at the cellular level in immune cells and gallbladder tissues. Given the higher risk of gallbladder cancer in Indigenous Chilean individuals of Mapuche ancestry, we will further investigate the association of germline and somatic structural variants with single-cell gene expression, revealing genes of interest, dosage and direction effects and pathways relevant for the physiopathological understanding of this cancer of high disease burden for South America. We will foster international collaboration while promoting local capacity building and training across LATAM. An endeavor of this caliber, rooted in community engagement and led by local experts is unprecedented for Latin America and will be of great value for biomedical research and global health.
recipient: Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN

title: MRC Novel human in vitro models of complex disease
description: The contribution of £5M will support a portfolio of 5 proposals for 4 years to develop novel human in vitro models of disease, which have been recommended for funding in the joint funding call with MRC, NC3Rs, BBSRC and EPSRC.  MRC will be contributing £10M for a total budget of £15m, with each proposal costed at just under £3M.  Wellcome funding would contribute to supporting all 5 proposals. These proposals were reviewed by a panel of experts convened by the MRC.

title: Driving Climate Action and Sustainable Development through the NDC Partnership
description: The NDC Partnership is proposing a grant of USD 1,298,810 from Wellcome, to support implementation of its Work Program. This contribution will enhance the Partnership’s ability to respond to growing demand for support from developing countries to advance health-related climate action. The Partnership brings together countries and institutions to create and deliver on ambitious climate action that help achieve the Paris Agreement and drive sustainable development. Governments identify their NDC implementation priorities and the type of support needed to translate them into actionable policies and programs. Based on these requests, the membership offers a tailored package of expertise, technical assistance, and funding. This collaborative response provides developing countries with efficient access to a wide range of resources to adapt to and mitigate climate change and foster more equitable and sustainable development. Collectively, the Partnership has mobilized over USD 1.8 billion to deliver coordinated support to more than 100 developing countries. As of March 2025, 101 developing countries have received support to implement and enhance their NDCs from 310 Implementing Partners. Yet, 43% of all requests are still unmet, including most health-related requests. Wellcome’s support will enable technical assistance and strengthen the Partnership’s Support Unit to effectively coordinate and maximize impact.

title: Diversifying Climate and Health Modelling Capacity Programme
description: Global climate modelling depends on a linked workflow of scenario frameworks (such as the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs)), Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs), Earth System Models (ESMs) and the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) to generate and compare projections of future climate conditions. Historically, this entire process has been led by researchers in high income countries (HICs), leaving low and middle income countries (LMICs) under resourced and under represented despite facing the greatest climate risks. To tackle this imbalance, we propose a capacity strengthening programme that offers hands on training in IAM development and alignment with climate attribution methods and health focused climate services. By prioritizing researchers based in LMICs, the programme will build vital local expertise where it is needed most and foster more inclusive, context driven climate health modelling.
recipient: International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis

title: ICTP - IAP - IPCC WGII Collaborative Research Assistance Grant
description: Climate change is threatening human health, biodiversity and the eradication of sustained poverty. Many Global South (GS) regions are affected by climate change more than other regions, and may therefore be considered as hotspots of high human vulnerability. This programme is to support IPCC WGII AR7 Global South Coordinating Lead Authors (CLAs) in the evaluation of climate change risks to GS regions and to enhance their knowledge of climate change adaptation for this particular IPCC cycle. This will ensure a more comprehensive reflection of global scientific knowledge. For this purpose, a Call for all eligible GS IPCC WGII AR7 CLAs will be opened for a one-off grant for the selected CLAs Institute in early 2026. The grant will be available from spring 2026, but can be split into installments, according to the needs of the CLA awardee. This grant will allow the CLAs to recruit research assistants. The funds include the stipends for the chapter research assistants as well as open-access publication fees. The 'ICTP- IAP - IPCC WGII Collaborative Research Assistance Grant Programme' will also deal with the monitoring the reporting from the selected CLAs, and implement a Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning process
recipient: The Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP)

title: Countering the evolutionary threat to malaria vector control in Africa - Major changes to national malaria elimination strategy in the Senegambia region as a model system for investigating strategies to block adaptation in Anopheles mosquito populations
description: Vector control has significantly reduced the burden of malaria in Africa. However, reliance on bednets impregnated with pyrethroid insecticides has caused rapid evolution of pyrethroid resistance in Anopheles mosquitoes. To combat this threat, dual active ingredient insecticide-treated nets (dual AI ITNs) have been developed and proven effective against pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes. Furthermore, dual AI ITNs combining a pyrethroid with the proinsecticide chlorfenapyr are promising for resistance management, because molecular mechanisms which cause pyrethroid resistance also activate and increase susceptibility to chlorfenapyr. This potential for antagonistic pleiotropy could create an evolutionary trap, delaying the evolution of resistance. However, little is known about how Anopheles mosquitoes will evolve in response to dual AI ITNs. We will exploit the first mass distribution of dual AI ITNs across the Senegambian region to study the evolutionary response of Anopheles mosquito populations to combined use of pyrethroid and chlorfenapyr insecticides. To complement this, we will use directed evolution experiments to investigate and validate the selective pressures generated by insecticide combinations. Finally, we will develop models to forecast the evolutionary risk of different insecticide combinations and intervention strategies. These advances will accelerate the design of future vector control interventions that exploit evolutionary vulnerabilities to ensure long term efficacy.

title: Super Pollutant Action Alliance
description: The Super Pollutant Action Alliance (SPAA) seeks £2,000,000 in foundational support from Wellcome Trust to catalyze a step-change in the integration of health goals and evidence into global action on super pollutants, namely methane, black carbon, nitrous oxide, f-gases, and tropospheric ozone. This proposal responds to Wellcome’s goals of protecting and improving health outcomes and strengthening the health case to avoid near-term warming. With Wellcome’s early engagement and participation on the Steering Committee, SPAA will be well placed to expand the super pollutant ecosystem in a way that is focused on the dual climate and health benefits of reducing these harmful pollutants.

title: Pollution and Rising Environmental Drivers of Illness under Climate Threats in Asia (PREDICT-ASIA)
description: Air pollution and extreme heat pose escalating health risks in Asia, especially in densely populated Southeast Asia, yet their synergistic effects remain unclear. Emerging evidence indicates that co-exposure to multiple pollutants (e.g., PM2.5, O3, NO2) and heat amplifies cardiovascular/respiratory morbidity and mortality, but region-specific data are lacking. We propose a new program—Pollution and Rising Environmental Drivers of Illness under Climate Threats in Asia (PREDICT-ASIA)—to investigate the individual and combined health impacts through two integrated work packages: WP1 will employ multi-city epidemiological analyses (Singapore, Chiang Mai, Kuala Lumpur, Taipei and Hong Kong) to quantify exposure-response relationships, identify risk thresholds, and project future burdens under climate change using national health records and climate models, while WP2 will conduct a biomarker-based panel study on outdoor workers across the five cities to unravel biological mechanisms (e.g., inflammation, oxidative stress) underlying acute and synergistic effects. By integrating big data, advanced modeling, and clinical biomarkers, PREDICT-ASIA will deliver region-specific risk thresholds, mechanistic insights, and policy-ready frameworks to guide public health interventions. This interdisciplinary initiative, leveraging a regional consortium of climate and health experts, aims to equip policymakers with evidence to mitigate compound climate-air pollution threats, ultimately reducing health disparities in Asia’s most vulnerable populations.

title: Scoping Phase of Greentree Acceleration Plan
description: The Greentree Acceleration Plan aims to scale up global mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) in humanitarian settings beginning in Chad and Lebanon, fostering systemic, sustainable change. This proposal seeks support for a scoping phase of the Greentree Acceleration Plan Grant Proposal, with a special focus on building scientific readiness in country. A core component of the Plan is its contribution to the IASC’s MHPSS research agenda (MHPSS-SET-2) as well as to the broader field of global mental health research. The scoping exercise will examine how multisectoral, multilayered approaches to MHPSS can be effectively designed, implemented, and scaled across contexts. The first countries to take part—Chad and Lebanon—were carefully selected for their contrasting contexts: both face acute humanitarian needs but are at different stages in developing their MHPSS systems and capacities. This reflects the Plan’s commitment to fostering cross-context learning, leveraging diverse experiences to generate adaptable models that can strengthen MHPSS efforts worldwide. With the Wellcome Trust’s support, this scoping initiative will build the groundwork for a transformative research program that advances the understanding of effective, context-sensitive, and integrated MHPSS interventions.

title: Supporting the Roles of Science Granting Councils in Africa’s Sustainable Development
description: The third phase of the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI-3), running from 2026 to 2030, is designed to reinforce the leadership and institutional capacity of Science Granting Councils (SGCs) as pivotal actors in strengthening national science, technology, and innovation (STI) systems across sub-Saharan Africa. Building on the progress of SGCI Phases 1 and 2, this phase will deepen support for SGCs to manage and fund high-quality, priority-driven research and innovation that addresses national development challenges. SGCI-3 recognizes SGCs as key enablers of robust STI ecosystems. It will enhance their ability to shape and implement evidence-informed policies, foster inclusive research environments, and catalyze partnerships with the private sector and other funders. The initiative will also support the development of internal systems and services, particularly for new and emerging Councils, ensuring they can effectively steward national research agendas. Aligned with the STI Strategy for Africa 2034, SGCI-3 will promote African ownership and sustainability through increased co-funding, alignment with continental priorities and Council-led decision-making. By strengthening the institutional foundations and strategic influence of SGCs, the initiative aims to build resilient national STI systems that are essential for long-term, inclusive development.

title: Migrant worker health equity: transforming health interventions for migrant workers
description: The health impact of hazardous work conditions, precarious employment terms and healthcare exclusion on low-wage migrant workers—the world’s largest migrant group—remains severely under-researched. Our Consortium’s work indicates the disproportionate risks faced by migrant workers, including high workplace injury rates, and elevated morbidity and mortality. The global burden of these conditions worsens health inequalities, particularly as social, technological, economic, environmental, and political (STEEP) transitions accelerate. Yet, migrant workers remain invisible in health metrics, absent from surveillance systems, and overlooked in health interventions. Addressing this systematic neglect is crucial for equitable and inclusive health protections. Building on long-standing collaborations with interdisciplinary academics, UN agencies, and migrant worker networks, we will pioneer advanced methodologies and migrant-sensitive survey instruments to generate national and global burden estimates of migrant worker health and support scalable, worker-centred health interventions in Egypt, Malaysia, and the UK, alongside building research capacity. We will develop: 1.Migrant- inclusive health measurement strategies: Co-develop, with migrant workers, standardised, validated measures to assess labour conditions and worker health and generate evidence pathways to guide policy and programming. 2.Scalable, replicable health interventions: Co-design interventions to enhance healthcare access and use, including mobile clinics, migrant insurance schemes, and climate-adaptive heat protection protocols.
recipient: City St George's, University of London

title: The Humanitarian Archive Emergency (HAE)
description: This programme evaluates a critical shortfall in the digital infrastructure supporting humanitarian and global health research. Recent political shifts amplify sharp declines in international funding, such as the abolition of USAID, cuts to Sweden's SIDA, the disbandment of DFID, and decreases in international aid and Official Development Assistance (ODA). These cuts have a disproportionate impact on the generation and preservation of data in vital areas such as demographic health surveys, records of attacks on healthcare and education, food security indicators, and most health-related datasets. This erosion of resources undermines archival capabilities of key international bodies like UN agencies (e.g., UNHCR), international NGOs, and faith-based organizations (e.g., Catholic Relief Services), as well as the historical records of USAID itself. Whilst this data erasure will impact dramatically future research and operational decision-making, we currently lack the means to quantify the scale of these losses (both ongoing and imminent) to humanitarian aid records. This programme aims to address this crisis by consolidating global partnerships focused on archives and essential records (AER) to establish a census of the AER at risk, develop a mechanism for their report and rescue, an ethical approach to triage, and a medium-term strategy to address the issue.

title: Africa Psychosis Research Network: Inaugural Meeting
description: This application supports the inaugural meeting of the Africa Psychosis Research Network, a continent-wide collaboration of researchers, experts by experience, clinicians, and policymakers working to strengthen psychosis research in Africa. Taking place on 13 November 2025 in Cape Town, following the Global Mental Health Summit, this strategic one-day meeting will identify shared priorities, build trust, and lay the groundwork for a sustainable, inclusive Africa-led network. The network responds to longstanding fragmentation in psychosis research across the continent and the need for African leadership in shaping future agendas. Funding will support equitable participation, particularly for delegates from low-income countries (LICs) and people with lived experience of psychosis, who are frequently underrepresented in research and policy discussions. The meeting will include structured sessions to map ongoing efforts, highlight gaps, and co-develop a shared framework for collaboration. It will also establish working groups to take forward specific themes and prepare for a larger convening in 2026. Outputs will include a network structure, a summary of agreed priorities, and a follow-up plan for joint activities and future funding opportunities. Keywords: psychosis, Africa, research network, lived experience, equity, mental health.

title: SAFER-MH: Improving Safety Evaluation and Regulatory Capacity for AI-Enabled Mental Health Care
description: In this proposal, we aim to address three key challenges to ensure that AI has safe and equitable impact in mental health (MH): we and our partners will collaborate with the South African Health Products Regulatory Agency (SAHPRA) to create a regulatory pathway for AI-enabled (MH) products; we will define a taxonomy of potential harms caused by AI-enabled MH products and develop new ways of detecting those harms; and we will establish a standard for how information about user engagement is recorded so that we can draw better links between products and real-world outcomes. Taken together, these three strands of work will help developers monitor and maintain user safety, regulators understand how to evaluate the safety of AI applications, and patients access quality care. More succinctly, our work will reduce the friction, complexity, and cost associated with regulatory compliance, making it easier for developers to innovate safely. Our focus will be to deliver these solutions in low-resource settings, but since the application of AI to MH and the field of regulatory science for AI-as-a-medical-device is so nascent, many of our outputs will have global relevance for advancing these fields.

title: Emergency fund to rescue FlyBase Curation
description: FlyBase provides an essential resource for those using Drosophila in their research. The emergency funds provided by a discretionary award will cover some of the sudden loss of funding for FlyBase from the US National Institute of Health. This award will enable FlyBase to retain the two most experienced members of the Cambridge FlyBase team, ensuring that essential knowledge it not lost, and that current curation efforts can be maintained. We are optimistic that contributions from the research community will provide the funding for the other three curators previously funded by the NIH. This award will provide the necessary time for the Principal Investigators to establish a new longer term funding stream for the Cambridge FlyBase team.

title: Climate Change and Health Support for COP 30 - Brazil
description: The Climate Change and Health Support for COP30 – Brazil project, led by PAHO/WHO, aims to strengthen Brazil’s leadership in aligning climate and health agendas ahead of COP30. Anchored in the Belém Health Action Plan, the project promotes equity-driven, evidence-based adaptation strategies within the health sector. Its main goals are to foster national and international dialogue, enhance institutional capacity within Brazil’s Unified Health System (SUS), and generate actionable knowledge to guide climate-health policy and practice. A major outcome will be the 2025 Global Conference on Climate and Health, co-organized by WHO and the Brazilian government, to be held in Brasília from 29 to 31 July 2025. The conference will highlight themes of health equity, climate co-benefits, and just transitions, engaging diverse stakeholders across all levels of governance. The project will also produce two strategic knowledge products. The first is a Synthesis Report on Social Participation, analyzing participatory approaches and proposing ways to strengthen engagement with Black, Indigenous, local, and traditional communities. The second is a Supporting Document on Climate and Health Policies, offering evidence-based, equity-focused recommendations and no- regrets actions to support the Belém Plan’s implementation. Together, these initiatives aim to position Brazil as a global leader in the climate-health nexus.

title: Policy Solutions
description: The grant will support collaboration between civil society organisations (CSOs), to build the evidence base required to make a compelling political case for increased mental health ambition in the UK. This will include jointly commissioning pieces of new analysis in response the current political context and prevailing evidence gaps. Policy analysis priorities will be informed by a joint political influencing strategy, with a likely focus on increasing available data and evidence on early intervention, mental health waiting lists and economic activity. The grant will also enable more responsive and reactive policy analysis, providing capacity to draw on and synthesise new insights generated by a sector data hub. The new sector hub will bring together data from multiple sources, including unique data held by CSOs, to build a more nuanced picture of the current mental health context. The data will be used to enable real time and coordinated influencing targeted at MPs, Ministers and No10.

title: Wellcome UK Mental Health CSO Discretionary Grant: Constituency Engagement
description: Current UK Government plans fall short in addressing the urgency and scale of mental health need across the country. Given the complex political landscape and economic constraints, securing major new investment in mental health care will be difficult without increased, consistent political and public pressure. To drive change, public pressure—particularly from those directly impacted —is essential. However, sector-wide funding cuts have made it difficult to build and sustain the pressure needed to secure government action. At the same time, current media narratives risk undermining progress we’ve made in shifting attitudes to mental health. This grant will amplify the public support we know exists across the UK for transformational changes in mental health care. This will include supporting young people aged 16-25 who are currently most impacted by negative media and political narratives to engage directly with decision-makers, share their perspectives and advocate for and inspire positive change. The grant will enable young advocates to explore and utilise a range of public engagement tactics — including media, PR, and creative advocacy —to begin to increase public and political cut-through for mental health.

title: The Africa Asia Alliance for Clinical Trials (A3CT)
description: We propose the establishment of the Africa Asia Alliance for Clinical Trials (A3CT)—a collaborative platform to strengthen clinical trial capacity and coordination across Clinical Trials Units (CTUs) embedded within Wellcome’s Major International Programmes (MIPs) in Africa and Asia. LMICs remain underrepresented in global health research and face persistent challenges in delivering cost-effective, high-quality trials. A3CT will address these gaps by harmonizing practices, fostering operational excellence, and building sustainable trial infrastructure led by regional research institutions. The Alliance brings together AHRI, MORU, MLW, KWTRP, and OUCRU to co-develop scalable solutions to shared barriers, including fragmented systems, workforce shortages, and high operational costs. Over four years, the Alliance and it's working groups will implement aligned governance, interoperable IT platforms, shared trial tools, a cross-site monitoring network and tailored workforce training. We will also establish accreditation mechanisms and an evaluation framework to monitor progress and impact. By further developing the CTUs maturity and strengthening institutional readiness, the Alliance seeks to establish an LMIC-led platform for delivering high-impact, efficient, and locally relevant clinical research—driving regional research excellence and attracting a diverse range of funders to enable sustainable growth.

title: Convening and elevating civil society and community visions towards reimagining the global health architecture
description: As multi-stakeholder processes begin to discuss the future of the development, financial and health architectures, it is critical that all key stakeholders are involved from the beginning. Some global institutions and processes, in particular within global health, have a strong track record of engaging and involving civil society and communities in governance and decision-making. However, meaningful civil society and community involvement still need to be advocated for and won. In parallel, there is a need to support civil society and communities to come together to articulate and advance what progressive visions of a more sustainable and equitable future global health architecture might look like. We are a small group of diverse and well-informed civil society and community organisations. Through a 10 month project beginning June of 2025 and concluding in March 2026, our goal is to ensure that civil society and communities across global health, at global, regional and national level, are supported to develop and articulate their own visions for the future of the global health ecosystem and that they are able to share those visions in all existing and new processes looking at reforming the global health ecosystem to become more inclusive, equitable, and responsive to their needs.

title: Facilitating Local and Indigenous Ownership of Water Ecosystems and Health (FLOW): centring Indigenous and Traditional Knowledge (ITEK) in solutions identification and implementation
description: The FLOW project expands community-led research on the health impacts of climate change and extractive industries on Indigenous Peoples (IPs) in East Africa and the Niger Delta. Building on Phase I findings, Phase II focuses on Lake Turkana, Lake Bogoria, the Omo River Basin and Niger’s Niger Delta—regions experiencing severe ecological degradation due to damming, oil drilling, deforestation, and climate change. FLOW integrates Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) with scientific methods using a community-based participatory research approach. It empowers IPs—including the Turkana, El Molo, Daasanach, Endorois, and Ogoni—to co-create research questions, define key concepts like “health” and “livelihood,” and identify local solutions to water-related health issues. Key objectives include documenting ecosystem changes, analyzing their causes, assessing impacts on health and cultural heritage, and facilitating locally driven solutions. Key activities include partner training, regional workshops, ITEK knowledge exchange sessions, community storytelling, and policy dialogues. The project will generate research documentation, advocacy briefings, and ITEK preservation outputs (e.g., toolkits, reports). Advocacy efforts will target sub-national, national, and international platforms. Keywords: Indigenous Peoples, Indigenous and Traditional Ecological Knowledge, participatory research, water ecosystems, climate change, extractive industries, Lake Turkana, Lake Bogoria, Niger Delta, health equity, environmental justice, community-led adaptation, East Africa, biodiversity, displacement.

title: BRAIN-CLIMA: Investigating the Combined Impact of Heat and Air Pollution on Blood-Brain Barrier Integrity and Brain Aging in Latin America
description: BRAIN-CLIMA is a transdisciplinary project investigating how heat stress affects brain health, and whether people in areas of higher air pollution are particularly vulnerable. The project aims to identify biomarkers for and elucidate the mechanistic links between these stressors and brain damage in populations across Latin America. We hypothesize that heat stress exposure disrupts blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, an early pathomechanism contributing to brain inflammation, aging, cognitive decline and neurodegeneration, and that this effect is exacerbated by air pollution and interactions with other factors, including socioeconomic status and comorbidities. Leveraging several cohorts in Latin America, which integrates harmonized, multimodal, and georeferenced cohort data from 7 countries (2010-2025), we will analyze environmental, clinical, and biospecimen data to identify early warning signs and point of no return for neurodegeneration. In work stream (WS)-1, we will assess heat-related, PM2.5-modified, blood- and extracellular vesicle-based biomarkers of BBB and brain damage. In WS-2, we will develop computational aging clocks of cognitive function, and brain aging linking exposure to climate-related stressors and socioeconomic disparity to accelerated aging. In WS-3, by integrating mechanistic and epidemiological insights, we will generate evidence to inform climate mitigation policies that protect brain health and identify novel interventions including early warning systems.
recipient: The Trustees of Columbia University in the City of New York

title: Conference on implementing climate-health indicators in Africa
description: To hold a 2-3 day conference for around 100 delegates in Kigali, Rwanda in November or December 2025 to disseminate the outputs of the Standards for Official Statistics on Climate-Health Interactions (SOSCHI) project and promote the adoption of climate impact indicators across the African region. We will bring together international/regional organisations and national government institutions from several countries along with members of the extended SOSCHI partnership (UK, Ghana, Rwanda). Speakers will be from the SOSCHI project, Rwanda and Ghana governments, and other national and multilateral institutions e.g. Mozambique Climate and Health Observatory, WHO AFRO, Africa CDC. Subjects will include examples of national adaptation policies and public health interventions and their use of climate-health impacts data, findings and proposals of the SOSCHI project, and discussion of approaches to the challenges of climate-health data quality improvement and indicator implementation in African settings. We aim to build a network for future collaboration on building capability for climate-health statistics in Africa and promoting policy use of statistics. Participative sessions will highlight government priorities and share understanding of data gaps, practical barriers and opportunities.

title: Catalysing Evidence-Based Climate Policy through Health-Centred Action
description: Climate change is one of the greatest threats to the planet and humanity, intensifying environmental degradation, economic instability, and public health risks such as heat-related illness and the spread of infectious diseases. Yet, well-designed climate action can deliver powerful health co- benefits and foster more equitable, resilient societies. This proposal sets out a high-impact strategic partnership between the UN Climate Change secretariat and Wellcome to place human health at the heart of global climate action. As the principal UN body guiding the international climate response, UN Climate Change has unparalleled access to national governments and stakeholders, but lacks dedicated health expertise, tools, and funding to deliver on this agenda. The project will strengthen the secretariat’s capacity to integrate health systematically into adaptation, mitigation, communications, and partnerships. It will embed health evidence in Nationally Determined Contributions and National Adaptation Plans, promote recognition of health co-benefits, and mobilize diverse actors through strategic communications and engagement platforms. Working alongside WHO, UNDP, the IPCC, the NDC Partnership, and GESDA, this project will deliver four outcomes: health-centred adaptation, mitigation with health co-benefits, strengthened amplification of climate–health evidence and narratives, and expanded multi- stakeholder partnerships. Beneficiaries include governments, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, health professionals, and non-state actors.
recipient: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Strengthening the Global Response to Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) is among the top 10 threats for global health and development. With an estimated 1.1 million deaths directly attributable to AMR in 2021 and nearly 5 million deaths associated with AMR, it is projected that AMR will cause a GDP shortfall of at least USD $3.4 trillion annually and push 24 million more people into extreme poverty. In response, the 79th UNGA Political Declaration on AMR was adopted, with Member States committing to key targets and actions. The Standing Quadripartite Joint Secretariat on AMR (QJS) hosted by the WHO was recommended to be formalized as the central coordinating mechanism to support the global response to antimicrobial resistance. Through QJS facilitation and coordination, the establishment of an Independent Panel on Evidence for Action (IPEA) should be completed by 2025. The Global Action Plan on AMR (GAP-AMR) should be updated based on recent evidence by 2026, along with its monitoring and evaluation framework. Project goal: to strengthen the global response to AMR by synthesizing evidence to inform the update of the GAP-AMR, its monitoring framework, while establishing the IPEA as a sustained mechanism to inform future policy decisions.

title: UK CSO Mental Health Influencing: Data and Evidence
description: The grant will support collaboration between civil society organisations (CSOs), to build the evidence base required to make a compelling political case for increased mental health ambition in the UK. This includes bringing together mental health data held across CSOs into a central data hub, to build live insight into mental health need and trends across the UK. Data collection will be informed by a joint political influencing strategy, with a focus on increasing available data on early intervention, mental health waiting lists and economic activity. A newly established sector data and evidence network will analyse available data on an ongoing basis to inform joint sector policy and influencing. The data will be used to enable reactive and coordinated influencing targeted at MPs, Ministers and No10.

title: TB Vaccine Development Activities at World Health Organization
description: In 2023, 10.8 million people fell ill with TB disease, and 1.25 million died, globally. New TB vaccines for adults and adolescents could be licensed by 2028. However effective engagement and strategic coordination across civil society, developers, manufacturers, regulators, policy makers, donors, procurers and TB programmes will be needed to accelerate policy and uptake. The WHO TB Vaccine Accelerator aims to expedite new TB vaccine development, introduction and access though technical and strategic co-ordination across the vaccine value chain. This grant will support and integrate the activities of working groups in the areas of clinical development, regulatory and policy strategy, finance and access and potentially also country readiness for introduction. Key goals include: • Provision of expert advice on regulatory and policy pathways for late-stage TB vaccine candidates intended for global use; • Assessment of the feasibility of and regulatory / policy pathways to novel clinical endpoints, including asymptomatic TB; • Development of global demand and supply forecasts, and novel financing options; • High-level political advocacy for new TB vaccines through forums such as G20 ministerial meetings and the WHO TB Vaccine Accelerator Council; • Consultation with country and regional level stakeholders on demand, evidence needs and policy pathways to accelerate introduction and uptake.

title: Supporting implementation of the Lusaka Agenda through technical health financing analytics, guidance, and research
description: As highlighted proposed “Strengthening Health Financing Globally” World Health Assembly (WHA) Resolution, immediate action is needed to provide guidance and share best practices on how to better align external with domestic health financing flows, systems, and priorities to sustain coverage efficiently and feasibly. This need is only exacerbated by the dramatic shifts in the global health financing architecture in the past weeks, with donor nations radically reducing or reorienting their official development assistance (ODA). The activities put forward primarily reflect the Wellcome Trust’s Global Health Financing’s priorities related to: (1) supporting the implementation of the Lusaka Agenda and (2) expanding engagement and dialogue on global health financing and architecture. They focus on immediate actions that are needed to support knowledge sharing to constructively respond to the dire challenges posed by domestic and external health financing constraints. The related support and information capturing/sharing are needed to inform longer-term shifts in global health financing architecture. To accomplish this aim a three-level approach is needed to inform sustainable health financing architecture informed by country-level experiences and priorities.

title: Wellcome UK Mental Health CSO Discretionary Grants: Political Engagement
description: Accelerate collaborative influencing across mental health civil society, to increase political support for mental health in Westminster. This will include streamlining political monitoring and stakeholder management across CSOs, expanding the number and impact of political champions for mental health and building strategic partnerships with political influencers. This will be enabled by funding additional public affairs capacity for the sector alongside dedicated budget to deliver consistent mental health events and engagement with Parliamentarians, including Ministers, backbench Labour MPs, and Opposition Parties. Central to this will be the development of a new ‘sector pitch’ to government, which builds a stronger political argument for increased mental health ambition, identifies opportunities for mental health breakthroughs during this parliament and sets out how the sector can support this. This will include increasing our understanding of current public attitudes to mental health and identifying target audiences to engage. Through insight and message testing we will build a new messaging framework to reach and engage target audiences and increase public pressure on UK Government.

title: CLEAR-IT: Climate-Lung Effects via Airborne Risks - an International Translational Network
description: We have led advances in the understanding of biological mechanisms in chronic respiratory, including paediatric, respiratory disease and how the airborne exposome, particularly fungi, affect respiratory health. Super pollutants created by climate change, some created and accumulating indoors, accelerate climate change further, affect wider indoor air quality and are linked with worse respiratory health. The mechanism by which indoor air pollution, including super pollutants, affect respiratory function remains incompletely understood. Through this new international collaborative interdisciplinary project, we will accelerate discovery of biological mechanisms linking indoor air pollution with risk of chronic respiratory disease and define the mechanisms underpinning the observed associations. To achieve this goal, we will use new indoor air pollution measurements building on studies of the EMBER consortium, and integrate with advanced lung cell models, multi omics datasets and state-of-the-art statistical approaches to discover and validate novel ‘in vivo’ biomarkers. This research will contribute to the improvement in diagnosis and prevention of respiratory diseases caused by indoor air pollution through mechanistic discovery and define climate-adaptive interventions for air quality and lung health based on the mechanistic insights gained from this project through Lungs Europe, a Brussels-based collaboration between the European Lung Foundation and the European Respiratory Society.

title: Supporting Longform output Open Access
description: Scholarly monographs are an important vehicle for sharing research, advancing education, and informing practice in the health and biomedical sciences. While mandates from Wellcome, UKRI, and other research funders increasingly require long form outputs to be made openly available, there is a lack of consolidated infrastructure that would support seamless deposit, processing, and dissemination. This project will establish an integrated, scalable workflow to support the open access archiving and discoverability of life science books and book chapters. A collaboration across OAPEN, Europe PMC, and NCBI Bookshelf will develop and implement an end-to-end process for compliant book deposit, XML transformation, and full text storage and display in Europe PMC. The project will be delivered in three phases: initial technical setup, full scale processing of eligible content, and ongoing delivery as a business-as- usual process. Once established, this workflow will enable policy compliance, strengthen open infrastructure, and enhance the visibility and reuse of long form outputs. Ultimately, this initiative will bolster equitable access to publicly funded research and support future participation by additional Europe PMC funders.

title: Strengthening cross-sectoral approaches to global health in German policy- making
description: The proposed project aims to strengthen cross-sectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration on global health in German policymaking, reinforcing Germany’s commitment and leadership in this field. It is implemented by the Global Health Hub Germany (GHHG), a network that brings together over 2,000 members from eight diverse stakeholder groups to foster dialogue, exchange, and joint action on pressing global health issues. Activities include two to three policy-events for Members of Parliament, the organization of the flagship Global Health Talk 2026, and the implementation of two high-level Catalyst Dialogues to deliver actionable recommendations for policy. The project also deepens collaboration between the global health and climate sectors through targeted events and communications activities. Emphasizing equity, diversity, and inclusion, the GHHG ensures broad representation, including from the Global South, in all its activities. By combining interactive engagement formats with evidence-based policy input and strategic communication, the initiative seeks to build new global health champions in Germany’s government and parliament. In doing so, it supports more coherent and impactful policymaking and contributes to the achievement of the health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 3. This effort positions Germany as a key actor in shaping a fairer, more resilient global health architecture.
recipient: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH

title: NRDC Extreme Heat Campaign: Raising Heat Awareness Through Film and TV
description: NRDC will leverage its cross-sector expertise—led by its Rewrite the Future (RTF) team, in collaboration with Entertainment Partnerships, the Environment, Equity & Justice Center (EEJC), and the Science Office—to create a two-year Extreme Heat Campaign in pursuit of the following goals: 1\. To convey the dangers of extreme heat and solutions to heat illness in ways that reach a broad audience and increase public awareness (which could have a secondary benefit of increasing support for policies that protect vulnerable populations); and 2\. To contribute to the reduction of avoidable heat-related illness and death. The campaign will adapt the existing strategies and relationships built by the RTF team and focus them on increasing public awareness of the dangers of extreme heat, as well as safety measures and adaptation strategies, through the onscreen representation of extreme heat related issues in film and TV. The campaign will leverage the exceptional reach of storytellers across Hollywood to influence broader attitudes on extreme heat and motivate action to help people stay safe and care for their communities amid rising temperatures.

title: Genomics-led Impact on African Population Health (GEN-IMPACT)
description: GEN-IMPACT is a five-year, African-led initiative designed to advance equitable precision medicine by integrating genomics into population health research. It addresses the urgent need to understand the genetic and environmental determinants of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) within the context of Africa’s persistent infectious disease burden. Leveraging the African Population Cohorts Consortium (APCC), the Science for Africa Foundation (SFA), and the African Bioinformatics Institute (ABI), the project will generate genomic, phenotypic, and exposure data from approximately 10,000 participants across underrepresented African cohorts. The programme includes deep phenotyping, genome-wide genotyping, and whole genome sequencing, with a strong emphasis on capacity building, data governance, and ethical community engagement. A landscape phase will identify priority health areas, followed by sub-studies addressing region-specific research questions. Data will be analysed locally and across sites using federated platforms. GEN-IMPACT will contribute to the African reference genome, support development of predictive models, and enhance data sharing infrastructure. By embedding training, ethical frameworks, and sustainability planning into all phases, it aims to empower African institutions and researchers to lead in genomic science. Ultimately, GEN-IMPACT will catalyse systems change and establish a model for integrating genomics into public health to improve health outcomes and research sovereignty across Africa.

title: Developing Climate and Health Data Services (Based on Pathfinder Studies in Pakistan and Malawi)
description: Climate change will significantly escalate health risks, particularly in low- resource settings, threatening vulnerable populations and disrupting health systems. However, the absence of reliable, comprehensive, long-term datasets linking climate change and health impacts limits effective decision-making and forecasting. To address this, we propose establishing Climate and Health Data Services in Malawi and Pakistan, aiming to enhance climate-informed health decisions, optimize resource allocation, and inform risk-reducing policies. Recent events underscore urgency: Pakistan’s 2022 floods affected over 33 million individuals, while Malawi faced climate shocks impacting more than 6.5 million people. Partnering with national health and climate ministries, we will integrate fragmented climate and health data, creating information assets and tools to inform decision making. The proposed program comprises four work packages: co-designing data services, operationalizing via local technology partners, building local research and communication capacity, and ensuring sustainability. Our consortium (PATH, Aga Khan University, Impetus, Malawi University of Business and Applied Sciences, and Columbia University’s IRI) offers robust expertise across climate-health modeling, public health, technology development, policy advocacy, and applied research. By leveraging alternative funding streams, this initiative will establish scalable, climate- resilient health systems and position both countries to attract sustainable financing from international sources.

title: From Data to Action: Identifying Harms and Critical Windows of Combined Environmental Exposures to Air Pollutants and Heat Using Integrated Epidemiological and Toxicological Evidence
description: Air pollution and climate change represent converging global health crises, with the most vulnerable—especially children—bearing the brunt. This international, interdisciplinary project tackles these challenges by advancing our understanding of how complex and representative exposures to regulated (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, NO₂, O₃) and unregulated (black carbon, ultrafine particles) air pollutants, combined with heat, shape respiratory health across the life course. Leveraging four long-standing European birth cohorts (N=24,533; follow-up since 1994), spanning Spain to Sweden and birth to age 25, we integrate cutting-edge exposure science, toxicology, epidemiology, risk assessment, and causal inference to quantify health and equity impacts of current exposures, interventions and scenarios, and identify windows of susceptibility. Our focus is on asthma—the most prevalent chronic disease in children—and lung function, a key predictor of adult cardiopulmonary morbidity and mortality. We go beyond single-pollutant approaches to address mixtures and heat interactions using harmonized, high-resolution exposure surfaces, mechanistic biomarkers in standard and novel mouse models, and life-course modeling. Through engaging key stakeholders, we will co-create and evaluate actionable, equitable interventions and feed results back into policy processes. Major advances over our foundational work include addressing more nuanced questions about mixtures, temperature interactions, susceptible windows, and underlying mechanisms as observed in experimental models.

title: Unraveling Biological Pathways and Health Impacts of Air Pollution Components to Inform Climate Mitigation
description: This research program addresses the urgent need to quantify dose-response relationships of real-world air pollution exposures on biology to inform climate mitigation. It directly tackles critical Wellcome Trust research gaps: understanding cumulative and combined pollutant exposures and identifying critical exposure thresholds for adverse health effects. The program is structured around two integrated projects. Project 1 (Mechanistic Studies) will characterize source-specific PM2.5 from urban hotspots to define their toxicological profiles and disease pathways in 3D human airway models. This includes assessing susceptibility in diseased airway cells (asthma, COPD) and investigating systemic links to cancer, immune dysregulation, and cardiovascular diseases. Project 2 (Population Studies) will develop high- resolution US air pollution models (PM2.5 components, NO2, O3) to link with nationwide health datasets (Medicaid, Medicare, HCUP). It will produce pollutant-, mixture-, and source-specific dose-response functions for respiratory, cardiovascular, neuropsychiatric, and cancer outcomes. This novel, integrated approach provides essential, policy-relevant evidence, including an interactive online tool to quantify potential health benefits of mitigation activities, enabling policymakers to effectively target hazardous pollutants and optimize public health outcomes. Keywords: Air pollution, PM2.5, climate change mitigation, health impacts, dose-response, cumulative exposures, pollutant mixtures, source apportionment, toxicological profiling, epidemiology, policy relevance, public health, computational modeling, environmental health.
recipient: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
